big.title: Atoms
big.text: Matter consists of atoms that have internal structures that dictate their chemical and physical behavior.

big.title: Bonding
big.text: Bonding: Atoms interact via electrostatic forces to form chemical bonds.

big.title: Structure and Function
big.text: Structure and Function: Chemical compounds have geometric structures that influence their chemical and physical behaviors.

big.title: Intermolecular Interactions
big.text: Intermolecular Interactions: Intermolecular forces—electrostatic forces between molecules—dictate the physical behavior of matter.

big.title: Chemical Reactions
big.text: Chemical Reactions: Matter changes, forming products that have new chemical and physical properties.

big.title: Energy and Thermodynamics
big.text: Energy and Thermodynamics: Energy is the key currency of chemical reactions in molecular-scale systems as well as macroscopic systems.

big.title: Kinetics
big.text: Kinetics: Chemical changes have a time scale over which they occur.

big.title: Equilibrium
big.text: Equilibrium: All physical and chemical changes are, in principle, reversible and often reach a state of dynamic equilibrium.

big.title: Experiments, Measurement, and Data
big.text: Experiments, Measurement, and Data: Chemistry is generally advanced via experimental observations.

big.title: Visualization
big.text: Visualization: Chemistry constructs meaning interchangeably at the particulate and macroscopic levels.

nodes.title: Atoms, particulate nature & composition
nodes.mech: matter is composed of discrete particles whose identity and count fix its behaviour
nodes.lo: Identify what a substance is and how much of it is present by reasoning from the particles it is made of — their kind, their number, and what lies inside them.

nodes.title: Chemical amount / the mole
nodes.mech: a counting convention that bridges particulate count to macroscopic mass, volume and charge
nodes.lo: Convert between a number of particles and a measurable mass, volume or charge, using the mole as the bridge between the two scales.

nodes.title: Periodicity
nodes.mech: recurring electronic configuration produces recurring property trends
nodes.lo: Predict an element's properties from its place in the periodic table by reasoning from electron arrangement rather than recalling group facts.

nodes.title: Bonding & molecular structure
nodes.mech: electrons are shared or transferred between nuclei to lower total energy
nodes.lo: Explain why atoms combine, and in what ratio, by tracking how electrons are shared or transferred to lower the total energy.

nodes.title: Structure–property relationships
nodes.mech: spatial and electronic arrangement determines observable property
nodes.lo: Explain an observable property of a material from the spatial and electronic arrangement of its particles.

nodes.title: Interparticle interactions, states & solutions
nodes.mech: attraction between particles competes with thermal motion
nodes.lo: Explain the state of a substance and its behaviour in solution as a contest between attraction and thermal motion.

nodes.title: Chemical change & reaction mechanisms
nodes.mech: bonds break and form along a pathway that conserves atoms and charge
nodes.lo: Predict what a chemical change produces, and represent it as a pathway that conserves atoms and charge.

nodes.title: Reaction stoichiometry
nodes.mech: balanced equations fix mole ratios between species
nodes.lo: Use a balanced equation to work out how much is consumed or produced, reading coefficients as ratios of amount.

nodes.title: Redox
nodes.mech: electrons transfer between species, changing oxidation state
nodes.lo: Identify which species loses electrons and which gains them, and use oxidation state to keep track of the transfer.

nodes.title: Electrochemistry
nodes.mech: redox driven or resisted by an electrical potential difference
nodes.lo: Relate electron transfer to an electrical potential difference, and predict what happens at each electrode.

nodes.title: Energy & thermodynamics
nodes.mech: energy is conserved and redistributed; spontaneity is set by free energy
nodes.lo: Account for the energy a change releases or absorbs, and judge whether it is feasible in itself — a separate question from how fast it goes.

nodes.title: Equilibrium
nodes.mech: opposing processes reach equal rates, fixing a state ratio
nodes.lo: Predict the state a reversible system settles into, and how that state shifts when conditions change.

nodes.title: Acids & bases
nodes.lo: Predict which species are present in an acid or base solution from proton-transfer equilibrium, and use pH to describe it.

nodes.title: Solubility equilibria
nodes.mech: dissolution and precipitation reach equal rates
nodes.lo: Predict whether a solid dissolves or comes out of solution by treating saturation as two opposing processes running at equal rate.

nodes.title: Kinetics
nodes.mech: rate is governed by the barrier and the frequency of effective encounters
nodes.lo: Explain and predict how fast a reaction goes, from the energy barrier and the frequency of effective collisions.

nodes.title: Nomenclature & symbolic conventions
nodes.lo: Read and write the names, symbols, formulae and equations of chemistry precisely enough that the meaning cannot be mistaken.

nodes.title: Practical & laboratory technique
nodes.lo: Choose the laboratory procedure that suits the substance and the purpose, and carry it out safely.

nodes.title: Quantitative methods
nodes.lo: Handle the arithmetic of chemistry — units, ratios, percentages, estimates — so that a calculation is valid rather than merely completed.

nodes.title: Experiments, measurement & data
nodes.lo: Plan and interpret an investigation: what is varied, what is measured, and what the data can and cannot support.

nodes.title: Visualization & models
nodes.lo: Move between the macroscopic, particulate and symbolic pictures of the same chemistry, and know where each model stops working.

nodes.title: Applications & contexts
nodes.lo: Apply chemical reasoning to a real material, process or environmental situation outside the laboratory.

edges.lo: Stoichiometry needs the mole first: coefficients give ratios of amounts, never ratios of masses — mass follows only after multiplying by molar mass.
Thermochemistry needs the mole first: 'per mole of reaction' scales with the equation as written, not with any single species in it.
Rate laws need the mole first: concentration is amount per volume, so diluting a solution changes the rate without changing the rate constant.
The equilibrium constant needs the mole first: K compares amounts per volume raised to stoichiometric powers, not masses or molecule counts.
Electrochemical calculation needs the mole extended to electrons: charge becomes an amount that can be counted exactly as atoms are.
A cell can only be read once the electron transfer has been located: redox bookkeeping comes before any potential is introduced.
Cell potential is a free-energy statement per unit charge — a claim about direction, not a property belonging to the metal.
Potential shifts with concentration: a standard potential is a reference state, not an absolute property of the couple.
Combining behaviour follows from recurring valence-electron configuration, not from memorised group facts.
A property trend needs a mechanism — effective nuclear charge and shielding — not a table to read the answer off.
A weak acid is a dynamic equilibrium, not a partial one-way reaction; buffering cannot be explained without that.
A saturated solution is two opposing processes running at equal rate; the common-ion effect cannot be explained without that.
Breaking bonds costs energy and forming them releases it — the single most inverted relation in school chemistry.
Energy that overcomes attraction between molecules is not energy that breaks bonds within them.
Interparticle attraction needs the particles first: melting, boiling and dissolving rearrange particles that keep their identity — and it is their thermal motion that the attraction has to overcome.

The mole needs the atom's fixed characteristic mass first: isotopes mean not every atom weighs the same, but each element has a fixed average atomic mass — and only because of that do counting particles and weighing a sample become the same act. The laws of definite and multiple proportions are the evidence.
Periodicity needs the atom's electron shells first: without electron configuration there is nothing to recur, and the periodic law regresses to an unexplained ordering of elements.
Chemical change needs atom persistence first: a reaction rearranges atoms that survive it — remove that and conservation of mass is an unexplained fact about weights.
Collision thinking needs moving particles first: the frequency of encounters is a count of particle collisions, unstatable for continuous matter.
Structure–property reasoning needs bonding first: shape, polarity and lattice type are properties OF the bonded arrangement — remove bonds and there is no arrangement to reason from.
Chemical change as pathway needs the bond first: 'bonds break and form' has no referent without them, and reactions regress to before-and-after bookkeeping.

Oxidation state needs bonding's assignment convention first: for shared electrons it is the charge an atom would carry if bonds were fully ionic — without that convention, covalent redox is undefined.
Solubility equilibrium needs dissolution first: its two opposing processes are solute–solvent events owned by the solutions node, not by equilibrium.
Rate needs the reaction pathway first: rate is how fast the bond-breaking-and-forming process advances — remove the pathway and there is nothing in motion to time.
The activation barrier needs energy first: a barrier is a height in energy, and an 'effective' collision is one that clears it — without energy neither is statable.
Dynamic equilibrium needs rate first: 'opposing processes at equal rates' is a kinetic sentence — without rate, equilibrium collapses into mere standstill.

I.title: Atoms
I.text: Matter consists of atoms that have internal structures that dictate their chemical and physical behavior.

A.text: Atoms have unique chemical identities based on the number of protons in the nucleus.

l3.text: The number of protons specifies the atomic number, which is used as an identifier of the atom/element.

l4.text: The atomic number is given in most periodic tables, so students should be able to provide the number of protons of any element.
Atomic symbols are important representations and students need to know most of these symbols to function efficiently in the chemistry classroom.

l3.text: Atoms may have the same chemical identity but different masses and this explains the existence of isotopes.

l4.text: Protons and neutrons sum to contribute the mass of an atom.
Atoms of one element have the same number of protons but can have differing numbers of neutrons. These are called isotopes.
Measures of mass are made at scales much larger than individual atoms, so elements have atomic masses that are the weighted average of all naturally occurring isotopes.
The isotopic abundance of any given element is not a constant of nature, and may vary depending on the origin of the sample being studied.
Ultimately, the atomic mass system is a relative one, based on the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

organic.text: The atomic number and mass number are used to determine average atomic weight and identify isotopes, which play a part in understanding techniques such as MS, NMR, or IR and rates of reactions via kinetic isotope effects.

inorganic.text: The identity of an element is associated with the atomic number, or number of protons within the nucleus.
All neutral atoms of the same element have the same number of protons and electrons although the number of neutrons can vary.
Descriptive chemistry involves the identification of the elements based on their unique chemical and physical properties.
Isotopes have many important applications in Inorganic Chemistry.

Isotope notation includes the mass and atomic numbers, and can be used to calculate the number of protons and neutrons for a specific nuclide. The charge of an atom or monatomic ion can be used to determine the number of electrons.
The nuclear spin of an atom arises from the individual spins of the protons and neutrons, and isotopes with a nonzero nuclear spin can be observed by NMR and Mössbauer spectroscopies.
The kinetic isotope effect can be used to justify reaction mechanisms and assign absorptions in infrared spectroscopy. The isotopes of hydrogen are most commonly used to demonstrate this effect.

physical.text: The nuclear charge Z of an atom is an important variable for quantum calculations.
The nuclear charge, Z, is a factor in the energy levels present in an atom.
Hydrogen atom like ions allow the analytical solutions of the H-atom problem to be used with higher nuclear charge (Z) systems.
Some nuclei have a net spin that allows them to be observed via NMR spectroscopy.
Any nucleus with an odd number of either protons or neutrons or both will have a net spin that results in a magnetic moment.
A nucleus with a magnetic moment will interact with an external magnetic field, splitting otherwise degenerate nuclear energy levels by an amount that depends on the strength of the external field.
NMR spectrometers work by splitting nuclear energy levels in an external field and then inducing transitions between the split levels.
Isotopic masses can have observable effects on experimental observations.
Reduced mass is used in several theories as the expression by which isotopic masses influence energy levels or transition frequencies
The most direct experimental observation related to isotopic mass is the mass spectrum of atoms or compounds.

B.text: Electrons play the key role for atoms to bond with other atoms.

l3.text: For a neutral atom there are as many electrons as there are protons, but the electrons can be categorized as core (inner) and valence (outer) electrons.

l4.text: Valence electrons, which determine the properties of elements, are correlated with the groups in the periodic table.

l3.text: The quantum model of the atom is capable of explaining many observations, and it organizes electrons into “orbitals”, which are wave functions that are identified using quantum numbers.

l4.text: The quantum mechanical model of the atom introduces the concept of orbitals, including atomic orbitals.
Quantum numbers specify the wave functions that are the orbitals.

l3.text: The occupation of atomic orbitals by electrons is summarized in the electron configuration, and this tool is helpful in understanding which atoms form chemical bonds, what type, and how many bonds they form.

l4.text: Electron configuration is a shorthand notation that summarizes the orbital occupations of electrons in an atom or ion.
Electron configuration notation for transition metal ions reflects that they can differ slightly from the patterns observed for main group ions.
Electrons will occupy atomic orbitals following both the aufbau principle and Hund’s rule.

organic.text: Electrons play a role in understanding the relative stability of resonance structures.
Stabilization of anions helps to explain pKa values and relative acidities of protons.
Some reactions occur because molecules that are electrophilic are prone to react with regions where electron density is high.
Electron-deficient atoms that seek electron-rich atoms are called electrophiles (meaning “electron seeking”). Electrophiles are commonly neutral or positively charged.
Alkenes and alkynes are electron-rich and therefore are susceptible to electrophilic addition. Alcohols and alkyl halides are often formed from alkenes via electrophilic addition.
Some reactions occur because molecules that are nucleophilic are prone to react with regions where electron density is low.
Electron-rich atoms that seek electron-deficient atoms are called nucleophiles (meaning “nucleus seeking”). Nucleophiles are commonly neutral or negatively charged.

inorganic.text: Quantum mechanics is used to explain electron behavior in atoms.

Historical developments leading to the modern view of quantum mechanics include the Bohr model of an atom, the Einstein and deBroglie descriptions of the particle/wave duality of light and matter, and the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle.

The Schrödinger equation is used to describe wavelike properties of electrons within atoms. Wavefunctions derived from the Schrödinger equations are used to describe the electron density within atoms and molecules.
Quantum numbers within wavefunctions describe the size, shape and orientation of the orbitals in an atom.
Orbitals derived from the Schrödinger equation are described using the quantum numbers n, l, and ml. The quantum number ms is derived from the Dirac equation.
Orbital shapes are related to the quantum numbers n, l, and ml, and the different types of orbitals can be identified by the differing number and locations of angular and radial nodes.

An electron configuration describes the electron distribution amongst the orbitals within a particular atom or molecule. The aufbau principle, Hund's rules, and the Pauli exclusion principle can be used as guides to estimate the ground state, or lowest energy, electron configuration. Known exceptions to these rules have been observed for electron configurations of the heavier elements (n > 4)

Atomic term symbols are used as a shorthand notation to describe the electron configuration of a molecule, and are used to express the relative energy, angular momentum, and spin multiplicity associated with the configuration.

The Schrödinger equation cannot be solved exactly for multi electron atoms or molecules. In most cases, combinations of hydrogen-like wavefunctions are a reasonable approximation to represent the electron density within molecules.
Coulombic forces play an important role in the energy associated with an electron configuration
Coulombic attractions between electrons and the nucleus lower the energy associated with the electron configuration.
Coulombic repulsions between electrons give rise to a pairing energy, which raises the energy associated with an electron configuration.
Shielding is a phenomenon in which the negative charges of electrons occupying lower energy orbitals affects the positive charge felt by electrons in higher energy orbitals.
Electrons within atoms can be classified as core or valence electrons.
Penetration effects for different orbitals can be compared using radial distribution functions.
The effective nuclear charge felt by an electron can be calculated by subtraction of shielding effects due to inner electrons from the positive charge of the nucleus.
Slater's Rules provide a method for estimation of the shielding factor that applies to a given electron.
Magnetism arises from the spins of electrons.
Paramagnetism arises from unpaired electrons in atoms. Atoms containing no unpaired electrons are diamagnetic.
Cooperative effects between paramagnetic nuclei gives rise to ferromagnetism, antiferromagnetism, and ferrimagnetism.

Oxidation states of atoms play an important role in the reactivity of and bonding interactions observed in inorganic compounds. Many elements can be stable in several oxidation states depending on the surrounding environment.
The inert pair effect is observed in lower row metals of the p-block.
Most transition metals have more than one accessible oxidation state. In contrast, many metals of the f-block display a limited number of stable oxidation states.
Nonmetals typically have more than one accessible oxidation state.

physical.text: Atomic wavefunctions describe an atom’s electrons and these functions include quantum numbers.
Atoms, molecules and subatomic particles (electrons) have combinations of mass and speed that their wave/particle duality becomes important and requires a quantum model.
Quantum numbers associated with wavefunctions provide a description of the characteristics of an electron within an atom or molecule.
Quantum numbers arise from the function indices of the central force problem solution of an atomic system using quantum mechanics
Atomic term symbols are shorthand notation to describe the sum of the electron microstates and their interactions.
Atomic term symbols describe the total orbital and total spin angular momentum in many electron atoms.
Atomic term symbols capture the importance of spin-orbit coupling in multielectron atoms.
Pauli Principle requires that the wavefunction of a multielectron atom must be antisymmetric with respect to electron exchange
No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers as a result of the Pauli Principle.
The square of the wavefunction describes the electronic probability distribution.
Because electrons must be found someplace, wavefunctions must be normalized.
The normalization constant is the expression that guarantees the square of the wavefunction integrated over all space is 1.
The wavefunction can be used to determine where the electron is probably located in an atom.

C.text: Atoms display a periodicity in their structures and observable phenomena that depend on that structure.

l3.text: Some properties of atoms, such as atomic radius, ionization energy, and electron affinity, follow periodic trends.

l4.text: Sizes of atoms and ions can be assigned and they demonstrate periodic trends.
Definitions of ionization energy and electron affinity are important concepts for relating observable phenomena to periodic trends.
In addition to atomic radii, other properties, such as ionization energy, electron affinity, and effective nuclear charge, are relatable to periodic trends.

l3.text: Effective nuclear charge is a useful model for explaining periodic trends in atomic properties.

l4.text: Effective nuclear charge accounts for both the nuclear charge and the effect of shielding of that charge by core electrons.
Relative sizes of atoms and ionization energy can be predicted based on effective nuclear charge.

l3.text: Reactivity trends of elements show periodic trends that are also relatable to the atomic structure of the atoms of the elements.

l4.text: Elements in the same group have similar chemical and physical properties and valence electron configurations.
Atomic ratios within individual compounds, when related to periodic trends, can be used to identify what elements are present in a compound.
The organization of the periodic table is identified with group numbers and names that are useful for categorization purposes beyond correlations with atomic structure.

organic.text: The valence of the various atoms commonly found in organic molecules shows the periodicity in structure and the phenomena that result from it (e.g., nucleophilicity trends, pKa properties).
Organic molecules reflect the periodicity of atoms via bond strengths and bond lengths.

inorganic.text: Effective nuclear charge can be used to understand many of the periodic trends in atomic properties.
The magnitudes of ionization energy, electron affinity, and electronegativity increase with increasing effective nuclear charge.
Atomic and ionic radii decrease with increasing effective nuclear charge.

The lanthanide contraction, which is related to the poor shielding ability of electrons in 4f orbitals, is used to explain the similarities between the properties of the d and p-block elements in rows 5 and 6 of the periodic table. A similar effect, sometimes referred to as the "scandide contraction" is also observed in the p-block between rows 3 and 4.
Elements within the same group contain the same number of valence electrons, and will exhibit similarities in reactivity, structures, formulas, etc.

Main group elements in the second row of the periodic table (B-F) often exhibit anomalous properties in comparison to the other elements of the group due to the small size of the 2p orbitals and efficiency of forming pi bonds. The 3d transition metals also have anomalous properties compared to the lower elements of the same group.

An increase in effective nuclear charge upon moving to the right one column on the periodic table is offset by the increase in size moving down a row. This causes elements located diagonal to each other to have similar chemical properties. This phenomenon is commonly known as the diagonal rule.

Elements located within the same group on the periodic table will display the same oxidation states within their compounds. Therefore, they tend to form compounds with similar stoichiometries (i.e NaCl, KCl and CH4, SiH4).

The inert pair effect arises in the lower p-block element because electrons in the valence s and p orbitals experience higher effective nuclear charges due to better penetration compared to d and f orbitals. This causes metals in the lower p block to have two accessible oxidation states.

Elements from the d-block of the periodic table form many compounds and ions with the same stoichiometry as p-block elements occupying similar positions on the periodic table. The A/B numbering system used on earlier versions of the periodic table is used to reflect this similarity.

The reactivity of main group elements displays a systematic variation dependent on their location on the periodic table. Excluding the noble gases, the highest reactivity is displayed by elements on the left and right sides of the periodic table, and reactivity decreases as you move towards the middle.
An element's location on the periodic table can be used to determine whether it will exhibit behaviors that are characteristic of metals, nonmetals, or metalloids.

Metallic character increases moving down a column of the periodic table. Physical properties of metals include luster, conductivity, malleability, ductility. Chemical characteristics of metals include low ionization energies, tendency to form cations, low to negative redox potentials, and formation of ionic compounds.

Nonmetals are located in the upper right corner of the periodic table. Physically, nonmetals are typically gases at room temperature, elements that are solid have a dull appearance. Nonmetals typically behave as insulators, and are typically brittle. Chemical characteristics of nonmetals include high ionization energies, tendency to form anions, larger positive redox potentials, and covalent bonding,
Metalloids/Semimetals are located on the periodic table in between the metals and nonmetals, and exhibit properties characteristic of both.
Elements in the p-block exhibit a variation in metallic properties, with metallic behavior increasing as you go down a group.

physical.text: The periodicity of electronic structure around atoms is well explained by the quantum model of atoms.
The set of quantum numbers, n, l, and m, identify the wavefunctions of atoms and can be related to periodic trends in multielectron systems.

Periodicity in bonding behavior of elements is often referred to as valence, and can be explained by the similarity in electron configurations that arise from the quantum mechanical model of the atom.
The concepts of electron shells is an approximation to the wavefunctions of an atom, and helps describe periodic tendencies of elements.
The radial portion of the wavefunction of atoms peaks further away from the nucleus as the quantum number, n, increases.

D.text: Most information about atoms is inferred from studies on collections of atoms often involving an interaction with electromagnetic radiation.

l3.text: Electromagnetic radiation can be characterized by wavelength or frequency , and different wavelengths of radiation are useful for different measurements of matter.

l4.text: The interaction of photons with molecules and atoms provides information about energy levels.
Atomic spectra are unique for a given element.

l3.text: Kinetic molecular theory is an important bridge between particulate and macroscopic models of behavior.

l4.text: Postulates of kinetic molecular theory can be listed for ideal gases, and their implications identified.
The manner in which these postulates for ideal gases fail for real gases depicts important concepts related to the volume of gas particles and the interactions between them.

l3.text: Many measurable properties of matter require bulk quantities, and qualitative trends can be used to categorize these properties .

l4.text: Phases of matter are an important bulk quantity.
Some properties of matter depend on individual atoms (or ions) of an element, and others are meaningful only for bulk quantities of atoms.
Trends in bulk properties, such as conductivity and reactivity, can be used to identify elements present in an unknown substance.
Some bulk properties are extensive and others are intensive.
Important categorization schemes of matter, such as metal versus nonmetal, are useful at both atomic and bulk scales.

organic.text: A discussion of the major historical developments in organic chemistry highlights how organic chemistry discoveries were made.
Key techniques for structural elucidation include UV, IR, NMR, and MS.

inorganic.text: Spectroscopic methods involve the use of electromagnetic radiation to probe the differences between energy levels within atoms.
Transitions between nuclear ground and excited states of atoms typically occur with energies in the γ-ray or X-ray region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
X-ray absorption, X-ray photoelectron, and X-ray fluorescence spectroscopies are used to probe energies associated with transitions involving core-level electrons.

Transitions involving valence electrons within atoms typically result in emission or absorption of light in the ultraviolet or visible regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. Atomic emission, atomic absorption, and ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopies are techniques that are commonly used to determine the energies associated with these transitions.

The degeneracy of nuclear and electronic spin states within atoms can be changed in the presence of a magnetic or non-spherically symmetric electric field. Transitions between the resulting magnetic states is typically observed using radio or microwave radiation in the nuclear magnetic resonance and electron paramagnetic resonance techniques.
The wavelength of X-rays is similar to the distance between atoms in solids, and powder and single-crystal X-ray diffraction techniques can be employed to measure these distances.
Interaction of coherent input X-rays with a crystalline (regular repeating) solid's electrons causes scattering (a regular array) of spherical X-rays.
Constructive interference of scattered X-rays leads to a pattern of bright scattered X-rays amid mostly dark destructive interference called a diffraction pattern.
Computation of an X-ray crystal structure results from the back-calculation of the positions of the atoms responsible for the diffraction pattern.
X-ray crystallography is the most powerful tool for determining the 3D structure of crystalline solids.

physical.text: Historically, the development of an understanding of quantization of energy states arose from spectroscopic observations.
Atomic line spectra were among the observations that could not be explained using classical theories, leading to the development of the quantum model of atoms,
The photoelectron effect requires a quantum model of light to be adequately described.
Selection rules dictate what electronic transitions can be observed.
Allowed transitions between electronic states in atoms have a change in the l quantum number of +/- 1 and no change in the m quantum number.
Atomic absorption and emission spectra can be described with quantum mechanics.
Atomic transitions due to electromagnetic radiation are understood via the calculation of the transition dipole moment.
Atomic absorption and emission spectra can be described with atomic wavefunctions.
The parity of the ground and excited state wavefunctions dictate whether or not a transition dipole will be non-zero.
The vibronic nature of atomic absorption or emission is understood in terms of Franck- Condon factors.
Time dependent wavefunctions are necessary to describe fully interactions with electromagnetic radiation.
Time dependent perturbation theory defines a Hamiltonian, H0 + H1(t) where the time dependence is captured in the perturbation term.
Time dependent perturbation theory is used to treat spectroscopic transitions in quantum mechanics.

E.text: Macroscopic samples of matter contain so many atoms that they are counted in moles.

l3.text: The mole is defined based on the relative mass scale for atoms, and this results in Avogadro’s number being equal to 6.02  1023 .

l4.text: The translation between atomic-level understanding and macroscopic understanding is facilitated by the concept of the mole.

l3.text: Conversions involving the mole (molar mass, g/mol, mol/# of atoms, etc.) are critical to being able to describe matter at both the particulate level and the macroscopic scale.

l4.text: Quantitative conversions with the concept of the moles are important.

l3.text: The size scale of atoms is roughly the picometer scale, which helps explain why Avogadro’s number is so large.

l4.text: A sense of scale of sizes of atoms and the distance between the nucleus and electrons is integral to understanding fundamental concepts in chemistry.

organic.text: Mole-based stoichiometry calculations (i.e., molar equivalents and limiting reagents) are used to determine percentage yield, particularly in the laboratory.

inorganic.text: Mole based stoichiometry calculations (i.e., molar equivalents and limiting reagents) are used to determine percent yield, particularly in the laboratory.

physical.text: Models in chemistry have a demonstrated correspondence between microscopic (atomic or molecular) models and macroscopic models.
The Boltzman constant relates the average kinetic energy of a gas to its temperature and is the gas constant, R, divided by Avogadro's number.

F.text: Atoms maintain their identity, except in nuclear reactions.

alt.inorganic: Atoms maintain their identity, except in nuclear reactions

l3.text: Conservation of macroscopic mass in chemical reactions is due to the conservation of atoms.

l4.text: Equations describing chemical reactions can be balanced based on conservation of atoms.

l3.text: Atoms change identity in nuclear reactions; it is possible to write nuclear equations that follow these changes.

l4.text: Balancing nuclear reactions is based on the simultaneous conservation of both atomic and mass numbers.

l3.text: Measurements of radioactivity can be used to identify which unstable isotopes are present in a sample and in what quantity.

l4.text: Radioactive half-lives are unique and may be used to identify what isotopes are present.
Radioactivity may occur via alpha, beta, gamma or other decay events and the type of radioactivity observed is often an important component of identifying the decaying isotope.
In a mixture, the amount of a radioactive isotope can be determined via quantitative measurement of radioactive events.

inorganic.text: Several different types of nuclear reactions can transform the identity of an element.
Unstable nuclei undergo decay processes that produce radioactive emissions.
Larger unstable nuclei undergo nuclear fission reactions. This is especially true of the elements with atomic numbers greater than 92.
Relative stabilities of isotopes are measured by comparing binding energies and half-lives.
Nuclei that do not undergo spontaneous decay may undergo nuclear fusion.
Nucleosynthesis is the process by which elements form from fusion reactions in stars.

physical.text: Atomic number may increase, decrease or stay the same in nuclear reactions.
Alpha decay, electron capture and positron emission are all processes that decrease the atomic number.
Beta decay increases the atomic number.
Gamma decay releases energy in nuclear processes but does not change the atomic number.

G.text: Ions arise when the number of electrons and protons are not equal, and can be formed from atoms.

alt.inorganic: Ions arise when the number of electrons and protons are not equal and can be formed from atoms.

l3.text: Anions form from atoms when additional electrons are added, while cations form from atoms when electrons are removed.

l4.text: The charge on monoatomic anions and cations can often be predicted by their position in the periodic table.

Symbolic representations of ions include the charge in addition to the atomic symbol, thereby imparting knowledge of both the number of protons and electrons present (and neutrons, if mass number is also given in the representation).

l3.text: Ions have chemical properties that differ from the atoms from which they are derived.

l4.text: The formation of ions often imparts stability to otherwise very reactive atoms.

organic.text: Metal–nonmetal bonds have a large dipole and can function in organic reactions as a strong base or strong nucleophile.

inorganic.text: Electrons can be gained or lost by atoms forming anions or cations respectively. Orbital energy and electron configuration dictate whether cation or anions are formed.
Due to low ionization energies and electron affinities, metallic elements typically lose electrons to form cations.
Due to high ionization energies and electron affinities, nonmetals typically form anions.
Core electrons are strongly attracted to the nucleus and are normally not removed when cations are formed.
Isoelectronic series consisting of atoms or ions having the same number of valence electrons are useful for comparison of properties.

physical.text: Ionization energy/electron affinity for atoms based on wavefunctions.
The ionization energy is obtained from the Bohr model equation for DE, by setting the final n to infinity.
Energy level spacings decrease in the quantum mechanical H-atom model, until ionization is reached at which energy the spacings are effectively continuous.
The formation of ions is a critical step in mass spectroscopy.
All forms of mass spectroscopy rely on the formation of ions to detect the analyte, but the specifics of the ionization process can be selected to optimize detection limits or sensitivity.
Generally the electronic structure of an ion starts from the framework of the electronic structure of the neutral atom.
Monatomic ions that have only one electron have Schrodinger equations that can be solved analytically in the same way as a hydrogen atom, but with nuclear charge being greater than 1.
Koopman's theorem indicates that the negative value of the HOMO is approximately equal to the ionization energy.

II.title: Bonding
II.text: Bonding: Atoms interact via electrostatic forces to form chemical bonds.

A.text: Because protons and electrons are charged, physical models of bonding are based on electrostatic forces.

alt.inorganic: Because protons and electrons are charged all models of bonding are based on electrostatic forces.
alt.physical: Because protons and electrons are charged all models of bonding are based on electrostatic forces.

l3.text: Ionic bonding is described via the interaction of positive and negative charged ions via Coulomb forces.

l4.text: Lattice structures of ionic substances display the alternation of opposite charges, which leads to a net attractive force.

l3.text: Covalent bonds can be distinguished from ionic ones and trends can be predicted based on the elements involved in the bonding.

l4.text: Bonds formed between two nonmetals tend to be covalent, while bonds formed between a metal and a nonmetal tend to be ionic in character.

l3.text: There is essentially a continuum of bonding behavior from ionic, through polar covalent, and ultimately nonpolar covalent bonding.

l4.text: Differences in electronegativity of elements involved in bonding can be used to predict the extent of charge separation when a bond forms.
Electronegativity trends for elements have periodic tendencies, with electronegativity tending to increase towards the top and right of the periodic table, excluding the noble gas group.

organic.text: Organic molecules are held together with covalent bonds that arise from the sharing of electron pairs between nuclei.
In alkanes, carbons can be labeled as primary, secondary, tertiary, or quaternary, depending on the number of non-hydrogen substituents (i.e., 1, 2, 3, or 4 respectively) on the labeled carbon.
An uneven sharing of the electrons in a chemical bond leads to a bond dipole moment.
Polar bonds (such as cyano groups) result from unequal sharing of electrons (due to electronegativity differences) between two covalently bonded atoms, resulting in a bond dipole moment.
Carbonyls are an extremely polar functional group; the carbon is partially positive and the oxygen is partially negative. Therefore, the carbon of a carbonyl is very electrophilic.

Conversion of an alkyl halide to an organomagnesium (or lithium– lithium and copper) results in a partially negative carbon that functions as a nucleophile. Organometallic reagents (e.g., Grignard or Gilman) are strong nucleophiles and participate in a variety of reactions that involve nucleophilic substitution or addition.

inorganic.text: Orbital energy dictates the type of bond formed.
Bonding between atoms can be described as lying within a continuum spanning ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding.
Polar covalent bonds result when electron density is asymmetrically distributed due to electronegativity differences between the atoms involved.
The Ketelaar triangle relates the position of a bond within the ionic/covalent/metallic continuum to the mean electronegativity of and electronegativity difference between the atoms involved.
Electrostatic parameters (z/r) can be used to rationalize types of bonding within molecules
Crystal field theory is an electrostatic model used to describe the electronic structure in transition metal complexes.

The energy separation between the d orbitals (Δ) is related to the interactions between ions within the crystal field, and is dependent on complex geometry and the metal and ligands involved. Common geometries observed in coordination compounds are octahedral, square planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and square pyramidal.
Pairing energy (Π or P) is a measure of the energy cost associated with pairing electrons within the same orbital.
The spectrochemical series is a ranking of ligands by their effects on the magnitude of Δ within complexes they form.
Depending on the relative magnitudes of Δ and Π, transition metal complexes can be high spin (Δ < Π) or low spin (Δ > Π).
Complexes containing asymmetrically occupied degenerate sets of orbitals may exhibit Jahn- Teller distortions.
Ionic bonding involves electrostatic interactions between ions formed when electron transfer occurs between two atoms.
The Born-Lande and Kapustinskii equations are used to model lattice energies of ionic compounds using the Coulombic interactions between the ions of the lattice.
The Maadelung constant for a solid-state lattice incorporates geometric and distance factors for nearest neighbor and longer range electrostatic interactions between ions.
The Born-Mayer equation accounts for repulsion of electron clouds of adjacent ions, which improves lattice energy calculations.
Various electron counting rules have been devised to rationalize bonding within molecular and ionic compounds.

The octet rule is used to rationalize the bonding within main group compounds. Common exceptions to the octet rule are observed in hypervalent compounds of the nonmetals of the lower p-block and electron deficient compounds of beryllium and boron.
The 18-electron guideline is used to rationalize bonding within transition metal complexes. A common exception is the stability of 16 electron square planar complexes containing 8 metal d electrons.
The "neutral ligand" and "ionic" methods are commonly used to determine ligand electron counts within transition metal compounds.

The covalent bond classification (CBC) method is an alternative electron counting method that classifies ligands within organometallic compounds based on electron donating properties as "L," "X" and "Z" type ligands.
Formal charge and oxidation state calculations are used to represent electron density on individual atoms within structures.
Lewis structures are used to represent electron distribution and bonding within molecules.

physical.text: Summing all electrostatic interactions between electrons and protons provides the potential energy operators of the quantum description of atoms and molecules.
The potential energy portion of the Hamiltonian for atoms or molecules is given by pairwise Coulomb’s Law interactions between all charged particles (nuclei & electrons).
Atomic units are often used to express the Hamiltonian and have the advantage of accounting for a number of constants that would otherwise be part of the potential and kinetic energy operators.
In the quantum model, electron-electron interactions are captured via electron correlation energy.
The electron-electron interaction renders analytic solutions for multielectron atoms in quantum mechanics impossible.
The core conceptual underpinning of the Hartree-Fock approximation is that each electron interacts with the average charge of the other electrons.
The Hartree-Fock approximation is written as a single Slater determinant, and electron correlation effects can be obtained by using more than one determinant to express the wavefunction.
The Born-Oppenheimer approximation allows separation of the nuclear wavefunction from the electronic wavefunction.
Because of the large differences in mass, electronic and nuclear motion can often be separated in a quantum mechanical calculation.

The Born-Oppenheimer approximation allows electronic motion to be solved first with the "clamped nuclei" approximation, followed by separate calculations for vibrational, rotational and translational motions of the nuclei.

B.text: Because chemical bonds arise from sharing of negatively charged valence electrons between positively charged nuclei, the overall electrostatic interaction is attractive.

alt.organic: Because chemical bonds arise from sharing of negatively charged electrons between positively charged nuclei, the overall electrostatic interaction is attractive.
alt.physical: Because chemical bonds arise from sharing of negatively charged electrons between positively charged nuclei, the overall electrostatic interaction is attractive.

l3.text: Electrons occupy “shells” so that the outer, valence electrons are the ones involved in chemical bonding.

l4.text: Valence electrons are responsible for bonding.
The number of valence electrons shows periodic trends that result in predictable numbers of bonds being formed by an atom.

l3.text: Covalent bonds arise when valence electrons are shared, in pairs, between nuclei.

l4.text: The build up of (negatively charged) electron pairs between (positively charged) nuclei leads to a bonding interaction.
Prior to bond formation, shared electrons may be either on one atom involved in the bond or both. The former distinguishes a coordinate covalent (or dative) bond.

organic.text: Chemical bonds result from shared electrons; nuclei involved in the sharing and number of electrons shared results in differences in bond energy.
Single, double, and triple bonds between atoms give rise to patterns in bond energies and lengths.

inorganic.text: The bond order can be used to represent the magnitude of the attractive interaction between atoms.
Bond order is an indication of net electrons in bonding molecular orbitals.
Bond order = 1/2(number of bonding electrons - number of antibonding electrons).
For bonds between the same element, the attractive forces follow the trend triple bonds > double bonds > single bonds.
Because bonds in coordination compounds form when ligand electrons are donated into empty metal orbitals, they are considered to be dative bonds.
In coordination complexes, the metal is the Lewis acid and the ligand is the Lewis base.
Since both electrons come from the ligand, it is usually simple to identify the ligand molecule within the "complex" ion.
In MO Theory, the source of electrons is irrelevant–only the number and location of all bonding and antibonding electrons is important.
Ionic compounds are held together by electrostatic interactions between ions.

physical.text: For a bond to form, there must be some buildup of electrons between nuclei.
The square of wavefunction, integrated over available space, is used to find the probability of an electron in that space.
If electron density has not increased between two nuclei, the internuclear repulsion would cause them to fly apart, thus not forming a bond.
The quantum description of a molecule includes overlap, Coulomb, and exchange integrals.
The Coulomb integral captures the interaction of electrons on one nucleus with another nucleus and corrects for nuclear-nuclear repulsion.
The exchange integral has no classical mechanical analog and arises from the requirement that electrons must be indistinguishable.
The overlap integral captures the extent to which the wavefunctions of two different quantum particles are located in the same region of space, and thus overlap each other.

C.text: When chemical bonds form, the overall energy of the bonding atoms is lowered relative to free atoms, and therefore energy is released.

alt.inorganic: When chemical bonds form, the overall energy of the bonding atoms is lowered, and therefore energy is released.

l3.text: The net result of the formation of any stable chemical bond is a lowering of the energy of the system. If the energy is not lowered, the bond is not stable.

l4.text: Not all atoms combine to form stable chemical bonds, but when a bond forms it is always accompanied by a lowering of the energy.

l3.text: Graphical depiction of the potential energy for a chemical bond as a function of interatomic distance shows both the stabilization for intermediate distances and repulsion for very short distances.

l4.text: The energy of interaction between electrons and nuclei is captured graphically by plotting potential energy as a function of distance between atoms.

l3.text: Valence bond theory describes bonds in terms of overlap of electron wave functions.

l4.text: The concept of atomic orbital overlap leading to chemical bonding as embodied in valence bond theory represents a useful tool for understanding the basic components of the quantum mechanics of bonding.
Sigma and pi bonds are a key way to distinguish chemical bonds , as obtained from valence bond theory.

organic.text: A chemical bond results in the lowest energy orbitals being filled such that the overall energy change of the system is negative.
Chemical bonds can interact in ways to lower the overall energy of the molecule.
Conjugated alkenes are uniquely stable due to conjugation (p-orbital overlap).
Benzene is uniquely stable (i.e., aromatic) due to cyclic conjugation of π- bonds.
Aromatic compounds are flat, continuous cyclic arrays of p-orbitals that contain 4n+2 electrons (anti-aromatic compounds have 4n electrons).

inorganic.text: Bond strength is determined by orbital overlap.
The amount of energy released when a bond is formed is equal to the bond dissociation energy.
Bond energies increase in magnitude with increasing bond order.
Lattice energies are used to express the energy released upon formation of ionic compounds.
Theoretical Born-Haber cycles can be used to explain why alternative ionic compounds (i.e. NaCl2 or NaO) are not formed.
The ligand field stabilization energy (LFSE) is a measure of the stability of a metal ion in a coordination compound.
LFSE's can be used to explain the formation of specific geometries for specific d-electron configurations.
LFSE indicates stabilization beyond bond formation that is due to d-orbital arrangements in particular geometries.

High spin (maximum unpaired electrons) and low spin (minimum unpaired electrons) arrangements are sometimes possible for the same complex geometry, and depend on the relative energetic cost of pairing electrons in the same orbital (P or Π) versus promoting the electron to a higher energy d-orbital (Δ, D).

physical.text: Graphical depiction of the electrostatic interaction is referred to as the potential energy diagram.
Because there are both repulsive and attractive forces present, a minimum of energy occurs in the depiction of a bond, and this is the most probable distance/length of that bond.
The minimum on the potential energy diagram occurs at a negative value if a bond is formed, and thus energy must be released to the surroundings during bond formation.
Because of the existence of zero point energy, care must be taken to define bond energy and bond dissociation energy.
Functions that fit the ground state potential are important for different models of bonds and bond vibrations.
The region near to the energy minimum may be fit by a harmonic oscillator potential, but anharmonicity becomes important as the energy increases.
The anharmonic depiction of bond energy can be fit using functions such as the Morse potential, or using a series expansion.
While the ground state lowers energy relative to separated atoms, there are also excited states, some of which are bound while others are purely dissociative.
Molecular term symbols provide a short-hand method to describe molecular orbital occupations for either ground or excited electronic states.
Interactions between electronic states depend on the symmetry and multiplicities of the states.

D.text: To break a chemical bond requires an input of energy.

l3.text: The energy required to break a chemical bond is the bond dissociation energy.

l4.text: Bond dissociation energy is useful at the level of individual molecules; for calculations on macroscopic quantities, the value used is the bond dissociation enthalpy.
Bond dissociation enthalpies can be used to estimate the change in enthalpy for a reaction.

organic.text: The breaking of a bond homolytically requires the input of energy, measured as the bond dissociation energy.

inorganic.text: The bond dissociation enthalpy is the amount of energy required to break a bond. Bond dissociation enthalpies increase with bond order.
Vibrational energies increase in magnitude with increasing bond order.

physical.text: The energy needed to break a chemical bond can arise from molecular collisions, or from the absorption of light or electrical energy.
High energy collisions between molecules may impart enough energy to break chemical bonds, and weaker bonds tend to be more frequently broken under these conditions.
Absorption of light energy may break bonds in processes such as photodissociation or predissociation.
Electrochemical systems may provide energy for the breaking of bonds, and this often occurs as a process on an electrode surface.
Bond breaking may be heterolytic or homolytic.
In homolytic bond breaking, shared electrons are divided equally among product molecules.
In heterolytic bond breaking, both shared electrons end up on a single product molecule.

E.text: A theoretical construct that describes chemical bonding utilizes the construction of molecular orbitals for the bond based on overlap of atomic orbitals on the constituent atoms.

l3.text: Molecular orbital theory describes chemical bonds via molecular orbitals derived from atomic orbitals.

l4.text: In the quantum model of atoms and molecules, the combination of atomic orbitals leads to the formation of bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals.
Bond order can be defined in terms of the occupation of bonding and antibonding orbitals by electrons.
Hybrid atomic orbitals are useful in describing bonding, particularly for organic molecules.
Molecular orbital theory helps account for unpaired electrons in molecules and can thereby explain the observation of paramagnetic behavior. O2 is a common example.

organic.text: Hybridization, resonance, and molecular orbital theory provide information about bond formation.

Molecular orbital theory is based on the wavelike nature of electrons. Atomic orbitals (i.e., s, p, d, f; based on the atomic orbitals of hydrogen) are mathematical probability functions for finding an electron in the circumscribed space for a given atom. Orbitals can be “hybridized” through a process of linear combinations of atomic orbitals’ hybridized orbitals (such as sp or sp3), and are used to better represent actual bond lengths, angles, and energies for molecules. Atomic and hybridized orbitals can be overlapped to form bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals and thus theoretical models of electronic structure and molecular geometry.

Resonance structures are two or more Lewis structures that differ only in the absolute location of electrons. A weighted linear combination of resonance structures for a given molecule best represents the “actual” electron density of the molecule.
Allylic radicals, cations, and anions are uniquely stable due to resonance stabilization.
The stereochemistry and regiochemistry of cycloaddition reactions is related to the symmetry of the orbitals.
The products formed in a Diels–Alder reaction retain the stereochemistry of the starting materials.
Atomic orbitals mix to form bonding, nonbonding, and antibonding molecular orbitals such that the number of molecular orbitals produced equals the number of atomic orbitals used initially.
Hybrid orbitals are necessary to describe the geometry of substituents on individual atoms (e.g., the tetrahedral geometry of carbon in methane).
Orbital diagrams reduced to just p-orbitals are used to understand the differences between aromatic and anti-aromatic compounds.

inorganic.text: Molecular orbitals are formed by overlapping atomic orbitals having the same symmetry.
Linear combinations of overlapping orbitals result in bonding, antibonding, and nonbonding combinations.
Molecular orbital shapes can be derived from the parent atomic orbitals.
Interactions of atomic orbitals influence energies of molecular orbitals.

Electrons occupying bonding orbitals stabilize the molecule relative to the component atoms, while electron occupation of antibonding orbitals will destabilize the molecule relative to the component atoms.
The energy that molecular orbitals are displaced relative to the atomic/component orbitals is inversely proportional to the difference in energies of the participating atomic orbitals.
Nonbonding orbitals are formed when one orbital does not have a complementary orbital with the same symmetry, or, in some cases, when more than two sets of orbitals interact with each other.
The relative energies of molecular orbitals typically increase with the number of nodes.
Molecular orbital diagrams provide a visual depiction of relative energies of molecular orbitals as well as correlation to the parent atomic orbitals.
Second-order mixing can lead to energy level diagrams that do not follow the simple patterns of more splitting for sigma and less splitting for pi bonds. (e.g. N2)
Photoelectron spectroscopy probes energy differences between atomic or molecular states.
Computational methods can be used to calculate the energies of molecular orbitals.
The energies of frontier molecular orbitals can be used to rationalize the results of acid-base and reduction-oxidation reactions.
Electron configurations of molecules can be generated using molecular orbitals.
Ground state molecular electron configurations are derived using the same rules (Aufbau principle, Hund's rules, and the Pauli exclusion principle) used for atomic electron configurations.

The bond order for a molecule can be calculated from the number of electrons occupying bonding and antibonding orbitals in the molecular electron configuration. Bond orders do not have to be integers.
Molecules with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic and molecules with no unpaired electrons are diamagnetic.
Isoelectronic molecules and ions have analogous valence molecular electron configurations.
Using symmetry, the principles of molecular orbital theory can be applied to polyatomic systems.

In molecules containing a central atom, Molecular orbitals are constructed by combining atomic orbitals on a central atom with Symmetry Adapted Linear Combinations of orbitals on the surrounding atoms.
The molecular orbital approach can also be used to construct molecular orbitals for extended pi bonding systems in linear or ring shaped molecules.
Molecular orbital theory is also applied to delocalized systems in inorganic chemistry. Examples include 3-center-2-electron bonds and cluster bonding.
Ligand Field Theory uses a molecular orbital theory approach to describe metal-ligand interactions in coordination compounds.
The effects of σ-only, π-donor, π-acceptor ligand interactions on the metal d orbitals can be used to explain the ordering of ligands in the spectrochemical series.

Changes in intra-ligand bond lengths may be observed when ligand bonding or antibonding orbitals are involved in metal-ligand bond formation. One common example is the lengthening of the C-O bond length upon coordination to a metal center.
The Jahn-Teller effect may be observed in compounds having asymmetrically occupied sets of degenerate orbitals.

The symmetry properties of molecular electron configurations can be represented using molecular term symbols. Energies associated with different terms are usually depicted using Orgel and Tanabe-Sugano Diagrams.
The Angular Overlap Model is used to calculate the effects of ligand sigma and pi interactions on the splitting of d orbitals based on the extent of overlap occurring in different geometries.

physical.text: Different computation models can be used to describe how electrons interact in multi-atom, multi- electron systems.
Because quantum mechanical calculations for multi-electron systems inevitably include more than two-body problems, analytic mathematical solutions do not exist, and approximations must be used.
The Hartree-Fock, Self Consistent Field (HF-SCF) approximation begins with an initial guess for a trial wavefunction, and is iterated until electron density and energy converge.
Models improve on the Hartree-Fock assumption by somehow accounting for the electron correlation energy.
Density functional theory describes the electron density as a functional which is a function of both time and space.
In semi-empirical calculations, some integrals required for the quantum mechanical problems are replaced with experimental information in order to reduce the time for calculation.
Different types of approximations, including variational theory or perturbation theory, may be used to solve quantum mechanical problems.
The variational theorem states that if an approximate wavefunction is used with an exact Hamiltonian, the calculated energy will be greater than or equal to the true energy.
Variational calculations are used to model quantum systems by inserting parameters into trial wavefunctions and minimizing energy with respect to these variational parameters.
In perturbation theory, the Hamiltonian is described as with an unperturbed term that is often a model for which answers are well established, that is modified by a small perturbation term.
Both bonding and antibonding orbitals arise when molecular orbitals are constructed from atomic orbitals.
One model for describing molecular orbitals is to use linear combinations of atomic orbitals (LCAO-MO).
Molecular orbitals produced from atomic orbitals can be bonding, anti-bonding or non- bonding.
An increased probability of finding an electron between two nuclei indicates a bonding orbital.
Because nodes indicate regions of space with no electron probability, nodes that occur between nuclei will indicate an antibonding orbital.

F.text: Covalent bonds can be categorized based on the number of electrons (pairs) shared. The most common categories are single, double, and triple bonds.

alt.inorganic: Covalent bonds can be categorized based on the number of electrons (pairs) shared. The most common categories are single, double and triple bonds.
alt.physical: Covalent bonds can be categorized based on the number of electrons (pairs) shared. The most common categories are single, double and triple bonds.

l3.text: Single bonds share one pair of electrons, double bonds share two pairs of electrons, triple bonds share three.

l4.text: Bond energy increases as the number of shared pairs increases.
Bond length decreases as the number of shared pairs increases.

organic.text: Single, double, and triple bonds are discussed in terms of sigma and pi bonds, and the differences in the relative bond lengths and strengths.

Bonds formed by the overlap of s-orbitals or s-containing hybrid orbitals result in the formation of sigma (σ) bonds; sigma bonds are also formed from the end-to-end overlap of p-orbitals; bonds formed by the side-to- side overlap of p-orbitals result in the formation of pi (π) bonds.

The “degree(s) of unsaturation” (or index of hydrogen deficiency) is equal to the number of π-bonds or rings in a given molecule. In general, it is the difference between the number of hydrogens in a corresponding fully saturated molecule minus the actual number of hydrogens in the molecule divided by two. Incorporation of heteroatoms (e.g., N or halogens) impacts the way in which unsaturation is calculated.
Sigma and pi bonds have effects on geometric structure; in particular, rotation about a single bond occurs readily, while rotation about a double bond is hindered.

Molecules can adopt conformations based on free rotation around σ- bonds. Relationships between atoms and substituent groups can be described as staggered or eclipsed, gauche or anti using Newman projections. Each conformation has a relative energy; molecules, in general, seek the lowest energy conformation. However, any conformation at an energy minimum can potentially be observed via spectroscopic methods.
Cylcohexane adopts three main conformations: chair (major conformer), boat, twist-boat. With sufficient energy, a cyclohexane molecule can interconvert between all possible conformations.

inorganic.text: Lewis structures are a shorthand representation of the electron distribution within ions and molecules.
When constructing a Lewis structure, central atoms typically have a smaller electronegativity than terminal atoms.
The bond order is calculated by counting bonds between atoms in a lewis structure can be compared to the bond order calculated from molecular orbital theory.
Bond orders < 3 are observed in main group compounds.
Quadruple bonds can occur in compounds of the transition elements, and some examples of quintuple bonds have been reported.
Resonance structures are used to explain delocalized bonding in pi systems and 3 center-2 electron bonds.
Valence Bond Theory is a localized description of bonding within molecules.
In valence bond theory bonding molecular orbitals are constructed from overlapping the constituent atomic orbitals.
Hybridization of atomic orbitals is often used in valence bond theory to explain observed molecular geometries.
Sigma (σ), pi (π), and delta (δ) interactions are defined by the number of nodal planes along the internuclear axis (0, 1, 2 planes respectively).
Bond strength and bond length are correlated with bond order.
Bond strength increases as bond order increases.
Bond length decreases as bond order increases.

physical.text: More than one molecular orbital may occupy the space between nuclei so long as the quantum numbers are different.
Sigma and pi orbitals between two nuclei are orthogonal to each other.
The orthonormality of wave functions is often expressed using the Kronecker delta, which is zero for functions with different quantum numbers.
The vibrational frequency of a bond is related to the bond order. These can be modeled by vibrational force constants.
The Harmonic oscillator is a simple quantum mechanical model which includes the relationship between bond strength and vibrational frequency in the force constant, k.
For polyatomic systems, the vibrational wavefunction can be approximately separated using normal mode coordinates.
The bond order can be determined computationally from the electron density using the full wavefunction of a molecule.
Bond order can be calculated as 0.5 x (# of bonding electrons - # of antibonding electrons).

G.text: Metallic bonding arises in many solids and fundamentally involves the sharing of valence electrons among many positively charged “cores” over extended distances.

l3.text: A simple model of metallic bonding invokes the concept of a “sea of electrons” that move relatively freely amid the positively charged cores.
A more rigorous model of metallic bonding depicts electrons occupying bands.

l4.text: The band gap between the valence band and conduction band can explain the difference between conductors, semiconductors, and insulators.

inorganic.text: The "electron-sea" model is a simple idea used to describe metallic bonding.
The electron sea is formed by the release of valence electrons to surround all of the cations.
Within metals, electrons are delocalized and behave as a collective.
Conductance of electrons and heat, as well as the malleability of metals, can be explained by the electron sea model.
The conductivity of solids can be explained by the band theory model.
The terms "valence band" and "conduction band" refer to the filled and unfilled molecular orbitals in the ground state electron configuration of a solid.

Molecular orbitals in metallic structures are very close in energy to each other, and electrons have no energetic barrier to overcome to be promoted from valence band to conductance band orbitals. Increasing the thermal energy causes increased vibrations of the metal atoms and lowers conductivity.

Semiconductors and insulators have an energy gap (band gap) between the valence and conduction bands. The size of the band gap relative to the available thermal energy distinguishes a semiconductor (small band gap) from an insulator (large band gap). The conductivity of a semiconductor depends on promotion of electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, and will increase with added thermal energy.

The conductivity of a semiconductor can be improved by doping with atoms that have empty energy levels close in energy to the valence band (p-type) or filled energy levels close in energy to the conduction band (n-type).
The Fermi level represents the energies of the highest energy electrons within a band structure at a given temperature.
Materials containing junctions of n and p type semiconductors have many useful applications.
Diodes are useful for switches, light emitting diodes, and photovoltaic cells.
Transistors are used as amplifiers within electronic circuits.
The Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory describes electrical conductivity in superconducting materials.
Cooper pairs of electrons form at low temperatures.
Cooper pairs push/pull each other through the cationic matrix of the material, thereby overcoming the attractions of cations that cause resistance.
All Cooper pairs in a material interact to form a "condensate" of electrons that better explains superconductance than individual electron pairs.

physical.text: Models for metallic bonding include the electron sea model and band theory.
In the electron sea model, valence electrons form a free flowing "sea" of charge around positively charged "cores" that are akin to metal ions.
Energy levels of valence electrons in metals are so closely spaced they form a band of allowed energies, and this phenomenon is described using band theory.

III.title: Structure and Function
III.text: Structure and Function: Chemical compounds have geometric structures that influence their chemical and physical behaviors.

A.text: Atoms combine to form new compounds that have new properties based on structural and electronic features.

alt.organic: Atoms combine to form compounds that have new properties based on structural and electronic features.
alt.inorganic: Atoms combine to form compounds that have new properties based on structural and electronic features.
alt.physical: Atoms combine to form compounds that have new properties based on structural and electronic features.

l3.text: Most compounds form using fixed ratios of atoms.

l4.text: Mass percentages can be converted to atomic ratios.
The chemical formula reflects the atomic ratios.

l3.text: In addition to chemical compounds, some elements themselves may form chemical bonds so that their most stable states are small molecules.

l4.text: Some elements may have stable molecular forms (e.g., diatomics) that include multiple atoms.
Some elements have allotropes—multiple, stable forms.

l3.text: The formation of molecules may lead to pure substances, but often mixtures of molecules are observed.

l4.text: It is possible to depict the difference between a pure substance and a mixture, particularly at the atomic and molecular scale.

organic.text: Molecular properties (e.g., boiling point) can be the result of differing combinations of atoms (such as –OH, the hydroxyl group), referred to as functional groups.

Molecular properties (e.g., chirality) can be the result of differing orientations of atoms (such as four different substituents bound to a tetrahedral configured carbon), referred to as stereocenters.
The properties of polymers and the different allotropes of carbon are related to their structure, and in the case of crystals, to their crystal structure.

inorganic.text: Coordination compounds are formed by Lewis acid-base interactions between metal ions and ligands.
The inner sphere environment of a coordination compound consists of the ligands bonded directly to the metal center.
Polydentate ligands, including chelating and macrocyclic ligands, contain multiple donor atoms.
Ambidentate ligands have different donor atoms available for formation of metal-ligand bonds.
Metals typically occur as coordination compounds in biological systems.
The properties of a coordination compound depend on its coordination environment.
Coordination number is influenced by atomic sizes, and reactivity is related to the degree of coordinative saturation of the atoms within a molecule.
Chemical properties of a ligand can be altered by coordination to a metal center.
Organometallic compounds contain metal-carbon bonds.
Carbonyl compounds provide a starting point for the understanding of organometallic compounds of the transition metals.
Phosphines are important ligands in organometallic chemistry for altering the electronic and steric environments around a metal center.
Organic ligands can be classified as alkyl, alkenyl, carbene, and carbyne types based upon their sigma and pi bonding interactions with a metal center.
Organic molecules with extended pi systems are common as ligands in organometallic compounds, and hapticity is used to describe different binding modes.
Three-dimensional cluster compounds are common in inorganic chemistry
Cluster molecules of boron are found in borides, boranes and heteroboranes.
Zintl ions are cluster shaped ions formed by p-block metal atoms.
Clusters containing transition metal vertices are common in organometallic chemistry.

Cluster structures are very prevalent in the chemistry of Group 5 and 6 transition metal polyoxometalates. Common structures include the Lindqvist structure for isopolyoxometalates and the Keggin structure for heteropolyoxometalates.
Compounds having chain and layer structures are prevalent in the chemistry of silicon, phosphorus, and sulfur.

physical.text: Both chemical and physical properties of molecules can be measured and they each depend on specific structural details.
Chemical properties ultimately require a reaction to be observed, but can often be predicted based on structures present within a molecule.

Physical properties of substances include both molecular scale characteristics that are usually observed spectroscopically and bulk scale characteristics commonly observed in thermodynamics experiments
Electronic, vibrational and rotational motions are associated with energy levels and transitions between levels provide important insight into molecular behaviors.

The spacing of energy levels varies for different motions, with electronic energy level much more widely spaced than vibrational energy levels which in turn are more widely spaced than rotational energy levels.

Electronic energy levels tend to be widely spaced, but transitions between them have spectroscopic signatures, and may be manipulated for applications such as building lasers or inducing photochemical reactions.
Vibrations of polyatomic molecules can be approximated by a set of normal modes.
Vibrational relaxation within a single electronic state plays a role in a diverse set of processes including spectroscopy and chemical reactions.
Rotational and vibrational spectroscopy are sensitive to the atoms' nuclear mass via I (moment of inertia), B (rotational constant) or reduced mass.
The harmonic oscillator model can be used to describe molecular vibrations and vibrational spectra allow observation of force constants.
Because the harmonic potential rises to infinity somewhat slowly, the quantum model of the harmonic oscillator shows tunneling.
The rigid rotor model can be used to describe pure rotational spectra and allows the determination of the rotational constant and/or the moment of inertia.
Rovibronic transitions that contain both vibrational and rotational information are observable, particularly for small molecular systems.

B.text: Models exist that allow the prediction of the shape of chemicals about any bonding atom in a molecule.

alt.inorganic: Models exist that allow the prediction of the shape of chemicals about any bonding atom in molecules.

l3.text: Many molecules exist with more than one isomer, species that have the same chemical formula but have atoms arranged differently in space .

l4.text: Structural isomers have distinctly different connectivity between atoms.
Stereoisomers have the same connectivity between atoms but different spatial arrangements.

l3.text: Drawing Lewis structures is a common, simple model for describing atomic connectivity in molecules.

l4.text: Lewis structures are an important model that allows one to keep track of bonding and nonbonding pairs of electrons in molecules.
Simple Lewis structure-level models of molecules are sometimes inadequate, and one key place where shortcomings occur can be explained by the concept of resonance.
The octet rule is an important guide in the drawing of Lewis structures, but many molecules do not follow the octet rule.

l3.text: Using the VSEPR (valence shell electron-pair repulsion) model in conjunction with Lewis structures makes it possible to roughly predict many chemical structures.

l4.text: The VSEPR model allows for the general prediction of shape about an atomic center in a covalent molecule.

organic.text: Molecular shapes can be predicted using VSEPR theory, bond angles, and polarity.

Lewis structures are used to note the location of valence electrons in bonds and lone pairs. Lewis structures can be used to predict bond lengths, angles, and energies; in addition, overall three-dimensional geometry of molecules can be predicted.

Substituent groups on a cyclohexane molecule can be labeled as axial or equatorial when the molecule is in the chair conformation. Axial groups are parallel to an axis drawn through the center of the ring; equatorial groups stick out from the ring at an ~109.5° angle from the axial groups. Larger, more bulky substituents preferentially orient in the equatorial direction to reduce torsional and steric strain.
