Cyclic structures can be strained due to non-ideal bond angles and steric repulsion; these causes are respectively called bond-angle and tortional strain.
Two or more rings can be bridged or fused. Fused cycles share 2 atoms (1 bond) and bridged cycles share 3 or more atoms (2 or more bonds).
The molecular shape is especially important with regards to stereochemistry.

Stereocenters are atoms with four different substituents, and are labeled R or S, depending on the three-dimensional arrangement of the four substituents based on substituent group priority as defined by the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules.

Nitrogens can be chiral; however, interconversion of the lone pair keeps the nitrogen in constant racemization. If interconversion can be stopped, the nitrogen can be chiral (the lone pair receives lowest Cahn– Ingold–Prelog priority when assigning R or S).
Alkenes can be labeled as terminal or internal. Likewise, through Cahn– Ingold–Prelog rules, E (trans) or Z (cis) isomers are used to identify the arrangement of the priority groups on alkenes.
Diels–Alder products can be labeled endo or exo, depending on the orientation of substituent groups in the product.

inorganic.text: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory is used to predict the arrangement of groups around a central atom based on steric repulsions between bonding and nonbonding electron domains.
Bonding and nonbonding electron domains will adopt a geometric orientation to minimize steric repulsion between domains.
Lone pairs derived from s and p orbitals are more sterically active than bonding domains, and will cause a decrease in the observed bond angles compared to the idealized geometry.
Chelating ligands may cause a distortion from the idealized geometry predicted by VSEPR.
Multiple bonds will cause distortions from ideal VSEPR geometries.
Deviations from idealized VSEPR geometries are observed in compounds containing diverse ligands due to electronegativity and size differences.
Wade's rules can be used to predict the structures of cluster compounds from cluster valence electron counts.
The isolobal concept can be used to determine the cluster valence electron count for a particular vertex in a polyhedral cluster.
Structures of clusters are generated by removing vertexes from or adding capping vertices to parent closo-deltahedra.
Peripheral ligands can coordinate to cluster compounds in terminal or bridging modes.

The Jemmis, or mno, classification scheme is a more involved electron counting scheme that can be used to predict the structures of a variety of cluster and related compounds of the main group and transition elements.

physical.text: Shapes of molecules dictate the point-group symmetry.
Point groups are generally identified by determining all symmetry elements present within a molecule.
High levels of symmetry can be reduced by replacing a single atom in the molecule, such as the relative symmetry of a methyl-halogen versus methane.
Orbital hybridization is sometimes used with simple bonding models to help explain the approximate shape about a given atom.
Rough estimates of shape provided by VSEPR theory can be used to motivate the use of hybrid orbitals to describe bonding in many small molecules.
The shape of a molecule is determined by the lowest energy total molecular wavefunction.
Within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, the nuclei of a molecule move within the electrostatic field determined by the electronic wavefunction.
Minimization methods generally maintain the symmetry of the molecule as dictated by the shape of the initial guess structure.

C.text: Theoretical models are capable of providing detailed structure for whole molecules based on energy minimization methods.

alt.organic: Theoretical models are capable of providing detail structure for whole molecules based on energy minimization methods.
alt.inorganic: Theoretical models are capable of providing detail structure for whole molecules based on energy minimization methods.
alt.physical: Theoretical models are capable of providing detailed structures for whole molecules based on energy minimization methods.

organic.text: Molecular modeling computer programs can provide information about structures, and are predicated on these theoretical models.

inorganic.text: Many computational methods exist for predicting the geometries of molecules based on minimization of energies.
Molecular mechanics calculations model bond stretches in molecules using a ball-and-spring approach.
Ab initio methods calculate orbitals and energies for a given set of nuclear coordinates from first principles.
Semi-empirical methods calculate orbitals and energies for a given set of nuclear coordinates based on fitting to experimental data.

In self-consistent field approaches, initial approximations of symmetry adapted linear combinations of orbitals are perturbed in a step-wise fashion until a consistent set of orbitals with minimized energies are obtained.
The Hartree-Fock method approximates the Schrödinger equation by using approximations to represent electron-electron repulsions.
Density functional theory is an alternative to the Schrödinger equation that works by acting on the electron density to determine the energy of a system rather than the wavefunction.

physical.text: Quantum mechanical calculations can use energy minimization to determine the molecular properties.
Energy minimization adjusts the nuclear coordinates within the field of the electronic wavefunction to minimize the energy.
Minimum energy structures are confirmed to be minima by checking the Hessian, the second derivative matrix.

Energy minimization can be used with any level of theory and improved results generally arise from using large basis sets along with some form of correlation energy in the quantum mechanical calculations.
Spectroscopic observations lend credibility to computational methods.
Structural details of molecules can be obtained through several experimental methods, and used to check the results of computational minimization in many cases of interest.
Quantum calculations can also provide information about the potential energy of geometries that are not minima.
Minimization methods work by finding a zero gradient (first derivative matrix).
Not all zero gradient locations on a potential energy surface are the global minimum of potential energy.

Energy minimization methods can also find transition states (by maximizing one degree of freedom), which can be an important way that computational methods contribute to the understanding of reactions and reaction dynamics.

D.text: Symmetry, based on geometry, plays an important role in how atoms interact within molecules and how molecules are observed in many experiments.

organic.text: Spectroscopy is related to the symmetry of the molecules being studied.
Symmetry impacts the visibility of some absorption peaks in an infrared spectrum.
The number of infrared spectrum peaks increase with the decrease of a molecule’s symmetry.
The symmetry of molecules may result in some 1H or 13C atoms having identical NMR characteristics (chemical shift and coupling patterns).
Equivalent protons do not couple with each other.

inorganic.text: The symmetry of a molecule is denoted by a point group classification.

A symmetry operation is a transformation performed on an object that results in an orientation that is indistinguishable from the original. Symmetry operations are classified as proper rotations (including the identity operation) and improper rotations/roto- reflections/roto-inversions (including reflection and inversion operations).
A symmetry element is a point, plane, or axis about which a symmetry operation is performed with respect to.

The point group of a molecule or object is the complete set of symmetry operations that render the molecule into an indistinguishable configuration. Flowcharts have been designed to assist in point group assignment.
Space groups combine point group operations with translational symmetry and are used to describe symmetry in 3 dimensional structures such as crystalline compounds.

Each space group is based upon one of 7 different Bravais lattices, each defined by the relationships of the side lengths and angles of the unit cell. Examples include cubic, rhombohedral, and orthorhombic.
There are 230 total possible space groups.
A representation describes how orbitals or vibrational modes of the atoms within a molecule transform when subjected to the symmetry operations contained within the point group of the molecule.
Many basis sets involve sets of orbitals or vibrations that transform as a reducible representation, which can be expressed as the sum of irreducible representations.
A character table summarizes the irreducible representations for a point group.
A symmetry operation can be expressed as a transformation matrix operating on the coordinates of a molecule or object. The character of the matrix is the sum of its diagonal elements.
The projection operator method can be used to generate symmetry adapted linear combinations of orbitals or vibrations that correspond to an irreducible representation.
Molecular symmetry can be used to interpret spectroscopic results.
Symmetry analysis of stretching and bending motions within a molecule can be used to predict the number of vibrational modes observable in infrared and Raman spectroscopies.
Identification of symmetry equivalent atoms within a molecule can be used to predict the number of chemical shifts observed in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.

Molecular term symbols can be derived from symmetry analysis and are used to describe the possible electronic states within a molecule. Term symbols are used in the interpretation and analysis of electronic spectra of molecules. Energies corresponding to specific terms are graphically depicted using Orgel and Tanabe-Sugano diagrams.
Selection rules based on symmetry considerations determine which transitions are allowed in a spectroscopic technique.
Certain physical properties of molecules can readily discerned from symmetry analysis.
Chiral molecules do not possess improper symmetry elements.
Whether or not a molecule is polar can be discerned from analysis of its point group.

physical.text: Molecular term symbols include information about symmetry.
In molecular term symbols, the presence or absence of inversion symmetry is indicated by the gerade/ungerade symbol.
Group theory allows description of symmetry, symmetry governs behaviors and selection rules.
Once determined, the symmetry elements for a molecule can be used to determine what vibrations are IR or Raman active.
The role of symmetry in an electronic wavefunction is captured by the parity.
For systems that have inversion symmetry, the wavefunctions can be assigned parity depending on whether their value is the same or opposite signed upon carrying out an inversion.

E.text: Three-dimensional structures may give rise to chirality, which can play an important role in observed chemical and physical properties.

alt.inorganic: Three dimensional structures may give rise to chirality isomerism which can play an important role in observed chemical and physical properties.
alt.physical: Three dimensional structures may give rise to chirality which can play an important role in observed chemical properties.

organic.text: Enantiomers and diastereomers describe structural relationships between stereoisomers.
Isomers are two or more molecules of the same molecular formula, but differ in either connectivity (i.e., constitutional isomers) or three- dimensional arrangement (i.e., stereoisomers).

Chiral compounds are nonsuperimposable on their mirror image. Chiral compounds lack an internal mirror plane; achiral compounds do have an internal mirror plane. A special class of achiral compounds is called meso: these compounds contain chiral centers; however, the presence of an internal mirror plane makes the overall molecule achiral.
Stereoisomers include cis (same) or trans (opposite) relationships of substituents; these terms are commonly used when describing substituents on cyclic alkene compounds.
Enantiomers are two stereoisomers that are nonsuperimposable mirror images of each other.
Diastereomers are two stereoisomers of the same connectivity, but are nonsuperimposable and nonmirror images.
Reactions can be regiospecific, regioselective, stereospecific, stereoselective, or neither.

Markovnikov’s rule—Addition across an alkene involves the addition of the electrophile to the least substituted carbon, resulting in a stable carbocation intermediate, followed by the attack of the nucleophile to the residual carbocation. Anti-Markovnikov reactions proceed via a different mechanism and add the nucleophile at the least substituted carbon.
Zaitsev’s rule—Using a nonsterically hindered base, the major product of an alkene forming reaction is the most highly substituted (non- hydrogen) alkene.
Hofmann’s Rule—Using a sterically hindered base, the major product of an alkene forming reaction is the least substituted (nonhydrogen) alkene.

Stereospecific reactions result in the formation of a single stereocenter configuration (R or S). SN2 reactions are stereospecific, resulting in inversion of the stereocenter at the site of displacement.
Stereoselective reactions preferentially form one stereoisomer in a greater quantity than another possible stereoisomer.
The stereochemistry of the starting material and reactive intermediates can affect the stereochemistry of the product(s).
Achiral starting materials give a racemic mixture of products or an achiral product (such as a meso compound).
The three-dimensional structure of molecules can lead to different transition states, reaction intermediates, and different isomeric products of a reaction.
Stereoisomers may be observed with polarized light; diastereomers may be separated based on differences in their physical properties.

Chiral compounds are optically active, meaning they rotate plane- polarized light. Specific rotation of a single enantiomer is an experimentally determined value (using a polarimeter) that can in turn be used as a constant to determine enantiomeric excess (i.e., optical purity).
A racemic mixture is a 1:1 mixture of enantiomers. Enantiomers can be separated from each other through a process called resolution.
Meso compounds contain two or more stereocenters, but have an internal mirror plane and therefore are achiral (optically inactive).

inorganic.text: Many coordination numbers and geometries are possible for coordination compounds.

Conformational isomers are possible when geometric isomers can be converted by rotations or bends of the bonds in a molecule. For example, four-coordinate complexes may adopt tetrahedral or square planar geometries, and five coordinate complexes can adopt trigonal bipyramidal or square pyramidal geometries. Fluxional processes usually involve mechanisms where one conformational isomer is converted to the other.
Octahedral and tetrahedral coordination are by far the most common for transition metals.
Stereoisomers have different geometric arrangements with the same bonds.
Different types of common isomers exist for square planar and octahedral complexes, including cis/trans, mer/fac, and Λ/Δ.
Optical isomers are stereoisomers that rotate polarized light differently.
Complexes containing chelating groups can often have optical isomers. An example is Δ/Λ isomerism in octahedral complexes.
Enantiomers are identical except they are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
Polymorphism is very common in solid state structures of inorganic compounds.
Polymorphs have different space groups and therefore different X-ray diffraction patterns.
Chiral catalysts can be used control the stereochemistry of products of chemical reactions.
Chiral ligands allow coordination of substrate in only one configuration.
Reaction on that single bound configuration yields, ideally, a single stereoisomeric product.

Constitutional isomers exist in coordination compounds having the same formula but different ligands attached to the central atom. Examples include solvent/hydrate isomers, ionization isomers, and coordination isomers. Linkage and ambidentate isomerism occurs when the same ligand can have different binding modes.
Several techniques exist for separation and resolution of mixtures of isomers.
Many geometric isomers possess different physical properties, such as dipole moment, that allow for resolution to be accomplished using physical techniques.
Optical isomers must be resolved using chemical techniques, such as selective precipitation with other optically active counterions or separation on a column with a chiral resolving agent.
Optical isomers can be identified in solution using optical rotary dispersion or circular dichroism.

physical.text: Chirality can be observed because optical rotation of light is sensitive to its existence.
Optical rotation is a macroscopic property that can be observed with collections of a molecule that has a chiral center.
The specific rotation is the quantity that measures the extent to which a particular molecule will rotate plane polarized light.

F.text: Reactions of molecules can often be understood in terms of subsets of atoms, called functional groups.

l3.text: Chemical formulas often designate the existence of functional groups in a molecule by listing those atoms as a group.

l4.text: The ability to identify functional groups in a molecule is an important skill for using representations.
An important reason to define functional groups is that they allow the prediction of reactivity patterns.

l3.text: Functional groups are important in acid–base chemistry and strengths of acids and bases can often be understood in terms of functional groups.

l4.text: The strengths of oxoacids follow identifiable trends.

organic.text: The reactivity of functional groups is related to their structures.
Functional groups can be stabilized or destabilized by resonance and inductive effects.

inorganic.text: Many types of ligands are found in coordination and organometallic compounds, and these ligands are typically classified based on the various types of bonding interactions with metal atoms.
"σ only" ligands do not undergo pi bonding with metal centers.

π donor ligands have filled orbitals having π symmetry that are capable of donating electrons to a metal center. Examples of pi donor ligands include alkylidenes and many ligands containing heteroatom donor atoms.

π acceptor ligands have low lying empty orbitals of π symmetry that are capable of accepting electron density from a metal center. Carbon monoxide is the prototypical πacceptor ligand, and other examples include nitrosyl, dihydrogen, alkene, alkyne, and neutral carbenes.
Extended π systems containing chains and rings can often have interactions with metals that span several atoms. Hapticity is used to designate the different binding modes of these ligands.
The same ligand may be involved in multiple bonding interactions in multiple binding modes. Common examples include bridging carbonyl groups and agostic interactions.
The isolobal concept can be used to rationalize the reactivity of ligands having similar electronic structures.
Isolobal analogies apply to fragments of tetrahedral, octahedral, and square planar compounds that contain analogous valence electron counts and degrees of coordinative unsaturation.

Pseudohalogens have electronic structures similar to the halogens and form analogous compounds. Examples of pseudohalogens include hydrogen atoms, the cyanogen radical, and the organometallic Mn(CO)5 fragment.
Synthetic strategies often employ interchanging isolobal fragments with each other in cluster molecules, organometallic compounds, and organic molecules. (e.g. N: for C-H in pyridine vs. benzene)
Reactivity of compounds can often be rationalized by taking the electronic and steric effects of the ligands present.
One common example is the alteration of activity of organometallic compounds utilizing phosphine ligands with different alkyl groups that affect the cone angle and electron donor/acceptor properties.
The basicity of amines can be enhanced by electron donating substituents and reduced by electron withdrawing substituents.

physical.text: Some computational methods rely on knowledge of functional groups or other small pieces of molecules to build a big picture.
Quantum-structure activity relationships (QSAR) can be enumerated to link the presence of functional groups to pharmacological activity for molecules.
Functional groups often have consistency of vibrational characteristics that are useful in spectroscopic characterization.
For polyatomic systems, vibrational normal modes are often relatable to certain bonding motifs which allow the identification of the presence of those motifs in IR spectra.

G.text: Periodic trends among elements can be used to organize the understanding of structure and function for related chemical compounds.

alt.organic: Many solid state, extended systems exist and geometric structures play an important role in understanding the properties of these systems.

l3.text: Atoms and ionic sizes influence how solids, such as metals or ionic salts, pack into condensed structures.

l4.text: Lattice energy of ionic substances is influenced by the size of the ions involved; therefore, periodic trends in ionic sizes can predict trends in lattice energy.

inorganic.text: Elements within the same group form binary oxides, hydrides, and halides having the same formula.
Nonstoichiometric compounds are often formed by metals capable of achieving multiple oxidation states (transition metals, lower p-block elements).
Elements with a diagonal relationship on the periodic table are often similar in size and can substitute for each other in solid state compounds.
The lanthanide contraction causes the 4d and 5d elements to have similar sizes and chemical properties.
The inert pair effect causes metals in the lower rows of the p-block to form compounds in oxidation states that are two less than the group valence.
Metals and nonmetals display characteristic differences in the compounds that they form.
Metals usually occur as cations in binary ionic compounds and nonmetals typically occur as anions.

The variation of bonds in the X-O-H system displays a systematic trend as you proceed through a group on the periodic table, with smaller effective nuclear charges on X favoring the strength of the O-H bond and larger effective nuclear charges resulting in stronger X-O bonds. This trend causes elements to be stable as aqua ions, hydroxo compounds, and oxoanions depending on their position in the periodic table.
The chemistry and structures of interhalogen compounds follows a distinct periodic trend.
Variation in atomic size results in higher coordination numbers as you move down the periodic table.

Synthesis of interhalogens is accomplished via oxidation of the less oxidizing element with the more oxidizing element. The structures of the resulting compounds contain the less oxidizing element as the central atom.
Groups of atoms with similar valence electron counts tend to form compounds with analogous structures.
Many structural analogs to compounds containing carbon-carbon bonds have been replicated with boron-nitrogen counterparts.
Compounds with structures analogous to silicon and diamond can be formed by 1:1 mixtures of III/V and II/VI elements.

physical.text: Many patterns for atomic properties can be explained using the quantum model of the atom.
Atomic size periodicity is largely described by the radial component of the atomic wavefunction.

H.text: Many solid state, extended systems exist, and geometric structures play an important role in understanding the properties of these systems.

l3.text: Bonding types in solids include metallic bonding, ionic, and covalent network.

l4.text: Many materials form crystalline solids that can be understood in terms of repeating (via translational symmetry) many units of a structure, called the unit cell.
Basic understanding of cubic unit cells provides a key example of this phenomenon, and should include some quantitative aspects.
Metals, ionic solids, covalent network solids, and molecular solids have distinctive macroscopic properties that allow them to be categorized.

l3.text: Macromolecules exist and their properties are often understandable in terms of the units that comprise them.

l4.text: Polymers are macromolecules that are synthesized by repeated incorporation of a limited number of monomer units.
Polymer properties are strongly influenced by their structures, including whether or not they are highly “branched”.
Natural polymers, such as polypeptides and polysaccharides, are important in biological chemistry.

l3.text: The practical implications of solid and extended systems are diverse and often focus on the availability of a specific element within a compound.

l4.text: Refining of metal ores is an important practical chemical reaction that is normally designed to obtain a specific element.
Chemical fertilizers may be small molecules, but are often ionic substances designed to deliver a specific element to crops.

inorganic.text: Solids consist of extended structures of atoms, molecules, or ions that are packed together in a variety of different motifs. The structure of a crystalline solid is described by its unit cell.

A crystal lattice is a a regular repeated three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, ions, or molecules. The seven crystal systems are defined by restrictions placed on their lattice parameters. Addition of centering operations results in the fourteen possible Bravais lattices. Many elements adopt body centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonally closest packed structures in the solid state under standard conditions.
The contents of the unit cell can be used to calculate the empirical formula.
The density of the unit cell can be used to estimate the density of the bulk material.
The structures of solid state compounds are often viewed as interconnected nets of polyhedra.
The symmetry of a unit cell is specified by its space group.
Many elements adopt body centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonally closest packed structures in the solid state under standard conditions.
The structures of ionic compounds can be visualized as smaller ions occupying the empty spaces in a lattice of the larger ions.
The structures of many simple binary ionic solids consist of smaller ions occupying the cubic, octahedral, and tetrahedral holes in a parent lattice of larger ions.
Binary ionic compounds with 1:1 stoichiometry often adopt the cesium chloride, rock salt, sphalerite, or Wurtzite structures.
Binary ionic compounds with 1:2 or 2:1 stoichiometries often adopt the fluorite, cadmium iodide, rutile, or antifluorite structures
More complex structures include the perovskite and spinel structures.
Radius ratios can be used to predict the structure adopted by binary compounds.
Many interesting properties of solids are due to the presence of defects or atoms on interstitial sites.
Solid solutions such as alloys are formed from heteroatoms occupying interstitial sites or substituting for atomic positions in the parent structure.
Nanomaterials can have zero, one, two, and three dimensional structures.
Nanoparticles such as quantum dots have electronic and optical properties that vary with particle size.
One dimensional nanostructures include carbon nanotubes and related materials.
Two dimensional nanostructures include graphene, self-assembled monolayers, and other layer materials.
Metal-organic frameworks synthesized using coordination chemistry are an example of a three-dimensional nanostructured material.
Many elements of the p-block have allotropes with a wide variation in their solid-state structures.
B, C, O, P, S, Sb, As, Se, Sn and Po have allotropes.
Many solid compounds have layered structures and exhibit useful properties.
Graphite intercalation compounds contain metal ions inserted between graphite sheets. Lithium intercalated graphite is used in lithium ion batteries.
Many oxides have layered structures. Examples include oxides of the late transition metals and aluminosilicate clays.
Layered sulfides are formed by early transition metals.
Silicates and their derived compounds have a wide variety of 1, 2, and 3 dimensional structures. The type of structure observed varies with the degree of condensation.
Zeolites are aluminosilicates that have porous 3 dimensional structures.
Many high temperature superconductors have crystal structures related to perovskite.
The archetype HTC Superconductor is YBa2Cu3O6.7, which is a 2-dimensional cuprate.

physical.text: Surface sites on solids and their structures play key roles in heterogeneous catalysis on solids.
Surfaces are often labeled using Miller indices.
Atoms on surfaces may reorganize relative to the bulk unit cells, and these structures are labeled with their reconstruction geometry in addition to the Miller indices.
Surfaces break translational symmetry and therefore have surface energy states that are not part of the bulk solid energy bands.
Catalysis sites may occur at steps on the surface or at defect sites on the surface.
Crystalline solids have translational symmetry and can be understood in terms of unit cells and lattice planes.
There are seven crystal systems into which all unit cells can be categorized based on rotational symmetry.
Cubic unit cells serve as a common example for crystalline systems and can be further categorized as primitive cubic, body-centered cubic or face-centered cubic.
Lattice planes are important to identify in terms of diffraction based observation of crystal structures.
Diffraction off crystal planes is understood using Bragg's Law.
All systems become solids at 0 K and perfect crystals at 0 K have zero entropy.
The Nernst heat theorem indicates that S --> 0 for any perfectly ordered system undergoing a physical or chemical change that occurs as the T --> 0 K.
The third law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of all perfect crystalline substances is 0 at 0 K.
The physical properties of solids can be measured and exploited in applications of technology.
Mechanical properties, such as strain and stress, play an important role in determining uses for solid materials.
The temperature dependence of electrical conductivity can be used to classify solid materials as insulators, conductors, semiconductors or superconductors.
The magnetic behavior of solid systems can often be understood in terms of behavior, such as diamagnetism or paramagnetism, of the constituted atoms or molecules.

IV.title: Intermolecular Interactions
IV.text: Intermolecular Interactions: Intermolecular forces—electrostatic forces between molecules—dictate the physical behavior of matter.

A.text: Intermolecular forces are generally weaker, on an individual basis, than chemical bonds, but the presence of many such interactions may lead to overall strong interactions.

l3.text: Substances exist as a gas at room temperature when intermolecular forces are weak. Models for gas behavior can be quite general because these forces are small—the most common is the ideal gas model.

l4.text: Gases have physical properties that are often independent of the identity of the gas; the conceptual understanding of the relationships between these properties is important.
Pressure is a key variable in describing gases; over time there have been many ways that the measurement of pressure has been carried out, leading to an array of units for measuring pressure.
The quantitative relationships between properties of gases are summarized for most systems using the ideal gas law.
Gases in mixtures generally act as independent species that can be quantitatively described using partial pressure.

l3.text: Properties that depend on intermolecular forces include phase, vapor pressure, surface tension, etc.

l4.text: Graphical summaries of the phase behavior of one-component systems, called phase diagrams, are useful tools for a compact understanding of the phase behavior of these systems.
For pure substances, quantitative measurement of physical properties may allow the identification of the substance.
Adhesion, cohesion, surface tension, and vapor pressure are observable bulk properties that rely on the same basic intermolecular forces present in the liquid.

l3.text: When intermolecular forces only are overcome (broken ), the chemical nature of the small molecules is not altered and the process is called a physical change.

l4.text: When a phase change occurs, the molecules involved do not change as they change phases.

Physical and chemical changes are most easily distinguished at the atomic or molecular scale. If the molecules involved in the process do not change, it is a physical change. Otherwise it is a chemical change.

For a given pure substance, the temperature at which a phase change occurs is a characteristic of that substance. Temperature does not change when a phase change is occurring, even though energy flow as heat is occurring.

organic.text: Intermolecular forces play a role in spectroscopy and the physical properties displayed by molecules.
Hydrogen bonding causes peak broadening in both infrared and NMR spectroscopy.
Intermolecular forces can lead to differences in solubility and melting and boiling points, and change the reactivity in polar versus nonpolar solvents.
Hydrogen bonding is a particularly important intermolecular force in organic chemistry.

inorganic.text: The melting point and boiling points of the halogens and noble gases display a periodic trend that reflects the magnitudes of the dispersion forces present.
Many self-assembly processes involve formation of intermolecular forces between molecules.
Langmuir-Blodgett films are self-assembled monolayers that are physisorbed to a substrate.
The structures of the host framework in many clathrates consist of hydrogen bonded molecules.

physical.text: The van der Waals radius is a convenient length scale for consideration of intermolecular forces.
In some models, the volume of atomic/molecular particles can be neglected, but it is often needed and the van der Waals radius provides an estimate of the volume.
The van der Waals radius can be defined as the contact distance between non-bonded atoms in molecules (or atoms) that are touching.

van der Waals radii can be estimated several ways including, measuring the critical volume of a gas, determining atomic spacing between non-bonded atoms in a crystal or via properties such as polarizability or refractivity.
The van der Waals surface is a rough estimate of the extent of a molecule and may be thought of as the surface at which the molecule interacts with other molecules.
Models of intermolecular forces include repulsive interactions.
While intermolecular forces are attractive at modest distances, they become repulsive as particles move too close together.
Mathematical models of intermolecular forces must capture both attraction and repulsion, and one example is the Lennard-Jones potential.
Gases characteristically exhibit weak intermolecular forces, large distances between particles or both.
Responses of gas volumes to changes in either temperature or pressure can be written as a total differential which may be simplified by defining thermal expansivity and isothermal compressibility.
One key way that real gases differ from ideal gases is that intermolecular forces become important.
Ideal gases provide a model system where intermolecular forces are so small they can be neglected.
As pressure approaches zero, all gases approach ideal gas behavior.
Because intermolecular forces can be neglected, the chemical identity of an ideal gas is not needed to describe its behavior.
Joule's Law defines how energy is independent of volume for ideal gases.
Equations of state describe relationships between macroscopic variables that arise from interactions of particles (gas laws).
The ideal gas equation of state relates P, V, n, and T in the familiar equation, PV=nRT.
Several examples of equations of state, such as the van der Waals equation and the Redlich- Kwong equation, have been devised to describe real gases.

B.text: For large molecules, intermolecular forces may occur between different regions of the molecule. In these cases, they are sometimes termed noncovalent forces.

alt.inorganic: For large molecules, intermolecular forces may occur between different regions of the molecule. In these cases, they are sometimes termed non-covalent forces.
alt.physical: For large molecules, intermolecular forces may occur between different regions of the molecule. In these cases, they are sometimes termed non-covalent forces.

l3.text: Macromolecules, including synthetics polymers and biochemical molecules , are examples of systems where nonbonding forces occur between atoms in the same large molecule.

l4.text: The specificity of base pairing in DNA and RNA is associated with hydrogen bonding interactions between nucleotide bases on opposite strands of the system.

organic.text: Noncovalent forces can play a role for compounds that disperse hydrophobic molecules or ions into aqueous layers.
For large molecules such as polymers, proteins, and DNA, intermolecular forces can affect their binding strength, and secondary and tertiary structure.

inorganic.text: Hydrogen bonding may play a role in the interaction between metal centers and ligands.
Intermolecular forces exist between crystalline and amorphous sub-domains in block copolymers.
Hydrogen bonding is the primary force involved in the secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structures of biomolecules.

physical.text: Large-scale structures of proteins are dictated by non-covalent forces.
Interactions between atoms within a large molecule that are not directly bonded are referred to as non-covalent forces.
The presence of electronegative atoms in side chains on certain peptide residues, plays a key role in the type of non-covalent forces they possess.
Both secondary and tertiary structures of proteins depend on non-covalent forces.
Large molecules, such as proteins, are often described in terms of possessing regions that are hydrophilic or hydrophobic.
Hydrophobic regions of proteins predominantly have non-polar residues while hydrophilic regions have predominantly polar residues.
Water soluble proteins will have hydrophilic regions on their exterior surfaces and membrane proteins will have hydrophobic regions that interact with the lipid bilayers.
Intermolecular interactions of lipids can lead to bilayer or micelle formation.
Lipids have both polar and non-polar regions and both of them tend to congregate when enough of the molecules are present.
Cell membranes are an important example of bilayers.
Langmuir-Blodgett films can be made in the laboratory and approximate important bilayer structures of lipids.

C.text: Intermolecular forces can be categorized based on the permanence and structural details of the dipoles involved.

l3.text: Key intermolecular forces include dispersion, dipole–dipole, and hydrogen bonding.

l4.text: All common intermolecular forces can be understood in terms of models that invoke either permanent or instantaneous dipole moments.

Forces are present between molecules, and the categories of these forces (dispersion, dipole–dipole, and hydrogen bonding in particular) are important organizational ideas for conceptualizing physical properties of chemical systems.
Hydrogen bonding is a specialized form of intermolecular interaction that is important in the physical properties of water and in the intermolecular forces present in many living systems.

l3.text: VSEPR structure, coupled with concepts of bond dipoles, can be used to determine the presence of a permanent dipole.

l4.text: In covalent bonding, electron-pair sharing is not always equitable and the model of electronegativity differences allows one to explain when polar covalent bonds will form.
Permanent molecular dipoles may be inferred qualitatively by considering vector addition of bond dipoles and the geometries predicted via the VSEPR model.

organic.text: Intermolecular interactions can play a role in how molecules collide.

inorganic.text: Intermolecular forces can be classified as London dispersion, dipole-dipole, or hydrogen bonding based on the magnitudes of the dipole moments involved.
Polarization of an atom's electron cloud can arise from the presence of nearby charges or dipoles.
Ion-dipole, ion-induced dipole, and dipole-induced dipole are interactions formed between different species.

physical.text: A bond dipole arises when bonding atoms have different electronegativities.

While there are several scales for electronegativity, all of them seek to quantify the tendency of electrons to be drawn towards the nucleus of atoms of different elements when connected by chemical bonds.
A bond dipole arises when the electrons shared between bonded atoms are, on average, closer to the atom with higher electronegativity.
Bond dipoles are vector quantities and net molecular dipoles can be estimated by vector addition of bond dipoles.
The concept of polarizability represents an important physical model for explaining the origin and strength of intermolecular forces.
Polarizability is the proportionality constant that relates the induced dipole moment of a species as a result of an external electric field.
Dispersion interactions can often be described by the London formula.
Dispersion interactions arise from fleeting fluctuations in the electron distributions of one molecule inducing a momentary dipole in a nearby molecule.
Dispersion interactions are modeled as London forces which are proportional to polarizability squared over distance to the sixth power.
An external electric field can induce a dipole in a molecule and the size of the induced dipole is dictated by the polarizability.
Because electrons are not very massive and carry a charge, they will respond to external electric fields more dramatically than more massive nuclei which can result in an induced dipole.
Polarizability is a way to estimate the ability of the electron cloud of an atom or molecule to respond to an external field and the more diffuse the electron cloud the more polarizable.
Instantaneous dipoles are short-lived and arise from fluctuations in the electron distribution.

The dynamic nature of electrons leads to fluctuations in their distributions in atoms and molecules and such fluctuations can lead to an instantaneous (short lived) dipole even in systems that have no permanent dipole.
All atoms and molecules, even those with permanent dipoles, will have instantaneous dipoles (and therefore show dispersion).
Dipoles on neighboring molecules will tend to align in order to minimize the Coulomb interactions.
Dipole-dipole interactions will tend to lead to negative poles near positive poles among adjacent molecules.
The hydrogen bonding interaction is a specialized form of dipole-dipole forces that arises when H atoms are covalently bound to very electronegative atoms.

Hydrogen bonding arises when H atoms are covalently bonded to highly electronegative atoms, leading to a relatively large partial positive charge on the hydrogen that interacts with negative charge on a nearby molecule.

Hydrogen bonding can also be described using MO theory, where mixing of the covalent bond that includes H atoms interacts with the lone pair orbital on the neighboring atom leading to lower energy for the four electrons present in the interaction.
Hydrogen bonding plays a key role in biochemical systems such as DNA where it is responsible for bonding of base pairs on opposite backbones.

D.text: For condensed phases that are not structures of extended chemical bonds, the physical properties of the state are strongly influenced by the nature of the intermolecular forces.

l3.text: Solutions can be characterized as electrolytes or nonelectrolytes, based on whether or not they conduct electricity.

l4.text: The aqueous solutions of some solutes will conduct electricity.
The origin of electrical conductivity in aqueous solutions is the solvation of ions because separate cations and anions can carry current in solution.

l3.text: Solution behavior is largely dictated by intermolecular forces between solute and solvent molecules.

l4.text: In a solution, there is a key distinction between solute and solvent molecules.

Intermolecular forces play a critical role in understanding the solubility of materials in each other. In the case of water as a solvent, the concepts of hydrophilic and hydrophobic summarize these ideas fairly succinctly.

Solutions have physical properties different from pure substances, and many of these properties are not dependent on the nature of the solute. Conceptual and quantitative understanding of such colligative properties is important.
Gases are capable of dissolving in liquids and the extent of solubility is governed by the nature of the molecules involved and the pressure.
Mixtures can be characterized as homogeneous or heterogeneous.
Solutions are homogeneous mixtures that can be separated by physical means, such as distillation.
Solution behavior can have qualitative practical applications, such as water hardness.

l3.text: Quantitative understanding of solutions is usually predicated on calculations based on solute concentrations.

l4.text: Calculations using molarity of solutions—including determination of molarity, making a solution of known molarity, and reaction stoichiometry of solutions—are key quantitative skills.
Depending on the nature of the quantitative property being determined, different concentration units may be needed when carrying out calculations related to solutions.

organic.text: The type of intermolecular forces present in reactants can affect what solvent is used in a reaction.
The nature of intermolecular forces can have an effect on green chemistry because choices of solvent can be environmentally important.

inorganic.text: Many important properties of solids result from the intermolecular forces present.
Intermolecular forces can affect the packing and densities observed in solid state structures. A very common example is the effect of hydrogen bonding within the structure of ice.
Intermolecular forces play a role in solid solutions (solid-solid, solid-gas), often leading to clathrate or other types of host-guest structures.
Many macroscopic physical properties are dependent on the magnitude of the intermolecular forces present. Examples include phase, melting and boiling points, wetability, and contact angles.
Hydrogen bonding can be used to explain the anomalous properties of compounds containing H-O, H-N, and H-F bonds.
Phase diagrams can be used to represent the physical states of a substance present as a function of temperature and pressure.

physical.text: Phase equilibrium occurs when the chemical potential of two phases are equal.
The chemical potential is defined as the partial derivative of the Gibbs energy with respect to the amount of a chemical component of interest.
The phase rule, F=C-P+2, describes the variance (F) as it relates to the number of components and phases at equilibrium.
For pure substances, one component phase diagrams summarize temperature and pressure conditions for phase stability.
For a one component system with 2 phases present, the phase rule indicates only one variance, and thus temperature and pressure are related and form the coexistence curve.

The Clapeyron equation for the coexistence curve indicates that the ratio of the change in pressure to the change in temperature equals the specific latent heat divided by temperature times the change in specific volume.
The relative sizes of ΔH(vaporization), ΔH(fusion) and ΔH(sublimation) reflect the extent to which intermolecular forces are altered in the phase change.
Vaporization must overcome intermolecular interactions, so ΔH(vaporization) is a greater magnitude than ΔH(fusion).
Because enthalpy is a state function, the ΔH(sublimation) = ΔH(vaporization) + ΔH(fusion)
Properties such as vapor pressure, viscosity and surface tension can be understood in terms of intermolecular forces.
Macroscopically observed physical properties are manifestations of motions of molecules and are therefore dependent on molecular scale intermolecular interactions.
Vapor pressure is measured when dynamic equilibrium is reached between gas and liquid phases at a given temperature and stronger intermolecular forces will lead to lower vapor pressures.
Viscosity is a measure of the flux of momentum of a fluid system and can be conceptualized as the resistance to flow, which will increase as intermolecular forces increase.

Surface tension generally increases with increasing intermolecular forces and is the proportionality constant between the infinitesimal work needed to make an infinitesimal change in the surface area of a substance.
The Clausius-Clapeyron equation describes phase equilibrium in terms of macroscopic variables.

Two reasonable assumptions (that the molar volume of a gas is much larger than that of a liquid and gases can be described as perfect gases) allow the simplification of the coexistence curve between liquids and gases into the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
The Clausius-Clapeyron equation can be used to estimate the heat of vaporization by measuring vapor pressure at two different temperatures.
Miscibility of two liquids is dependent on the relative magnitudes of intermolecular forces of the pure liquids.
Miscibility refers to the mixing of two, nonreactive, liquids, which will typically have similar strengths of intermolecular interactions.
Liquids that have significant differences in intermolecular forces, such as one polar and one non-polar liquid, will tend to be immiscible.
The partial molar volume describes changes in total volume when liquids are mixed.
Ideal solutions are characterized by Raoult's Law and may form between miscible liquids.
Immiscible liquids may be mixed by the addition of surfactants.
Beyond the critical point, gases and liquids are best characterized as fluids.
The critical point may be visually estimated by observing the disappearance of a meniscus between a liquid and its vapor.
The Law of Corresponding States still holds beyond the critical point and is commonly expressed in terms of the reduced pressure and temperature.
Solutions often behave non-ideally.
Deviations from Raoult's Law are observed in non-ideal solutions but they will approach Raoult's Law at one extreme of mole fraction and Henry's Law at the other.
The observation of an azeotrope in an indicator of a non-ideal solution.

E.text: The energy consequences of chemical reactions that take place in condensed phases (solution) usually must include intermolecular forces to be correctly and completely explained.

alt.inorganic: The energy consequences of chemical reactions that take place in condensed phases (solution) usually must include intermolecular forces to be correctly/completely explained.
alt.physical: The energy consequences of chemical reactions that take place in condensed phases (solution) usually must include intermolecular forces to be correctly/completely explained.

l3.text: Heats of solution and other thermodynamic factors (entropy of solution formation) are key factors in the formation of a solution.

l4.text: Salts may dissolve either exothermically or endothermically.

organic.text: Choice of solvents is an important factor in organic reactions.
Changing solvent polarity can cause a change in mechanisms and lead to different products.

inorganic.text: Intermolecular forces play an important role in solution formation.
The relative magnitudes of the lattice energy and enthalpy of solvation play a role in solution formation.
Solvation shells result from intermolecular forces being created between solvent molecules and metal ions.
Hard-Soft Acid Base theory can be used to understand the effects of solvent ion interactions on solubility.
Intermolecular forces between solutions and surfaces or nanoparticles are important in many applications
Stronger intermolecular forces cause a solution to be more resistant to flow and have a higher viscosity.
The formation of colloids in solutions is dependent upon the interactions of the forming particle with surrounding ions and solvent molecules.
Interactions between solutions and surfaces lead to surface tension and wetting phenomena.
Solvation plays an important role in many chemical reactions.
Solvation of ions often causes different trends in acidity and basicity than observed in gas phase reactions.
Choice of solvent may affect the rate of electron transfer reactions, and can be used to isolate electrides and related compounds.
Intermolecular forces play an important role in outer sphere electron transfer reactions.

physical.text: Solvent effects may play a role in reaction outcomes for solution phase reactions.
Molecules in solution are able to encounter each other readily in order to react, so solution chemistry plays an important role in the study of reactivity.
Molecules in solution often have measurably different properties, such as the frequencies at which they absorb light (called solvatochromism).
Enthalpies of solvation of reactants and products may be quite different and therefore may have a substantial effect on the energetics of chemical reactions that take place in solution.
Ions often form in aqueous solutions and the energy consequences of interactions with solvent molecules may be critically important.
Ions in solution are solvated and the solvation free energy is a critical thermodynamic variable to understand this process.
Endothermic reactions in solutions may obtain part of the reaction energy from solvation.
Solvation of molecules is often exothermic and this can provide one source of energy for reactions that take place in solution.
Heats of formation for molecules differ between phases.
Condensed phases have more intermolecular interactions than gases, so heats of formation include the energy implications of those interactions.

V.title: Chemical Reactions
V.text: Chemical Reactions: Matter changes, forming products that have new chemical and physical properties.

A.text: In chemical changes, matter is conserved and this is the basis behind the ability to represent chemical change via a balanced chemical equation.

l3.text: A fundamental skill for chemistry is the ability to write a balanced chemical equation.

l4.text: Chemical equations represent reactions symbolically, so they must be balanced and accurately portray reactants and products.
Predicting the reactivity of chemicals is a key skill that ultimately involves the ability to write a balanced chemical equation.
In some cases, a net ionic equation (in which spectator ions are removed) is an important tool in describing a chemical or physical process.

l3.text: An important observation of reactions is that mass is conserved.

l4.text: Conservation of mass in a chemical reaction can be observed in the laboratory or calculated based on the masses of the reactants and products.
When laboratory reactions include gaseous substances (including components of air), the conservation of mass must account for the mass of gases consumed or produced in the reaction.

l3.text: The chemical equation provides key information for quantitative problem solving in stoichiometry.

l4.text: Stoichiometric calculations of chemical reactions are based on mole ratios determined from balanced chemical equations.
Because chemical equations provide mole ratios, stoichiometry problems involving masses require the use of molar mass conversions.
Because chemical equations provide mole ratios, stoichiometry problems involving solutions will require calculations using molarity and volume.
Because chemical equations provide mole ratios, stoichiometry problems involving gases require using the ideal gas law for most systems.

organic.text: Equations for organic reactions are rarely explicitly balanced; reagents are often indicated over the arrow rather than to the left of it.
Reaction yields are important.
Organic reactions can be carried out and techniques for maximizing yield and purity can be determined experimentally.
Series of reactions are used to produce larger and more complex molecules.

Retrosynthetic analysis is a process of identifying a set of reagents that could be used to obtain the desired target. This backwards thought process continues until all reagents are commercially available or methods are known for the formation of the desired reagents.

inorganic.text: The balanced equation for an oxidation-reduction reaction in acidic, basic, or neutral solutions can be obtained by combining the appropriate half reactions. Within the balanced equation, the number of electrons lost by the reducing agent is equal to the number of electrons gained by the oxidizing agent.

physical.text: The balanced chemical equation represents reaction ratios that are important in defining expressions such as equilibrium constants or rate equations.
Stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced chemical equation are incorporated into the rate expression so that a single rate is reported regardless of what reactant or product is observed.
For the purpose of thermodynamic equations, stoichiometry coefficients of reactants are considered negative and products positive.
The extent of a reaction, xi, can be defined in terms of differential changes in amounts of substances present.

For a reaction progressing from reactants to products, the differential change in number of moles of reactants is the negative value of the differential extent of reaction, xi, and the differential change in the number of moles of products is the positive value of xi.

B.text: Chemical change involves the breaking or forming of chemical bonds, or typically both.

alt.inorganic: Chemical change involves the breaking or forming of chemical bonds, or typically both

l3.text: Line structures of reactants and products can depict the changes in chemical bonds while conserving the number of atoms.

organic.text: The synthesis of organic compounds involves breaking and forming chemical bonds; energetics plays a part in which bonds are broken or formed.

When carbocations are formed as intermediates, the opportunity for rearrangement arises. Rearrangement is the process of a hydride or alkyl shift to produce a more stable carbocation intermediate. Only one shift is normally observed.

Radicals and cations are stable relative to each other such that tertiary are more stable than secondary, more stable than primary, more stable than methyl carbons. Allylic radical cations and anions are more stable than respective nonallylic radical cations and anions. Carbanions follow an inverse relative stability scale (i.e., methyl more stable than primary, etc.).
SN2 reactions at α-allylic and benzylic sites are faster because of transition state stabilization by the allyl or benzyl group.
The rate of SN1 and E1 reactions is dependent on the stability of the intermediate carbocation.

The rate of nucleophilic substitution is dependent on the leaving group ability, nucleophilicity, solvent polarity and proton donation ability, and steric hindrance at the site of leaving group displacement.
Carboxylic acid derivatives have differing degrees of susceptibility to nucleophilic attack such that amides are the least, then esters, anhydrides, with acid chlorides as the most reactive.

inorganic.text: The relative energies of the reactant frontier molecular orbitals determine whether a chemical reaction will occur, and if an occurring reaction will result in bond formation or electron transfer.
Reactions between molecules are symmetry forbidden when the participating orbitals do not have the same symmetry.

physical.text: Chemical change is conceptualized as reactants converting to products, and thus (at least partial) bond breaking is viewed as the initial step.
The activation energy of a reaction is associated the initial the breaking of bonds in the reactants or reactive intermediates.
Net reaction energies arise from the differences in energy inputs needed to break bonds in reactants versus energy released in bond formation of products.

Because enthalpy and free energy are state functions, calculation of the overall energy change for either thermodynamic variable need not consider what bonds break or form when, just total bonds are present in reactants and products.
Reaction energies may be estimated using tabulated average bond energies.
Reaction energy diagrams summarize the overall energetics along a single reaction coordinate.
Reaction energy diagrams present relative energy numbers showing the relationship between reactants, products and transitions states, as a function of an idealized reaction coordinate.
Potential energy diagrams provide more information than schematic reaction energy diagrams about the energy changes associated with reactions.
Potential energy diagrams still reduce the number of degrees of freedom shown for a reaction, but capture more information than single coordinate reaction energy diagrams.
Potential energy diagrams are capable of providing information about the energy associated with vibrational motions that are not along the overall reaction coordinate.

C.text: Chemical change can be observed at both the particulate and macroscopic levels, and models exist that allow the translation between these two levels of observation.

alt.organic: Chemical change can be observed at both the nanoscopic and macroscopic levels, and models exist that allow the translation between these two levels of observation.
alt.inorganic: Chemical change can be observed at both the particulate and macroscopic levels and models exist that allow the translation between these two levels of observation
alt.physical: Chemical change can be observed at both the nanoscopic and macroscopic levels and models exist that allow the translation between these two levels of observation.

l3.text: The visualization of chemical change at the particulate level enhances reasoning about stoichiometry and should include the concept of limiting reactants.

l4.text: Schematic drawings at the particulate level are capable of depicting the inherent stoichiometry of a reaction, including whether or not limiting reactants must be accounted for.

organic.text: Visualizing molecules and how they react is a key skill for organic chemistry.
Different representations can be used to depict the structure of organic molecules.

Molecular geometry is depicted using several representational typologies, each with a specific purpose of communicating molecular geometry, properties, and reactivity. Representations include dashed- wedged line drawings, skeletal structures, and Newman and Fischer projections.

inorganic.text: Scanning probe microscopy can be used to observe reactions occurring on surfaces.

physical.text: The Arrhenius equation provides a macroscopic method to estimate activation energy at the particulate level.
The Arrhenius equation is derived from the temperature dependence of the equilibrium constant along with the concept that at equilibrium the forward and reverse rates of reaction must be equal.
The thermodynamic origin of the Arrhenius equation means the change in internal energy of the system is needed and has been assigned as the value of the activation energy.
Molecular beam and spectroscopic methods can be used to observe reactions at the molecular level.
Under high vacuum conditions beams of reacting species can be created while controlling initial conditions and allowed to cross to allow reactions to occur and product states analyzed.
The monochromatic nature of laser light allows state specific spectroscopic probing of reactants or products to provide molecular level information about reactions.

D.text: There are a large number of possible chemical reactions, and categories have been devised to organize understanding of these reaction types.

l3.text: Categories such as synthesis, decomposition, and double displacement are used to describe reactions.

l4.text: Precipitation reactions are common examples of double displacement reactions.
Removal of waters of hydration of ionic solids is a category of reactions that finds common use in introductory chemistry laboratory classes.

l3.text: Oxidation–reduction reactions are important and include combustion.

l4.text: Oxidation–reduction reactions are important to chemistry and are sometimes referred to as “redox” reactions.
Being able to identify an oxidation–reduction reaction often involves assigning oxidation numbers.
The use of oxidation–reduction reactions as a category includes the concepts of oxidizing and reducing agents.
Completion and balancing of oxidation–reduction reactions requires both mass and charge balance and is often facilitated by the concept of a half-reaction.
The oxidation–reduction of metals (with each other or with acids) yields a measure of the activities of metals.
Materials that are combustible are undergoing oxidation –reduction reactions, often with oxygen in air.

l3.text: Acid–base neutralization is an important category of reaction s that includes several definitions.

l4.text: Categorizing reactions in terms of acid–base chemistry, particularly in water, is important.
Categorizing acid–base reactions can be facilitated by a basic understanding of acid–base strength.
The definition of an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor is a key concept of acid–base chemistry.
The definition of an acid as an electron-pair acceptor (Lewis acid) and a base as an electron-pair donor (Lewis base) is a key concept of acid– base chemistry.

organic.text: Addition, elimination, rearrangement, substitution, and redox reactions represent broad categories that are helpful in understanding organic reactions.
Key categories of organic reactions that students should be able to recognize include: SN1, SN2, E1, E2, and electrophilic and nucleophilic aromatic substitution.

Nucleophilic substitution occurs when a nucleophile displaces a leaving group. Bimolecular substitution (SN2) occurs via a concerted mechanism in which the nucleophile directly displaces the leaving group. Unimolecular substitution (SN1) occurs when the leaving group first leaves in a rate-determining step, followed by nucleophilic attack at the resultant carbocation intermediate.

Bimolecular (SN2) and unimolecular (SN1) nucleophilic substitution reactions compete with elimination reactions (E2 and E1, respectively). Preference for substitution or elimination is governed by steric hindrance and basicity of the reagent.

Elimination reactions (E2 and E1) occur via beta deprotonation to the site of the leaving group displacement. The resultant electron pair after deprotonation forms a π-bond with the carbon at the site of leaving group displacement. Elimination reactions occur in the presence of a strong base nucleophile.
SN1 reactions result in racemization (or near racemization) at the site of displacement due to the attack of the planar carbocation from above or below.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution is a reaction between an electrophile and an aromatic compound (electron-rich component). The electrophile replaces hydrogen on the aromatic species. Electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions include bromination, nitration, sulfonation, Friedel–Crafts alkylation, and acylation.
Nucleophilic substitution occurs via an addition–elimination or elimination–addition mechanism. Electrophilic substitution occurs exclusively via an addition-elimination mechanism.
Radical reactions, which show single electron movement, represent another broad category.

Radical reactions are regioselective, dependent on the stability of all possible reactive intermediates. More than one product is possible for a radical reaction; products (two or more) are labeled major or minor corresponding to predicted or observed relative yields.
Radical reactions follow a sequence of initiation, propagation, and termination steps.
It is important to recognize reaction conditions in an environmentally responsible (green) manner whenever possible.

inorganic.text: Many constructs involving atom and electron exchange have been developed to aid in our understanding of acid-base reactions.

In certain classification schemes, acids and bases are viewed as electron transfer between reactants. In the Lewis concept, the base donates an electron pair to the acid resulting in the formation of a coordinate covalent bond. The Usanovich concept involves electrons being transferred from the base to the acid in a reaction that forms a salt. Hard-soft acid base theory includes the effect of polarizability on the equilibrium position of Lewis acid-base reactions.

Acid base reactions can also be viewed as a transfer of an ionic species between the reactants. Examples include the Bronsted-Lowry definitions based on proton transfer and the Lux-Flood system based on oxide transfer reactions.

Autoionization reactions occur within many solvents to produce ionic products, and within solvent system classification schemes, acids and bases are defined as species that increase the concentrations of the cationic or anionic autoionization products, respectively, upon dissolution. The Arrhenius description is an example of a solvent system classification applied to aqueous solutions.
Oxidation-reduction reactions involve electron transfer between reactants to form products.
Reduction and oxidation processes result in a decrease and increase, respectively, of the oxidation states of the atoms involved.
An activity series can be used to predict whether a oxidation-reduction reaction will occur between two compounds.
Changes in oxidation states can be used to identify the reactants acting as oxidizing and reducing agents within oxidation/reduction reactions.

Many elements have a variety of accessible oxidation states in their compounds, and graphic representations are often used to aid in the understanding of the relative stability of these oxidation states under different reaction conditions. Examples include Latimer, Pourbaix, Frost, and Ellingham diagrams.
The reduction potential for a half reaction is related to the relative stabilities of the oxidation states of the reactants and products.

Disproportionation reactions are redox reactions involving a reactant in an intermediate oxidation state forming products in higher and lower oxidation states. Comproportionation reactions involve two reactants in different oxidation states reacting to form a product in a more stable intermediate oxidation state.

The reactions of organometallic compounds can be classified based on the electron count and coordination geometries of the reactants and products. Catalytic cycles involving organometallic species can be described using the terminology associated with these basic reaction types.

Oxidative addition reactions involve the addition of a reagent that increases the coordination number and decreases the oxidation state of the metal center. The reverse reaction is called reductive elimination.
Ligand association and dissociation reactions respectively increase or decrease the coordination number of a metal center without a change in oxidation state.

A migratory insertion usually involves a neutral ligand with a pi-system reacting with an anionic ligand to produce a new anionic ligand that has a new sigma-bond between the two. The reverse reaction is called an elimination reaction.
According to the Chauvin mechanism, alkene metathesis reactions involving alkylidene complexes typically proceed through a metallocyclobutyl intermediate.
Several reactions can be described as an attack of an outer sphere nucleophile or electrophile on a coordinated ligand.
The type of reaction(s) possible for an organometallic complex depend on the relative coordinative saturation/desaturation and valence electron count of the metal center.
Catalytic cycles involving organometallic complexes typically involve multiple bond breaking and formation reactions.
Double displacement, or metathesis, reactions between compounds involve an exchange of counterions between the reactants to form products.
Precipitation reactions produce an insoluble solid in the net ionic reaction.
Arrhenius acid-base reactions produce water as a product in the net ionic reaction.
Heterogenous processes often involve interactions of molecules with the surfaces of solids.
Physical adsorption, or physisorption, involves molecules being attracted to surface by van der Waals forces.
Chemical adsorption, or chemisorption, involves a species forming a chemical bond with a surface atom.
Surface migration allows chemisorbed species to move around on the solid surface.

Condensation reactions involve a combination of two molecules to form a larger molecule and release a much smaller molecule, such as water. Hydrolysis reactions involve reaction of water with a larger molecule to decompose it into smaller fragments.

physical.text: Molecularity provides an important characterization in the study of reactions and their rates.
Regardless of stoichiometric ratios, most individual reactions are either unimolecular or bimolecular.

E.text: Many chemical properties of elements follow periodic trends that can be used to strategically design reactions to achieve desired outcomes.

alt.organic: Chemical change can be controlled by choices of reactants, reaction conditions, or use of catalysts.

l3.text: With some exceptions, elements in a single group or row on the periodic table have reactivity trends that vary in predictable ways when reacting with water or air.

l4.text: Reactivity trends vary in predictable ways as you move down and to the right on the periodic table, with a few exceptions.

organic.text: Organic chemistry can be understood by studying the structure and reactivity of different functional groups. Reactions can be understood in collections by functional groups, collections including reactions leading to formation of functional groups, and reactions using the given functional group to form other functional groups. While key reactions of functional groups can be listed, such lists are not intended to be exhaustive within this map.
Key reactions of alkanes include combustion and free radical halogenation.
Key reactions of alkyl halides include SN1 and SN2 substitution, E1 and E2 elimination, and the formation of organometallic reagents.
Key reactions that include alkenes are reduction to alkanes, Diels– Alder, formation of alkyl halides, electrophilic addition, free radical reactions, and oxidative cleavage reactions.
Alkynes undergo many of the same reactions as alkenes, and can also be selectively reduced to cis- or trans-alkenes.
Key reactions of alcohols include oxidation to aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, conversion to a chloride using sulfonyl chloride, and dehydration to form alkenes.
Key reactions of ethers include their formation by the Williamson ether synthesis and their reduction to alkyl halides.

Epoxides are highly reactive heterocyclic compounds; their key reactions include their formation via peroxy acid conditions and stereoselective opening in the presence of a strong acid or nucleophile.

Aromatic systems display a fairly broad array of important reactions, including: electrophilic or nucleophilic substitution; the oxidation of benzyl hydrogens to ketones, aldehydes, and carboxylic acids; reduction of aromatic nitro groups; and reactions of atoms that are alpha to aromatic rings, such as oxidation.

Aldehydes and ketones undergo many of the same key reactions, including: conversion to acetals; reduction to a –CH2– group via imine intermediates; combination into alkenes using Wittig reagents; nucleophilic attack at the carbonyl carbon; aldol and Claisen (reactions that depend on the acidity of hydrogens on the carbon alpha to the carbonyl group); conversion to complex alcohols by nucleophilic attack of organomagnesium and organocuprates; reduction to alcohols by hydride donors or Grignard reagents; and alpha-substitutions via basic and acidic conditions.

Key reactions of carboxylic acids and their derivatives include: interconversion via an addition–elimination mechanism; conversion to ketones or aldehydes by nucleophilic attack by organomagnesium; organocuprates; decarboxylation at high temperatures when the carboxylic acid group is beta to carbonyl groups; and conversion to enols or enolates when beta-carbonyl groups are present.
Key reactions of amines include their formation via substitution chemistry and Hoffman elimination reactions.

Substituents on an aromatic ring either activate or deactivate the ring (i.e., increase or decrease the electron density and susceptibility to electrophilic attack). Also, substituents serve to direct the adding group to an ortho, para, or meta relationship to it via resonance (electronic effect) stabilization of mechanistic intermediates, or via inductive effects.
The control of a reaction is important and is affected by time, temperature, catalysts, and solvent, etc.

inorganic.text: The half reaction reduction potentials for the elements follow a periodic trend.
Metals on the left side of the periodic table are strong reducing agents and nonmetals on the right side of the periodic table are strong oxidizing agents.
The reducing/oxidizing properties of elements strongly influence their terrestrial occurrence and extraction.
The hydration enthalpies of transition metal ions show a systematic variation with the ligand field stabilization energy associated with the aqua complex of the ion.
Acid base properties for similar compounds show systematic variations that follow periodic trends.
The acidity of an oxoacid is dependent on the number of oxo groups and the electronegativity of the central atom. The equilibrium constants for oxoacids can be estimated using Pauling's rules.
The acidity of binary acids varies with the size and electronegativity of the non-hydrogen atom.

There is a periodic variation of the acid-base character displayed by elements in aqueous solutions in which the oxidation state of the central atom determines where it lies on an aqua- hydroxo-oxo continuum.

The main group oxides show a systematic variation in acid-base properties across the period. Metal oxides react with water to produce basic solutions and nonmetal oxides react with water to produce acidic solutions. Amphoteric properties are displayed by the oxides of the semi-metallic elements in a group.
Polyoxoanions are formed from condensation reactions involving early transition metal oxo and hydroxo compounds.
The reactivity of Lewis acids and bases is influenced by steric and electronic effects, specifically including electron-withdrawing and electron-donating groups.

F.text: Chemical change can be controlled by choices of reactants, reaction conditions, or use of catalysts.

alt.organic: Controlling chemical reactions is a key requirement in the synthesis of new materials.
alt.inorganic: Chemical change can be controlled by choices of reactants, reaction conditions or use of catalysts.
alt.physical: Chemical change can be controlled by choices of reactants, reaction conditions or use of catalysts.

l3.text: Utilizing solubility and/or precipitation reactions allows for the qualitative analysis of ions present in a solution.

l4.text: Predicting the reactivity of chemicals is a key skill that can involve knowledge of solubility rules.
