l3.text: Control of chemical reactions is often not fully accomplished, so details such as limiting reactants and percentage yields are important in characterizing what occurs.

l4.text: Stoichiometric calculations must determine the limiting reactant when it is not clear that some reactant(s) are present in excess.
Stoichiometric calculations provide the theoretical yield, which can be used to determine percentage yield.

organic.text: Different reagents or reaction conditions can control the regio- and stereochemistry of a reaction.
Different reagents or reaction conditions can control the regiochemistry of a reaction. 

inorganic.text: Examples of control include sterics, sol-gels, surface adsorption, particle size, size of ligands, pH, solvent effects
The Nernst equation can be used to determine the effect of nonstandard conditions (including pH) on an electrochemical cell potential.

Solvents play an important role in the observed kinetic behavior of reactions. For example, solutions containing solvated electrons can be prepared by dissolving alkali and alkaline earth metals in ammonia.
Phase diagrams can be used to predict the products of reactions under different conditions.
The reactivity of acids and bases is affected by the presence of sterically encumbered functional groups.
Latimer, Frost, and Pourbaix diagrams can be used in the selection of appropriate reagents for reduction-oxidation reactions.
Coordinative saturation plays an important role in the reactivity of many chemical compounds.
Organometallic compounds are synthesized by reaction of appropriate metal and ligand containing compounds.
Templating reactions involve combination of ligands within the inner sphere of a coordination complex. This type of reaction can be used to make macrocyclic ligands.
Metal containing compounds are often used as homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts for chemical reactions.
Zeolites and other porous solids have high surface areas and can be used to introduce shape selectivity.
Many heterogenous reactions employ high temperature and pressure conditions due to the high activation energies involved.
Homogeneous catalysts have been developed for a many chemical reactions, including hydroformylation, carbonylation, hydrogenation, oxidation, and olefin metathesis.
Metals are important in many biochemical processes.
Metal atoms can play structural, catalytic, or redox roles in biological systems. Examples include chlorophyll, hemoglobin, cytochrome C, and zinc containing biomolecules.
Chiral catalysts can be used control the stereochemistry of products of chemical reactions.
The acid base properties of a compound can be altered in nonaqueous solvents.
The levelling effect determines whether an acid or base will behave as a strong or weak electrolyte.
Superacids are acids stronger than sulfuric acid which can be employed in reactions requiring protonation of hydrocarbons.
Interesting compounds of the elements can be synthesized using fluorine and similar strong oxidizing agents.
Compounds of the noble gases are prepared from reaction with fluorine at high pressure and temperature.
The trans effect and trans influence can be used strategically in the synthesis of coordination compounds.
The trans effect refers to the dependence of the site dependent rate of ligand substitution on the ligand positioned trans to the departing ligand.
The trans influence refers to the impact of a ligand on the strength of the bond located in the trans position.
While the trans effect is most often discussed in the context of square planar complexes, it also has an effect in the reactivity of octahedral and five-coordinate complexes.
The presence of chelating ligands within the coordination sphere may influence the geometry of the products formed.
Hard-soft acid-base theory can be used to control the products of chemical reactions.
"Hard" species are small, nonpolarizable, and ionic; "soft" species are large, polarizable, and covalent.
Hard/Hard and Soft/Soft interactions are more energetically favorable than Hard/Soft interactions.
Choice of appropriate Hard/Soft metal/ligand combinations can lead to the desired product.
Hard ions tend to be lithophiles while soft ions tend to be chalcophiles within the Goldschmidt classification.
Hard-soft principles govern the formation of complexes containing ambidentate ligands.
Photochemical reactions are initiated using electromagnetic radiation, most commonly in the ultraviolet or visible range.

physical.text: Changing reaction conditions affects the chemical potential which determines the equilibrium position.
Chemical potential reflects the important variables of the free energy and thus is sensitive to the reaction conditions.
Reactions from nanochemistry often have different behaviors than bulk quantity reactions of the same materials.
The size of nanoparticles that are synthesized often depends on the reaction conditions.
Some reactions can be influenced by changes in total pressure.
When there is a net production or consumption of gases in a reaction, total pressure will influence the equilibrium location.
The identity of reaction products cannot be changed by the addition of a catalyst.
The presence of a catalyst does not affect the products formed or the equilibrium constant, only the rate of the reaction.

G.text: Controlling chemical reactions is a key requirement in the synthesis of new materials.

l3.text: Modern materials represent an important example of the synthesis of new materials.

l4.text: Some solid-state modern materials, including those that compose applications such as LEDs, do not require whole-number stoichiometry.

inorganic.text: Properties of solid state materials are dependent upon reaction conditions.
Solid materials are typically prepared by direct combination, reaction in solution, or sol gel methods.
The degree of crystallinity of a solid or thin film can be controlled by employing different reaction conditions.
The shape of nanomaterials is highly influenced by the reaction conditions employed.
Metal oxides are used in the production of glasses to impart different properties to the final product.
Synthesis of inorganic compounds often employs air, water, and light sensitive techniques.
Schlenk and dry box techniques are often employed when working with air and moisture sensitive compounds.
The principles of coordination chemistry can be employed in the design and synthesis of self- assembled monolayers, metal organic frameworks, inorganic polymers, and other related compounds.
A self-assembled monolayer is an organized two-dimensional structure formed by interactions of long-chained molecules with a surface.
Coordination polymers are formed when metal ions react with polydentate ligands to form extended structures.
Metal-organic frameworks are ordered coordination polymers which often possess large pores within their structures.

physical.text: Catalysis affects only reactions under kinetic control, not thermodynamic control.
In some reactions, a less stable product may be formed, because the activation energy is lower on the pathway that leads to that product.

VI.title: Energy and Thermodynamics
VI.text: Energy and Thermodynamics: Energy is the key currency of chemical reactions in molecular-scale systems as well as macroscopic systems.

A.text: Most chemical changes are accompanied by a net change of energy of the system.

l3.text: The role of kinetic versus potential energy is a key aspect of understanding how energy plays a role in chemical reactions.
Energy changes can be considered in terms of heat and work.

l4.text: Concepts related to energy in chemistry require careful definitions that are more precise than are used in everyday language.
In thermodynamic treatments of chemical systems, the definition of the system of interest versus the surroundings is important.

l3.text: There are a wide variety of energy units, so care must be taken to use consistent units when considering energy changes quantitatively.
Within thermodynamics, it is important to distinguish between internal energy (the heat associated with a constant volume process) and enthalpy (the heat associated with a constant pressure process).

organic.text: Thermodynamics is important in explaining energy changes.
Energy diagrams provide an important tool for understanding and illustrating reaction energetics.
Energies for reactants, intermediates, and products can be combined to model energy diagrams for reaction mechanisms.

inorganic.text: A spontaneous process is indicated by a negative Gibb's free energy for that process.
The equilibrium established between two different states is a function of the Gibb's free energy difference between the states.
Hess's Law can be used to calculate the lattice energy or heat of formation of an ionic solid from a Born-Haber cycle.

physical.text: The careful study of energy implications for reactions requires the definition of the system and its surroundings and their ability to exchange energy.
The system is the part of the universe in which we are interested and the surroundings are everything else, but practically the region outside of the system where pertinent measurements can be made.
Systems may be open, closed or isolated depending on where matter or energy can be exchanged with the surroundings.
Boundaries that permit energy flow between the system and surroundings are called diathermic and those that do not are called adiabatic.
Conservation of energy requires that energy changes of a system are matched by those of the surroundings.
Because reactions will most often have reactants and products that differ in energy, they exchange that energy difference with the surroundings.
Energy itself is neither created nor destroyed, so the amount of energy lost (or gained) by the system is gained (or lost) by the surroundings.
Endothermic reactions absorb energy from and exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings
Measurements generally provide changes in energy rather than absolute energy, so sign conventions have been devised to distinguish energy release from energy absorption by the system.
Energy changes that occur during chemical changes can be measured (using calorimetry).
Under proper conditions, the energy change in the system can be determined by measuring a temperature change using a calorimeter, an apparatus that attempts to isolate the heat flow.

B.text: Many chemical reactions require an energy input to be initiated.

l3.text: Reactive chemicals may remain stable for long times because the reactions they undergo must be initiated by some form of energy input, such as a spark or flame.

organic.text: Reactions generally require an input of energy to overcome the energy of activation.

inorganic.text: Activation energy for a reaction determines the rate at which a reaction occurs at a given temperature.
A catalyst decreases the activation energy for a reaction by enabling a different mechanistic pathway.
An activated complex with higher energy than reactants or products is usually formed during the course of a reaction.
There are examples of reactions that do not require energy to initiate the process.

Many inorganic compounds are fluxional at room temperature because the activation energy associated with structural distortion is low. Dynamic NMR experiments are often employed to measure the activation energy for these processes.
Activation energies for substitution in transition metal coordination complexes can be influenced by the ligand field stabilization energy. (e.g. water exchange rates)

physical.text: Energy input may come from a variety of sources and is required to overcome the activation energy.
Activation energy may be supplied by any of several methods, such as flames, electrical discharge, light or molecular collisions.
Reactive chemicals may be in contact and not react, because initial energy input is required to start the reaction.
Hydrocarbon fuels can be stored in the presence of air and not react with the oxygen present until a spark or flame provides the initial energy.

C.text: The type of energy associated with chemical change may be heat, light, or electrical energy.

alt.inorganic: The type of energy associated with chemical change may be heat, light or electrical energy.
alt.physical: The type of energy associated with chemical change may be heat, light or electrical energy.

l3.text: Heat exchange is measured via temperature change.

l4.text: Heat flow into the system is defined as endothermic; heat flow out of the system is defined as exothermic.
Heat flow is quantitatively obtained from T via molar heat capacity or specific heat and the mass of the substance involved.
By convention, numerical estimates of exothermic processes carry a negative sign, while endothermic processes carry a positive sign.
When observed in the laboratory, exothermic processes will show warming (heat evolved), while endothermic processes will show cooling (heat absorbed).

l3.text: The enthalpy of reaction is a measure of heat exchange for reactions carried out at constant pressure.

l4.text: Enthalpies of reaction, such as those incorporated in a thermochemical equation, can be used to calculate energy flow for a given amount of reactant or product.

l3.text: Electrochemistry is predicated on oxidation–reduction reactions, and involves physically separating the electron production of oxidation from the electron consumption of reduction.

l4.text: Oxidation–reduction reactions can be considered in two halves, and can be physically separated to form electrochemical systems.
Electrical energy can be obtained from electrochemical systems operating as galvanic cells.

organic.text: Heat and light are common types of energy associated with reactions.
The source of energy input can affect mechanisms and change the products of pericyclic reactions.

inorganic.text: Many chemical and biochemical processes interconvert chemical energy with other forms of energy.
Light energy can be used to photodissociate chemical bonds.
Bioluminescent and chemiluminescent processes produce light from chemical energy, while photosynthetic process use light to effect chemical change.
Methods exist to measure or estimate energy differences within a system or a portion of the system.

physical.text: Heat provides reaction energy by increasing the number of fast moving molecules and therefore high energy collisions.
Heat transfer into a reaction system increases the temperature and therefore increases the average speed of the molecules present.
Photochemical reactions use light energy to initiate a reaction.
In photochemical reactions, a reactant absorbs light which often creates a reactive species that then initiates further reactions.
Electrical energy may either initiate a reaction or be generated by a reaction.
When electrical energy is produced by a reaction it may be used to power a galvanic cell.
Electrolysis occurs when electrical energy is an input that causes a reaction.
The Gibbs energy represents the maximum electrical work obtainable from a chemical reaction.
Some reactions release light as a product.
Products in chemical may be created in an excited state that releases energy as light, causing luminescence.
Fluorescence occurs when the light released occurs on a relatively short time scale and arises from allowed electronic transitions.
Phosphorescence occurs when the light released occurs on a relatively long time scale and arises from non-allowed electronic transitions.

D.text: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy; formation of chemical bonds releases energy.

alt.organic: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy, and formation of chemical bonds releases energy.
alt.inorganic: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy and formation of chemical bonds releases energy
alt.physical: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy and formation of chemical bonds releases energy.

l3.text: While breaking a chemical bond is always endothermic, chemical energy can be released via reactions because bonds are both broken and formed in the course of the reaction.

l4.text: The extent of energy release or absorption is dictated by the bonds broken in the reactants and the bonds formed in the products.

organic.text: In a reaction, often there is both bond breaking and bond formation, so the energy consequences depend on both.
The transition state of an SN2 reaction has concurrent bond making and bond breaking.

inorganic.text: Born-Haber cycles typically include the effect of bond dissociation enthalpy on the lattice energy of an ionic compound.
The activation energy for a reaction is often determined by bond dissociation energies.
Proton gain enthalpies are often used to measure and explain acid and base strength.
The identities of the metal and ligand are important to the energies observed in the reactions of coordination complexes.
Bond energies are often affected by ligand field stabilization energy in coordination complexes.
In dissociatively activated reactions, a linear free energy relationship typically exists between the log of the rate constant and the log of the equilibrium constant.

physical.text: Reactions are either exothermic or endothermic based on which bonds are broken and which bonds form.
Any chemical bond releases energy upon formation or absorbs energy when broken, but chemical reactions include both breaking and forming of bonds, so they may be either endothermic or exothermic.

E.text: The forces that are associated with energy change in chemical processes are electrostatic forces.

l3.text: Moving charge in an external circuit (electrochemistry) provides one lever by which this concept is measured.

l4.text: When an electrochemical system is built, it is possible to determine the cell potential.
Trends related to cell potential are summarized via tables of standard reduction potentials.
Calculations using standard reduction potentials can determine cell potential and the spontaneous direction of an electrochemical reaction.
Nonstandard situations are addressed via the Nernst equation.

External electrical energy can be used to drive an electrochemical system in the nonspontaneous direction. Quantitative information about stoichiometry of these systems can be derived from variables related to electricity flow.

organic.text: Interactions with solvent can be described in terms of dipole–dipole or induced-dipole interactions.

inorganic.text: The potential of an electrochemical cell can be related to Gibb's free energy for the cell reaction.
Half reaction potentials are used to calculate the standard cell potential for a chemical reaction. The Nernst Equation can be used to calculate cell potentials for non-standard conditions.
Electrostatic forces play an important role in the formation of coordination complexes.

The Irving-Williams series determines the effect of metal ion on the formation constant for octahedral coordination complexes, and results from a combination of electrostatic attraction due to increasing effective nuclear charge and ligand field stabilization energy of the electron configuration associated with the metal ion.
The Drago-Wayland equation is used to estimate the enthalpy of a reaction based on electrostatic and covalent factors.

physical.text: The Coulomb forces present in molecules give rise to potential energy that can be divided into electronic, vibrational and rotational components.
The electronic potential energy arises from all pairwise Coulomb forces between electrons and protons.
Within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, the nuclear motions associated with vibrations arise from the potential energy established by the electron distributions around the nuclei.
In addition to internal motions of electrons, and of vibration, the whole molecule may rotate or translate in space.
Electrochemical reactions directly tap the electrostatic nature of forces to do electrical work.
Oxidation reduction reactions have a net movement of electrons, and when carried out with some form of separation, the electron flow can be harnessed to do electrical work.

F.text: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or human-made devices.

alt.inorganic: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or man-made devices.
alt.physical: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or man-made devices.

l3.text: Pressure–volume (PV) work is a common means by which chemical changes, particularly combustion, are harnessed in human -made devices.
Electrochemical cells provide one way that chemical change is harnessed in human-made devices (batteries).

l4.text: Batteries and fuels cells are important applications of electrochemical systems.

organic.text: Hydrocarbon compounds are commonly combusted for energy.

inorganic.text: Galvanic cells, such as batteries or fuel cells, can be used to produce electrical energy from chemical energy, while electrolytic cells are use electrical energy to effect chemical change.
Diagrams representing electrochemical cells show the chemical identity of the anode and cathode, solution contents, and the direction of electron flow.
Line notation can also be used to represent the contents of an electrochemical cell.
Several devices exist for the conversion of electrical energy to other forms of energy.
Thermoelectric materials are used to interconvert heat and electrical energy.
Photoelectric and electro-optic materials are capable of interconverting light and electrochemical energy. Common examples include solar cells and light emitting diodes.
Piezoelectric materials are used to interconvert electrical and mechanical energy.

physical.text: The efficiency of engines is fundamentally limited as dictated by the 2nd Law of Thermodynamics.
One key statement of the second law of thermodynamics is that no process can occur where the only result is the complete conversion of heat energy into work.
Efficiency of a heat engine, defined as the ratio of work performed to heat absorbed, is maximized for a reversible engine.
Refrigeration does work to transfer heat, and the efficiency is captured by the coefficient of performance which is the inverse of the efficiency of a heat engine.
Efficiency may be improved by increasing the temperature of the hot reservoir or decreasing the temperature of the cold reservoir or both.
Converting heat into work in a system requires the production of waste heat into the surroundings.
Work is path dependent because of the production of waste heat.

G.text: Thermodynamics provides a detailed capacity to understand energy change at the macroscopic level.

l3.text: A key concept within thermodynamics is the state function, which can be defined as a quantity whose value is independent of its history.

l4.text: Standard states of substances play a key role in thermodynamic calculations.

l3.text: Hess’s law takes advantage of enthalpy being a state function to allow the determination of enthalpy change for a reaction based on combinations of more readily measured, or tabulated, reaction enthalpies.

l4.text: Enthalpy is a key thermodynamic state function for calculation of heat exchange for many processes; these calculations include Hess’s law.
Tabulated values for the calculation of thermodynamic variables often take advantage of the concept of the formation reaction.
The concept of Hess’s law is useful in calculating thermodynamic properties from both reactions and tabulated values.

organic.text: Bond energies of reactants and products can be used to estimate macroscopic enthalpy changes for reactions.

inorganic.text: Bond dissociation energies can be used to calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction.

physical.text: Heat flows from a warmer body to a cooler body until thermal equilibrium is established.

The zeroth law of thermodynamics indicates that if system A is in thermal equilibrium with system B and B is in thermal equilibrium with system C, then system A is in thermal equilibrium with C as well.
The zeroth law provides the basis of using a thermometer to measure temperature.
0 K is defined as the temperature at which the molar volume of an ideal gas goes to zero.
The idea that the total energy of isolated systems is conserved, allows for mathematical expressions for the transformation of energy from one form to another.
The first law of thermodynamics states that the internal energy of an isolated system is constant, and because the universe is an isolated system, its energy must be constant.
Thermodynamic systems may be described as isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric or isochoric.
Systems that are not isolated will exchange energy with their surroundings, unless the boundary does not allow energy transfer, or the surroundings maintain thermal equilibrium with the system.
When a thermodynamic system is held at constant pressure it is said to be isobaric, and these conditions favor the use of specific state functions such as enthalpy or Gibbs Free Energy
When a thermodynamic system is held at constant volume it is said to be isochoric, and these conditions favor the use of specific state functions such as internal energy or Helmholtz Free Energy
A boundary that does not allow energy exchange as heat leads to an adiabatic system.
Systems that are maintained at constant temperature are called isothermal systems.

Expansion or compression of gases may be carried out under different conditions, such as free expansion, expansion or compression against a constant pressure or reversible expansion or compression and these conditions influence the calculation of work and heat.
Compression or expansion of a gas may be carried out under adiabatic or isothermal conditions, and these conditions influence the calculation of work and heat for the process.
Measurable primary thermodynamic functions are T, P, V and composition.
P, V, T, and n may, in principle, vary so must be measured or held constant in thermodynamic experiments and mathematical manipulations.
Measurable primary thermodynamic functions are related to other thermodynamic properties via partial derivative relationships.
Heat capacity, Cp, Cv are defined as derivatives of enthalpy and internal energy with respect to temperature and they provide a proportionality constant between heat and temperature change.
Isothermal compressibility is defined as the partial derivative of volume with respect to pressure (at constant temperature) multiplied by (-1/V).
The expansion coefficient is defined as the partial derivative of volume with respect to temperature (at constant pressure) multiplied by (1/V)
The Joule-Thomson coefficient is defined as the partial derivative of temperature with respect to pressure at constant enthalpy.
The isothermal Joule-Thomson coefficient is defined as the partial derivative of enthalpy with respect to pressure at constant temperature.
Work and heat are the main forms of energy exchange, and their sum is the internal energy.
Energy is defined as the capacity to do work.
Energy that exchanges because the system is in thermal contact with surroundings at a different temperature is called heat.
Work is defined by moving an object against an opposing force.
Work is associated with organized particle motion while heat is associated with random particle motion.
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the sum of heat and work equals the change of internal energy of the system.
The change in internal energy, ΔU, is measurable under constant volume conditions.
Internal energy is a state function and the change in internal energy equals the heat under constant volume conditions.
Bomb calorimetry maintains constant volume conditions, and therefore represents a method to measure the change in internal energy.
A perfect gas is identified by the fact that the partial derivative of its internal energy with respect to volume at constant temperature is zero.
Enthalpy is defined as U+PV and describes the heat flow under constant pressure conditions.
Enthalpy is a state function.
The change in enthalpy equals the heat under constant pressure conditions, and because these conditions are more common in the laboratory it is often the thermodynamic function used for heat.
Because enthalpy is a state function, Hess's Law states that reactions can be summed and/or tabulated values of the enthalpies of formation can be used to calculate ΔH .

So long as the temperature difference is not too large, the enthalpy change of a reaction at a temperature T1 may be estimated from the enthalpy change at T2, by adding the integral over T1 to T2 of the difference in molar heat capacities times dT.
State functions in thermodynamics are path independent, and many mathematical relationships are built upon this property.
The value of a state function depends only on its state, not the path by which that state was reached.
Mathematically, state functions have exact differentials.
Key examples of state functions include: S, T, P, H, V, n, G, A, while heat and work are important variables that are not state functions.
Thermodynamic cycles can be used to determine changes in values of state functions.
Thermodynamic calculations do not provide information about the rates of reactions.
Knowing that a particular system is more thermodynamically stable in one state than another provides no evidence as to the rate at which a change could occur.

H.text: The tendency of nature to disperse, particularly in terms of energy distribution, is embodied in the state function called entropy.

l3.text: Spontaneous changes will always increase the entropy of the universe (practically speaking—the entropy of the system and surroundings).

l4.text: The definition of entropy and the ability to calculate change in entropy for a reaction are important.
A qualitative, conceptual understanding of processes that lead to more random physical distributions of particles with an increase in entropy is valuable.
An individual, nonspontaneous process can occur when linked to another process such that the combined events increase the entropy of the universe.

l3.text: Gibb’s free energy is a state function that simultaneously calculates entropy for the system and surroundings, and is useful for determining whether or not a process occurs spontaneously.

l4.text: Gibbs free energy is defined in such a way that the calculation of it provides insight into whether a process is spontaneous with a single calculation.
The Gibb’s free energy is defined in terms of enthalpy and entropy changes; students should be able to consider these components both quantitatively and qualitatively.
Calculations of Gibb’s free energy from tabulated values are important not only to obtain ΔG, but often to estimate equilibrium constants or cell potentials as well.

l3.text: The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is 0.

l4.text: Because the entropy has a specific value at 0 K, tabulated values for entropy need not be enumerated as changes relative to a standard reference state.

l3.text: Thermodynamic spontaneity alone cannot predict whether a process will occur. Some spontaneous processes occur too slowly to be readily observed.

l4.text: Even spontaneous processes may not be observed if there is a large activation energy for the process to begin.

inorganic.text: In chemical reactions where the changes in enthalpy are small, entropy can play a major role in predicting the direction of chemical reactions.

In the thermodynamic chelate effect, complexes containing polydentate ligands are favored in an equilibrium over complexes containing analogous monodentate ligands because formation of the chelated complexes results in an increase in entropy. An additional enthalpic term resulting from ligand pre-organization causes the macrocycle effect.
The Gibb's equation describes the change in free energy for a system with respect to the change in enthalpy plus the change in entropy times the temperature.
The temperature dependence of electrochemical cell potential can be used to calculate entropy of reaction.

physical.text: The direction of spontaneous change is towards the dispersal of energy into more disordered forms.
An increase in heat of a system is accompanied by a more disordered dispersal of the energy.
While more ordered systems can be created, the work required to do so is accompanied by an even greater amount of heat dispersal, so the overall change is towards more disordered forms of energy.
Entropy is a state function that reflects the dispersal of energy into disordered forms and can be defined in terms of either macroscopic variables (heat and temperature) or microstates.
Entropy change can be defined in terms of qrev/T.
Entropy can be defined in terms of microstates using the Boltzmann definition: S = k ln(W).
The entropy of any isolated system increases in a spontaneous change.
Because the universe is an isolated system, Δ Suniv increases for any spontaneous process.
For a system that is not isolated, the entropy change of the system and the surroundings must both be considered to determine the spontaneous direction of change.

Processes that do work are generally more ordered (at the particulate level) than heat flow processes, so creating work from heat sources is in the opposite direction as dictated by entropy of the system.
The relatively ordered nature of work when compared to heat justifies the macroscopic statement of the second law of thermodynamics that heat cannot be converted completely into work.
Perfect gases have no enthalpy change upon mixing, so the entire driving force for the spontaneous mixing of gases is due to the increase in entropy, i.e. a less ordered state.
The change in the Helmholtz Free Energy indicates if a process occurring at constant temperature and volume is spontaneous or not.
The Helmholtz Free Energy, A, is defined as A=U-TS
A process at constant volume and temperature will be spontaneous if the change in the Helmholtz free energy is negative or zero.
The change in the Gibbs Free Energy indicates if a process occurring at constant temperature and pressure is spontaneous or not.
The Gibbs Free Energy, G, is defined as G=H-TS
A process at constant pressure and temperature will be spontaneous if the change in the Gibbs free energy is negative or zero.

The definition of the Gibbs free energy essentially takes into account the entropy change of both the system and surroundings and allows the determination of the spontaneous direction of change via a single variable.
ΔG is the maximum amount of non-PV work.
Because the Gibbs Free Energy is a state function, summed reactions and/or tabulated values of the free energy of formation can be used to calculate ΔG.
The spontaneous direction of phase changes can be related to Gibbs energy and signs and relative sizes of ΔH and ΔS
The Third Law of Thermodynamics defines the absolute entropy scale.
Absolute entropies at a given T° can be calculated using the Third Law of Thermodynamics
Entropy can be calculated from the temperature dependence of the heat capacity.

I.text: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical changes.

alt.organic: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical change.
alt.inorganic: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical change.
alt.physical: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical change.

l3.text: Basic concepts related to energy in nuclear reactions derive from the conversion of mass to energy.

l4.text: Nuclear chemistry arises when there are changes in the nuclei of atoms.
Mass deficits in nuclear reactions arise from the conversion of mass to energy and are calculated via the equation: E = mc 2 .
Nuclear reactions give off radiation that may have biological effects.

inorganic.text: Nuclear energy levels are quantized, and transitions can occur between nuclear states to release energy. Nuclear fission and fusion reactions can be used to harness energy from these transitions.
The binding energy is a measure of the stability of a nuclear state with respect to free nucleons.
Concepts such as magic numbers, the even-odd rule, and the Island of Stability are used to rationalize the stability of certain isotopes in comparison with others.

physical.text: Energy of nuclear processes arises from mass changes and are calculated via E=mc2.
The mass deficit that arises in nuclear reactions leads to large energy changes via Einstein's equation.
Nuclear energy changes are much greater than energy changes associated with chemical changes.

VII.title: Kinetics
VII.text: Kinetics: Chemical changes have a time scale over which they occur.

A.text: Chemical change can be measured as a function of time and occurs over a wide range of time scales.

alt.physical: Chemical change occurs over a wide range of time scales.

l3.text: The rate of the reaction must be defined in a manner that is not dependent on which reactant or product is used to measure it.

l4.text: The reaction rate should incorporate reaction stoichiometry when it is defined.

l3.text: Rate is generally defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product as a function of time.

l4.text: Chemical reactions may occur at a wide range of rates, and a key aspect of rate is related to the concentration of species involved in the reaction.

l3.text: When solids are included in reactions, surface area is an important factor in the rate of reaction.

l4.text: A reactive solid with a large surface area will react more rapidly than the same solid with a smaller surface area.

organic.text: Differences between fast and slow reactions can play a vital role in determining what product forms in a reaction.

inorganic.text: Complexes are classified as inert or labile relative to the timescale that substitution reactions occur.
The relative rates of solvation for metal ions vary with the charge, size, and ligand field stabilization energy of the ion.
Fluxionality of complexes can occur and be observed at different timescales.

physical.text: Time scale for measuring or monitoring reaction rates must match the time scale on which a reaction occurs.
Some experiments may be studied using real-time analysis of the system composition while other reactions are studied using quenching methods.
Flow methods and stopped-flow methods provide access to different time ranges for reactions, with stopped-flow methods being used for faster reactions.
Relaxation methods can be used to study kinetics at the millisecond time scale.
Relaxation methods study the return of a system to an equilibrium state after a sudden change in conditions has perturbed that equilibrium system.
Temperature jump methods perturb the equilibrium with a change in temperature and pressure jump methods can be used with systems where equilibrium is sensitive to the total pressure.
Spectroscopic probes are often used to monitor concentration as a function of time.
Spectroscopic probes of reaction kinetics are particularly useful when one reactant or product has strong absorption properties in a particular spectral region.
Laser induced fluorescence is capable of providing state-specific monitoring of product molecules.
Multiphoton ionization techniques, often paired with mass spectrometric detection, can be used to monitor reaction dynamics.
Rates of reaction can vary depending on specific isotopes present.
The kinetic isotope effect refers to the decrease in reaction rate when a heavier isotope of an atom is present in a reactant.

The magnitude of the kinetic isotope effect is dependent on the ratio of the reduced masses between the heavier and lighter isotopes, thus the largest effect arises from replacing hydrogen with deuterium.

The primary kinetic isotope effect occurs when the rate determining step involves breaking a bond that includes the replaced isotope, while in the secondary kinetic isotope effect some other bond is broken in the rate determining step.
Rates of chemical reactions change over time.
Reaction rates can be determined as instantaneous or average rates.
The initial rate, an instantaneous rate measured at the start of a kinetics experiment, is often used to compare rates of different reactions.

B.text: Empirically derived rate laws summarize the dependence of reaction rates on concentrations of reactants and temperature.

l3.text: The “order” of a reaction is derived from the exponent on the concentration term of a given reactant in the rate law.

l4.text: Rate laws are always determined experimentally, and the methods of initial rates or graphical depiction of rates provide the key method for determining rate laws.
Once known, a rate law can be used to quantitatively predict concentrations of species involved in a reaction as a function of time.
The kinetics of nuclear processes is first order and can be quantitatively treated, often by indicating the half-life of a nuclear reaction.

l3.text: The temperature dependence of the reaction rate is contained in the rate constant. This temperature dependence is often well modeled by the Arrhenius model.

l4.text: Under most circumstances, an increase in temperature leads to an increase in reaction rate.
Empirical fits of temperature data in kinetics can be used to estimate the activation energy.

organic.text: Rate laws can provide clues to reaction mechanisms, particularly substitution and elimination reactions.
Rate laws can be developed from reaction equations or reaction mechanisms.

inorganic.text: Kinetic information is obtained experimentally by measurement of reaction rate under a variety of conditions.
Concentration dependence is used to determine order and rate constant of a reaction at a particular temperature and pressure.
The Eyring equation is used to determine the enthalpy and entropy of activation from temperature dependent measurements of the rate constant.
The volume of activation is determined from pressure-dependent measurements of the rate constant.

physical.text: Many reactions have integer exponents for concentrations that are in the rate law leading to 1st order, 2nd order and 3rd order rate laws as commonly (but not exclusively) seen expressions.
The fundamental goal of the rate law is to summarize the effect of changes in concentration on the rate of a reaction.
The rate law expression can be integrated to derive an expression of concentration vs. time.
Complex rate laws may not have an integer order but can be experimentally forced into an order such as a pseudo 1st order or 2nd order reaction.
The units on the rate constant, k, reflect the order of the reaction.
In many cases, integrated rate laws can be determined by monitoring either reactant disappearance or product formation.
The isolation method uses large excess of all but one reactant to determine the pseudo-rate order of the reaction for that one (not excess) reactant.
Experimental data can provide either absolute or relative reaction rates.
Absolute reaction rates are best measured in systems where the reaction of interest is the only reaction taking place.
Reactive species, like radicals, often participate in more than one reaction, and the study of such systems may rely on measuring relative reaction rates for the various reactions.
One way to characterize the rate of a reaction is to define the half-life which is particularly useful in 1st order kinetics.
The half-life is defined as the time it takes for the concentration of a reactant to reach half its initial value.
The half-life in a first-order reaction does not depend on the concentration of the observed species and thus provides a convenient way to rank the rates of such reactions.
Reaction rates depend on temperature and this dependence can often be captured by using the Arrhenius equation for the rate constant.
For many reactions, a plot of the natural log of the rate constant versus inverse temperature provides a straight line and the reaction is said to display Arrhenius behavior.
The Arrhenius equation has two parameters, the pre-exponential or frequency factor and the activation energy, which can be obtained from fits to experimental data.

C.text: Most chemical reactions take place by a series of more elementary reactions, called the reaction mechanism.

alt.inorganic: Most chemical reactions take place by a series of more elementary reactions, called the reaction mechanism

l3.text: The reaction stoichiometry does not imply the species actually involved in a reaction.
It is possible to devise a series of reactions that, when summed, yield the overall reaction and provide a mechanism for how the reaction occurs.

l4.text: Chemical reactions often occur via multiple steps, called the reaction mechanism.
One step in a mechanism, the rate determining step, is often much slower than others and this slow step tends to determine the overall reaction rate.
Given a reaction mechanism and knowing the rate determining step allows the rate law to be inferred. This rate law must match the observed empirical rate law for a mechanism to be valid.
A compatible rate law does not “prove” the correctness of a mechanism.

Species that appear in a reaction mechanism but not in the overall reactions are called intermediates and their identification can provide important evidence about how well the mechanism describes the reaction.

organic.text: Reaction steps are fundamental to understanding each functional group’s reactivity in organic chemistry.
The slowest step is the rate-determining step.
Functional groups consist of polar or polarizable bonds that dictate reactivity.
Curved arrow mechanisms show electron movement from nucleophiles to electrophiles in elementary reactions.
Reaction mechanisms can de depicted illustrating the movement of electrons for every bond broken or formed.

inorganic.text: Most reaction mechanisms involve the reactants colliding to form an activated complex, or transition state, that proceeds to form the products of the reaction.
The properties of the solvent often influence the stability of the transition state.
Steady-state approximations are often used to understand the relationship of a multistep mechanism and the observed rate law.

Redox processes are classified as inner-sphere or outer-sphere based on the mechanism of electron transfer. Inner-sphere electron transfer takes place through chemical bonds while outer sphere reactions involve through space interactions.
Outer-sphere electron transfer displays kinetic behavior that can be interpreted using Marcus theory.

Substitution reactions of coordination complexes can be explained by associative (A), dissociative (D), and interchange (Ia, Id) mechanisms. Mechanisms are classified as associative or dissociative if an intermediate can be observed by experiment, while interchange reactions proceed through an unobservable transition state.
The role of the incoming, outgoing, and spectator ligands in determining reaction outcome and stereochemistry is used in classification of a mechanism as dissociative or associative.

The coordination environment of a metal influences the mechanism of ligand substitution observed. Substitution in octahedral complexes is typically dissociative, while substitution in square planar complexes is typically associative at high ligand concentrations and dissociative at low ligand concentrations.
The relative coordinative saturation of a metal center will affect the mechanism observed. Dissociative mechanisms are often observed in complexes containing sterically bulky ligands.
Activation volumes can be used as further evidence in the classification of a reaction mechanism as associative (ΔV > 0) or dissociative (ΔV < 0).
pH dependence of a reaction rate is used as evidence to support mechanisms involving protonation or deprotonation of ligands.
The Fuoss-Eigen equation allows for the estimation of an equilibrium constant for formation of an encounter complex in dissociative reactions.
Rates of dissociative substitution reactions often have rate dependent on the ligand field stabilization energy of the reactants.
Dissociative substitution reactions typically exhibit a linear free energy relationship between the log of the rate constant and the log of the equilibrium constant for bond dissociation.
Mechanisms for reorganization in fluxional complexes involve distortion of the bond angles within the complexes.
Fluxionality in trigonal pyramidal complexes is explained using the Berry pseudorotation mechanism.
Fluxionality in octahedral complexes is often explained using the Bailar or Ray-Dutt twist mechanisms.
The kinetic chelate effect is used to explain the stability of complexes with polydentate ligands.
Binding of the donor atoms of chelate complexes occurs at the same rate as monodentate ligand complexes.
Fast rebinding of the first dissociated donor atom of a chelate due to that atom's huge "effective concentration" is the source of the chelate effect.

The macrocycle effect is a greater stability of macrocyclic complexes than can be explained by the chelate effect. The cause is the slow dissociation of the first donor atom due to the additional rigidity of the macrocyclic ring.
The cryptate effect is a further enhancement of complex stability when two macrocyclic rings are fused, which further increases rigidity.

physical.text: Kinetics mechanisms sum the elementary reactions to achieve the overall reaction.
There may be numerous ways to envision elementary steps for a kinetic mechanism, but any possible mechanism must ultimately be summed to provide the overall reaction.
Reaction intermediates can be built up if the elementary step producing them is faster than those that are consuming them.
The molecularity of elementary steps defines how many particles collide in the reaction.
Three body collisions are not likely to occur, so virtually all elementary steps are either unimolecular or bimolecular.
For elementary reactions only, the rate law can be obtained directly from the stoichiometry to the reactant particles.
The Lindemann-Hinshelwood mechanism provides an explanation of how unimolecular reactions can arise.
The overall rate law must be derivable from the mechanism in order for it to be a viable depiction of how the reaction takes place.
In addition to depicting the overall stoichiometry of a reaction, the kinetic mechanism must also give the overall rate law for the reaction.
Variability in rates and extent of completion (or reaching equilibrium) for elementary steps is considered when obtaining the overall rate law from expressions for each elementary step.

Some elementary steps may establish pre-equilibrium with a reactive intermediate, in which case both forward and reverse rate constants for the elementary steps are used in determining the overall rate law.
Reaction intermediates that build up may require an induction period before they reach a stable concentration.
The steady state approximation may be invoked to determine the overall rate law for mechanisms that produce reaction intermediates.
Reaction mechanisms cannot be generally proven, but observation of reactive intermediates is capable of providing important supporting evidence for a proposed mechanism.
For many/most reaction mechanisms, one elementary step is much slower than others and largely determines the overall rate.
The slow step in a reaction mechanism determines the overall rate of the reaction as is called the rate determining step.
Chemical intermediates are often important in reactions and the lifetime of intermediates dictates the observation time-scale.
Relatively long lived intermediates are often formed by a pre-equilibrium process prior to a rate determining step.
Methods exist to observe kinetics on a state-to-state level.
Experimental techniques can be used to cool molecules to limit the number of rotational and vibrational states occupied by reactants.
Experimental probes, such as laser induced fluorescence, may be able to measure rotational and vibrational states of the products of a reaction.
Typically for small molecular systems, initial vibrational states may be selected to be excited to determine state-to-state effects on reaction dynamics.
Atmospheric chemistry, including pollution formation, is usually described with a complicated kinetic mechanism.

Reactions in the upper atmosphere tend to have low collision frequencies because of the low pressures, and mechanisms proposed in such regions must account for how energy is removed from the reacting system by subsequent collisions.
A number of atmospheric processes are initiated by sunlight, so photochemical elementary steps are often an important component of the reaction mechanisms in the atmosphere.
Models that accurately account for the formation of key pollutants, like lung irritants, may include hundreds of elementary reactions.
In biochemical systems, many reactions take place in cycles, and the kinetics of the overall process depends on the rate of the steps.

Obtaining energy as part of cellular respiration involves the Krebs cycle, and the kinetics of each step in the cycle must be studied to understand the rate of the overall process and the effects of enzymes and other factors on that rate.

The study of the rate at which pharmaceutical molecules are metabolized and removed from the body is vital to the medical effectiveness of the treatment, and forms the basis of the field of pharmacokinetics.

D.text: An elementary reaction requires that the reactants collide (interact) and have both enough energy and appropriate orientation of colliding particles for the reaction to occur.

alt.inorganic: An elementary reaction requires that the reactants collide (interact) and have both enough energy and appropriate orientation of colliding particles for the reaction to occur

l3.text: The collision theory of reactions indicates that collisions result in products only if there is enough energy and if the orientation of the reactants is appropriate.

l4.text: The number of particles involved in a collision defines the reaction as unimolecular, bimolecular, or termolecular.
At the molecular scale, reactions are required to overcome an energy barrier, called the activation energy, in order to take place.

l3.text: The energy required to initiate a reaction is called the activation energy.

l4.text: In many cases, overcoming the activation energy is achieved by high - speed collisions between rapidly moving molecules in a sample.

organic.text: Transition state theory is used mainly to explain kinetics in SN2 reactions.

inorganic.text: Collisions occurring in aqueous solutions often involve a pre-arrangement within spheres or cages of water molecules.

physical.text: Molecular collisions lead to products through an activated complex. The relative energy of this complex dictates the activation energy.
All reactions involve a collision between reacting molecules.
When reacting molecules are in the act of colliding, they form a transient species called an activated complex, from which the reaction may or may not proceed to products.
The molecular scale definition of the activation energy is the amount of energy that the activated complex is higher than the reactants.
Kinetic molecular theory uses the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to describe the distribution of speeds of particles in a sample.
Gas kinetic theory begins with a set of postulates that describe the behavior of gases at the molecular scale.
The Maxell-Boltzmann distribution is temperature dependent and describes the fraction of particles moving at a particular velocity.
Integration of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution over all velocities must be equal to one because the probability must be 100% that any given particle has some velocity between zero and infinity.
Integration over the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution from some velocity to infinity provides the fraction of molecules that exceed that velocity.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the gas and for the Boltzmann-Maxwell distribution relationships can enumerate the average speed, the root mean square speed and the most probable speed.
Because kinetic energy depends on mass, heavier molecules will move slower than lighter molecules at the same temperature.
The mass dependence of the velocity distribution affects diffusion and effusion rates and as a result presents a way to measure the molar mass of a gas.
Temperature, pressure, volume, concentration and composition can influence collision rates and the mean free path.
The mean free path is the average distance that a gas molecule travels between collisions and it is inversely proportional to the collision frequency.
The collision energy is dictated by the relative velocities of the colliding particles.
Higher temperatures increase reaction rates because more molecules have higher velocities that lead to more energetic collisions.
Increased pressure at constant temperature leads to increased concentration which increases the number of molecular collisions.
The mean free path is inversely related to the number of particles per unit volume, so changing the volume without changing the number of particles will alter the mean free path.
Collision theory and transition state theory provide numerical models relating molecular scale dynamics to macroscopic reaction rates.
Collision theory describes the rate of reaction in terms of collision frequency, a steric factor, the activation energy and the temperature.
Even reactions that have enough energy to overcome the activation energy may not lead to a reaction.
The steric factor in collision theory accounts for the fact that the relative orientation of colliding molecules may affect whether or not a given collision will lead to reaction.
Transition state theory assumes that reactants reach a quasi-equilibrium with the activated complex in order to derive the expression for the rate of reaction.
The rate constant in transition state theory is proportional to an exponential of the free energy of activation.

E.text: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of subdisciplines of chemistry.

alt.inorganic: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of sub-disciplines of chemistry
alt.physical: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of sub-disciplines of chemistry.

l3.text: A catalyst is defined as an agent that increases the rate of the reaction while not being consumed by the reaction.

l4.text: Catalysts can be either homogeneous or heterogeneous.
Catalysts play an important role in applications, such as catalytic converters on cars, or environmental events, such as ozone depletion.

l3.text: A catalyst increases the rate of the reaction by providing a new reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

l4.text: Catalysts provide an alternative reaction pathway that lowers this activation energy.
Because a catalyst lowers the activation energy, it affects both forward and reverse reactions.

organic.text: Catalysis changes the path of a reaction to a lower activation energy, which can be shown through changes in the reaction rates.

inorganic.text: Catalysts influence reaction orientation and pathway, leading to an alteration of the potential energy surface and decrease in activation energy for the reaction.
A catalytic cycle is a mechanism proposed to explain the formation of products and regeneration of the active catalyst.
Catalysts for reactions are chosen based on their activity, selectivity, and lifetime.
Turnover frequencies and turnover numbers can be used to compare the activity of different catalysts.
The structure of a heterogeneous catalyst can influence the activity and selectivity of a reaction.

Activity of a catalyst increases with increased surface area. This can be accomplished physically by supporting the catalyst on a high surface area substrate, or synthetically using reaction conditions, as is done with zeolites.
Many reactions involving heterogeneous catalysts involve interaction with acidic and/or basic sites on the catalyst surface.
The porous structure of zeolites can be used to impart shape selectivity in various reactions.
Reactions of homogeneous catalysts are often studied as models for processes occurring in heterogeneous systems.

physical.text: A catalyst changes the reaction mechanism and the new mechanism has a lower overall activation energy than the uncatalyzed pathway.
Because the new pathway provided by a catalyst lowers the activation energy, it speeds the overall reaction.
Catalysis may occur in a single phase (homogeneous) or at a phase interface (heterogeneous).
Homogeneous catalysis may allow for desirable features such as asymmetric synthesis, but typically has greater challenges separating the products and the catalyst once a reaction has occurred.
Heterogeneous catalysis by solids occurs when reactive species chemisorb on the surface and the adsorbed species react then desorb.
Two key mechanisms for solid surface catalysis are the Langmuir-Hinshelwood and the Eley- Rideal mechanisms.
Electrochemical catalysis is a special category of heterogeneous catalysis that takes place at the surface of an electrode.
Enzyme catalysis is a critical component of many biochemical reactions.
The Michaelis-Menten mechanism provides a key model for understanding substrate binding in enzyme catalysis.
Specific mechanisms for enzyme activity are strongly dependent on the structure of the enzyme and the ligand.

F.text: Reaction products can be influenced by controlling whether reaction rate or reaction energy plays the key role in the mechanism.

alt.inorganic: Reaction products can be influenced by controlling whether reaction rate or reaction energy plays the key role in the mechanism

l3.text: When reaction rate is the dominating factor for an observed process , it is said to be kinetically favored. When reaction energy is the dominating factor , it is said to be thermodynamically favored.

l4.text: Observing changes over time can sometimes distinguish between kinetically and thermodynamically favored processes.

organic.text: Kinetic versus thermodynamic control of a reaction and reaction coordinate diagrams are used to discuss how to control the reaction products.
The role of reaction intermediates and concepts such as resonance and hyperconjugation inform the manner in which this type of reaction control is understood.

inorganic.text: The identification of kinetic vs. thermodynamic product as a function of the reaction is important to the understanding of a reaction mechanism.
Kinetic products are often isolated and later converted into thermodynamic products.
Kinetic factors, such as overpotential, can be used to control the observed products obtained from oxidation-reduction reactions.

physical.text: When thermodynamic control is present only the amount of products not the products themselves can be adjusted.
Catalysts, in particular, do not influence the equilibrium thermodynamic position of a reaction.

VIII.title: Equilibrium
VIII.text: Equilibrium: All physical and chemical changes are, in principle, reversible and often reach a state of dynamic equilibrium.

A.text: Both physical and chemical changes may occur in either direction (e.g., from reactants to products, or products to reactants).

alt.organic: Both physical and chemical changes may occur in either direction (e.g., from reactants to products, or products to reactant).
alt.inorganic: Both physical and chemical changes may occur in either direction (e.g. from reactants to products or products to reactant).
alt.physical: Both physical and chemical changes may occur in either direction (e.g. from reactants to products or products to reactant).

l3.text: Phase changes are reversible and provide a good example of dynamic equilibrium.

l4.text: Interpretation of phase diagrams can be tied to the understanding of equilibrium concepts.

organic.text: The position of equilibrium can affect the amount of product formed by a reaction.
Enols and enolate ions are in equilibrium with their respective ketones or aldehydes.

inorganic.text: Microscopic reversibility is important in the understanding of reaction coordinate diagrams for a variety of reaction mechanisms.

physical.text: Depending on conditions, either physical or chemical changes may be observed to proceed in either a "forward" or "reverse" direction, as defined by the chemical equation for the process.

Because reactions or physical changes may proceed in either direction, the equation describing a process is in some sense arbitrary, but the designation of the forward direction has implications on the details of the quantitative description of the system.

B.text: When opposing processes both occur at the same rate, the net change is zero.

alt.organic: When opposing processes both occur at the same rate the net change is zero.
alt.inorganic: When opposing processes both occur at the same rate the net change is zero.
alt.physical: When opposing processes both occur at the same rate the net change is zero.

l3.text: Dynamic processes that achieve equilibrium may be phase changes or chemical reactions.

l4.text: Concentration versus time profiles can be used to demonstrate kinetic versus equilibrium realm.
Equilibrium is dynamic because rates of opposing process are the same, but the rate is not commonly zero.

organic.text: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium.

inorganic.text: Equilibrium represents a steady state created by a dynamic process of forward and reverse processes.
A system is at equilibrium when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.

physical.text: Equilibrium is dynamic despite the observation that there is no net change.
Even when no net change in composition is observed for a system, processes in opposing directions are occurring, but at the same rate, leading to dynamic equilibrium.
For some reactions, the energy required to induce the reverse reaction is so large that it is impractical to attempt to observe equilibrium concentrations of reactants.
While, in principle, all reactions reach equilibrium, some reactions proceed so strongly towards products as to make observation of the reverse reaction impractical.

C.text: For chemical and physical processes, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.

alt.organic: For chemical reactions, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.
alt.inorganic: For chemical reactions, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.
alt.physical: For chemical reactions, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.

l3.text: The equilibrium constant can be used in calculations that determine the amount of reactants or products present at equilibrium for a given initial state.

l4.text: The equilibrium state is characterized by a constant, designated K, which provides quantitative information of the extent of a reaction and is related to the ratio of the concentrations of reactants and products.
The equilibrium constant, K, is a function of temperature.
The equilibrium constant, K, incorporates reaction stoichiometry as part of the ratio.
Calculations using equilibrium constants may determine K, or estimate equilibrium concentrations given initial concentrations of a system with a known value of K.

l3.text: Solubility of solids, particularly ionic solids, provides an example of chemical equilibrium.

l4.text: Dissolving of solids in water provides an example of equilibrium systems, for which quantitative understanding via Ksp can be derived.
There are limitations related to using molarity as the unit of concentration in this type of equilibrium problem, so answers obtained are subject to error.

organic.text: An equilibrium state can be shown using a reaction-coordinate diagram, by performing a conformational analysis or using instrumentation.
pKa is a measure of the equilibrium between the protonated and deprotonated forms of a molecule.

Terminal alkyne hydrogens are more acidic (pKa ≈25) than most C–H bonds due to the s-character of the hybrid orbital (sp) containing the conjugate base lone pair. Deprotonated terminal alkynes are good nucleophiles.
The acidity of phenols is the result of resonance stabilization within the aromatic ring of the conjugate base’s negative charge.

Alpha-hydrogens to carbonyl groups are acidic due to resonance stabilization of the conjugate base (i.e., an enolate). Enolates can be used as nucleophiles and therefore can be involved in any nucleophilic reaction (e.g., aldol or Claisen condensation).
Any H on an O is more acidic than carbon or nitrogen due to the ability of O to handle a negative charge.

inorganic.text: Standard equilibrium constants are used to describe many reaction types.

The acid dissociation constant (Ka) and base ionization constant (Kb) are used to compare the strengths of acids and bases. The Hammett acidity function can also be used to compare strengths of superacids.
Autoionization constants are used to describe ionization equilibria resulting from reaction between solvent molecules.
The dissolution of ionic solids results in an equilibrium described by the solubility product (Ksp).

Complexation equilibria are described using formation constants (Kf) and dissociation constants (Kd). Different expressions of these constants are used to represent stepwise and overall formation/dissociation of the corresponding metal complexes.

physical.text: Equilibrium occurs when free energy is minimized.
The reaction Gibbs energy is defined as the partial derivative of the Gibbs energy with respect to extent of reaction at constant pressure and temperature.
Equilibrium is reached in a chemical reaction when the reaction Gibbs energy becomes zero.

The direction a reaction will proceed can be inferred from the initial reaction Gibbs energy, where a negative value means the forward reaction is the spontaneous direction and a positive value means the reverse reaction is the spontaneous direction.
Equilibrium states occur when the chemical potentials of the involved components are equal.
Because the reaction Gibbs energy is the chemical potential of the products minus that of the reactants, it goes to zero and equilibrium is reached when those chemical potentials are equal.
The reaction will proceed towards products whenever the chemical potential of the reactants is greater than that of the products and vice-versa.
Equilibrium constants are defined in terms of the activity/fugacity of the species in the reactions.

The reaction quotient is defined as the activities (fugacity for gases) of products raised to their stoichiometric coefficient divided by the activities/fugacities of the reactants raised to their stoichiometric coefficients.
When equilibrium is reached, the reaction quotient is equal to the equilibrium constant.
The stoichiometric coefficients arise in the equilibrium constant because the extent of reaction inherently incorporates them.

D.text: When the equilibrium constant is very large or small, products or reactants, respectively, are primarily present at equilibrium. Systems with K near 1 have significant amounts of both reactants and products present.

alt.inorganic: When the equilibrium constant is very large or small, products or reactants (respectively) are primarily present at equilibrium. Systems with K near 1 have significant amounts of both reactants and products present.
alt.physical: When the equilibrium constant is very large or small, products or reactants (respectively) are primarily present at equilibrium. Systems with K near 1 have significant amounts of both reactants and products present.

l3.text: Very large or very small values of the equilibrium constant, K, indicate reactions strongly favoring products (in the former case) or reactants (in the latter).

l4.text: Reactions with very small values of K will have little formation of products, while reactions with very large values of K will proceed nearly completely to products.

l3.text: Because the equilibrium constant is determined for the reaction as written, the reverse reaction has the inverse equilibrium constant.

l4.text: Strong acids have very large K values and are considered fully ionized; weak acids have small K values and are only partially ionized.

For some reactions, particular acid–base chemistry, the concept of pKa, pKb , or pKw can both illustrate the relationship between the equilibrium constant of forward and reverse reactions, and provide qualitative reasoning for reaction extents.
Ksp values can be used to rank relative solubilities for sparingly soluble salts, or obtain numerical estimates of measureable solubility of these salts.

l3.text: The equilibrium constant for a series of reactions is the product of the individual equilibrium constants.

l4.text: Qualitative analysis methods, such as the formation of complex ions, take advantage of differences in Ksp or combined equilibrium constants to separate species dissolved in water.

organic.text: When the equilibrium constant K is very large, product formation is strongly favored.

inorganic.text: Relative sizes of equilibrium constants are used to describe periodic trends in properties.
Hard-Soft Acid-Base Theory can be used to rationalize the magnitudes of many equilibrium constants.

physical.text: The magnitude of the equilibrium constant indicates the propensity of the formation of reactants versus products for a reaction.
Because K = SUM [products]^n /SUM [reactants]^m, the value becomes very large if mostly products are present and very small if mostly reactants are present.
Systems with intermediate values of K will have significant amounts of both reactants and products present at equilibrium.
For similar systems, such as acid/base chemistry or precipitations, the propensity of chemical systems can be ranked based on the size of equilibrium constants.
Some reactions are product favored while others are reactant favored based on the value of their standard state free energy of formation and chemical potentials of the chemicals involved.
The standard state free energy reflects the difference between the chemical potentials of reactants and products, and thus indicates the expected direction of a chemical reaction.

E.text: If perturbed, a system at equilibrium will respond in the direction that tends to offset the perturbation.

l3.text: The direction of change in a system that is perturbed from equilibrium is predictable—it will change so as to minimize the perturbation.

l4.text: The ability to predict the direction a reaction will progress for a given perturbation is a key concept.
Reasoning based on perturbations of equilibrium can be used to determine conditions that maximize product formation in a reaction.

organic.text: It is possible to use Le Châtelier’s principle to force a reaction to form product.

inorganic.text: Industrial processes often use excess reactants, high pressures, and high temperatures to exploit LeChatelier's principle to favor product formation in reactions that have a high activation energy and/or result in a decrease in the number of gas molecules.
The Haber-Bosch process is used to synthesize ammonia from hydrogen and nitrogen at high temperatures and pressures using an iron based catalyst.
The contact process is used in the production of sulfuric acid to oxidize sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide at high temperatures and pressures using a vanadium(V) catalyst.

physical.text: The perturbation of the equilibrium system changes the chemical potential of at least one component, so chemical potential is no longer equal and equilibrium is not present.
When the chemical potentials are rendered not equal by a change in conditions, the reaction will proceed in a direction that allows them to regain the equality.
Temperature-based perturbations to equilibrium change the value of K.
A system will reestablish equilibrium with a new value for K when the temperature is changed.

F.text: Thermodynamics provides mathematical tools to understand equilibrium systems quantitatively.

l3.text: The equilibrium constant is related mathematically to the change in free energy.

l4.text: Calculations of the equilibrium constant of a system from the free energy of that system are important.
Systems achieve equilibrium when free energy is minimized.

l3.text: For electrochemical systems, the cell potential is also related to the change in free energy.

inorganic.text: Equilibrium constants and their connection to ΔG, ΔH, ΔS and E° are important in understanding quantitative measures of stability and reactivity.

The values for the electrical cell potential and the Gibbs free energy can be used to determine if a system is at equilibrium, and the direction of change that a system needs to undergo to attain equilibrium.
The proton gain enthalpy and proton affinity are often used to aid in the understanding of Bronsted acid strength.
Thermodynamic concepts are important in the understanding of the formation and reactivity of coordination compounds.
The strengths of metal-ligand bonds, acidity/basicity of ligands, and solvent interactions are important factors in equilibria involving complex ions.
The relative frontier molecular orbital energies of reactants can be used to predict the extent of electron transfer in Lewis acid-base and oxidation-reduction reactions.
The chelate and macrocycle effects cause equilibrium constants for the formation of complexes containing chelating ligands to be large.

physical.text: The condition that the sum of chemical potentials must equal each other at equilibrium allows the derivation of several important relationships.
Keq relates to ΔH and ΔS and thus ΔG.
The relationships between the equilibrium constant and free energy arise from statistical mechanics but can derived without it.
The overall equilibrium constant is defined in terms of the ΔG of the reaction.
The standard free energy is related to the equilibrium constant by the equation, ∆G° = -RT ln(K)
The van't Hoff equation describes how equilibrium constants depend on temperature.

G.text: Equilibrium concepts have important applications in several subdisciplines of chemistry.

alt.inorganic: Equilibrium concepts have important applications in several sub-disciplines of chemistry.
alt.physical: Equilibrium concepts have important applications in several sub-disciplines of chemistry.

l3.text: Many reactions categorized as acid–base are described via equilibrium.

l4.text: Acid–base chemistry, particularly in water, forms an important example of equilibrium systems. Conceptual and quantitative understanding of this form of equilibrium system is important.
The laboratory technique of titration serves as a key example for acid– base chemistry; interpretation of titration curves, both conceptually and quantitatively, is an important tool for chemists.
pH is used in quantitative descriptions of acid–base chemistry.
Conjugate bases of weak acids are strong, and conjugate acids of weak bases are strong. Thus, salts of weak acids and bases affect pH.

l3.text: Buffers resist changes in pH because both the acid and base of a conjugate pair are present.
