l4.text: Weak acid–base systems are capable of forming buffer systems that tend to resist changes in the pH of the system.
Conceptual and quantitative understanding of buffers is important.

l3.text: Protein–substrate binding can serve as another example of the application of equilibrium concepts.

organic.text: Protonation of functional groups in organic molecules is an equilibrium process (and it is essential to acid-catalyzed processes, for example).
Brønsted acids are proton donors; bases are proton acceptors. Lewis acids are electron-pair acceptors; Lewis bases are electron-pair donors.
The reversibility of many reactions is important in understanding mechanisms and in predicting reaction outcomes.

inorganic.text: Equilibrium constants can be used to determine the reactivity of inorganic compounds.
The levelling effect can be used to control acid-base behavior in different solvent systems.

Chemical speciation is dependent on a number of factors. The position of a chemical equilibrium depends on many conditions, including pH, temperature, pressure, and the presence of oxidizing/reducing agents.
Distribution diagrams are used to describe the speciation of acid-base species as a function of solution pH.
Phase diagrams can be used to determine the most stable form of a compound as a function of temperature and pressure.
Chemical sensors use chemical equilibria to quantify the amount of analyte present.

physical.text: Equilibrium plays an important role in many biochemical systems.
The binding and unbinding of oxygen to hemoglobin is an equilibrium process that illustrates the role of equilibrium in biochemistry.
In some cases, adsorption and reactions at surfaces may be described by equilibrium principles.
Gases are in equilibrium with adsorbed species that may or may not dissociate.

IX.title: Experiments, Measurement, and Data
IX.text: Experiments, Measurement, and Data: Chemistry is generally advanced via experimental observations.

A.text: Materials are frequently mixtures of chemical substances.

alt.organic: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance and/or time scales.
alt.inorganic: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance scales and/or time scales.
alt.physical: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance scales, energy, frequency and/or time scales.

l3.text: Mixtures may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

l4.text: Macroscopic samples of everyday objects and systems can serve as examples of homogeneous versus heterogeneous mixtures.

l3.text: Methods such as distillation and chromatography can be used to separate mixtures.

l4.text: A simple distillation apparatus can be used to separate mixtures in the laboratory.

organic.text: Data collected can be measured at the macroscopic level using chemical tests.
Data collected can be measured at the microscopic level using instruments such as X-ray, NMR, IR, MS, and EPR.
Wet chemical methods may take time to provide results and results may be unclear due to multiple functional groups, particularly when compared with instrumental methods.

inorganic.text: Microscopy allows for the observation of matter from the macroscopic to the atomic levels.
Optical microscopy allows for observation of matter at resolutions above 0.2 microns.
Nanoscale structures can be viewed using transmission and scanning electron microscopies.
Scanning probe microscopy can be used to observe structures on the atomic/molecular size scales. Examples of probe microscopy include scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy.
Fluxional processes in molecules can be observed at many timescales using spectroscopic techniques.
Many molecular rearrangements take place on the same timescale as the NMR experiment, and dynamic NMR experiments can be used to obtain thermodynamic and kinetic information for these processes.
Techniques employing pulsed lasers can be used to observe bond stretching and molecular vibrations occurring on the femtosecond timescale.
Structural information for a molecule, including bond lengths and bond angles, is based on observations of samples made at the macroscopic level.
The connectivity and structure of a molecule can be obtained using one- and two-dimensional NMR techniques.
Infrared spectroscopy can be used to determine functional groups present and bond strengths within a molecule, and is commonly used in the identification of compounds containing carbonyl ligands.
X-ray crystallography can be used to determine bond lengths and angles within a compound.
Phosphorescence and Fluorescence phenomena occur at different timescales due to the different relaxation mechanisms taking place within a molecule.

physical.text: Diffraction requires the wavelength of light/particles to be on the order of the spacing between particles to be observed.
X-rays represent a good tool for observations at the atomic scale because the wavelength is roughly equivalent to interatomic distances in solids.
The method of observation in kinetics has to be sensitive to time-scale of observation.
Femtosecond spectroscopy provides the fastest time scale for the study of reaction kinetics.
Temperature jump methods can access kinetics in the microsecond time range.
Shock tube methods provide conditions that allow the study of reactions on the millisecond time scale.
Most kinetics are observed based on collections of a large number of reactions, but individual collisions can be observed in crossed-molecular beams.

B.text: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance, energy, frequency, and/or time scales.

alt.organic: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.
alt.inorganic: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.
alt.physical: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.

l3.text: Laboratory observations are made and then often understood in terms of particulate-level models.

l4.text: While molecular-scale observations are not generally made in the introductory chemistry laboratory, interpretation of results often invokes molecular-scale reasoning.
Historically, the development of the atomic theory of matter was driven by experimental observations.

l3.text: Laboratory measurements are sometimes combined into ratios; for example, density is measured via a ratio of mass and volume.

l4.text: Calculations that use density may include both the determination of the density from mass/volume data or the use of a known density with the measurement of either mass or volume.
Practical implications for density include the concept of buoyancy.

l3.text: Laboratory observation of reaction rates helps to establish the concept of reaction time scales empirically.

l4.text: Rate laws and reaction order are determined using empirical rate data.

organic.text: In order to be able to organize observations on vast numbers of compounds, a systematic nomenclature system has been devised to name compounds.
IUPAC has outlined a set of systematic guidelines for naming all organic structures based on carbon chain length, rings, functional groups, and substituents.
Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen atoms. Hydrocarbons with only carbon–carbon single bonds are called alkanes; they can be straight-chained or branched.
Substituents on a di-substituted benzene ring can be labeled as ortho, meta, or para to each other.

inorganic.text: The nomenclature system for coordination and organometallic compounds is used to specifies composition and stereochemistry.
The systematic name of a coordination compound includes information about the number and type of ligands along with the oxidation state of the metal ion.
One type of stereoisomerism, geometric isomerism, has special nomenclature associated with it. Examples include cis/trans isomers and mer/fac isomers.

Many ligands have multiple binding modes that should also be specified within the name of the corresponding complex. Examples include the κ (kappa), η (eta), and μ (mu) designations for denticity, hapticity and bridging ligands and the nomenclature of ambidentate ligands.

Simple crystal structures are often identified by specific names associated with prototypical compounds. The hole concept is used to describe the relative locations of cations and ions within the structures of crystalline ionic compounds.
The cesium chloride structure contains cesium atoms in the cubic holes of a primitive cubic chloride lattice.
The sodium chloride, fluorite, and zinc blende structures contain counterions within the octahedral or tetrahedral holes of a parent cubic-closest-packed lattice.
The nickel arsenide and wurtzite structures contain counterions within the octahedral and tetrahedral holes of a parent hexagonal-closest-packed lattice.
The tetragonal rutile structure can be visualized as having titanium atoms occupying half of the octahedral holes within a distorted hexagonally-closest-packed oxide lattice.
The perovskite and spinel structures are observed in many tertiary ionic compounds.
Many catalysts and industrial processes are identified using common names associated with the people that discovered and/or worked on the development of the process/catalyst.
Students should be able to associate the common name of these compounds with their composition and structure, and the general type of reaction associated.

Homogeneous catalysts are employed in the hydrogenation, hydroformylation, oxidation and metathesis reactions of alkenes. Other common processes include acetic acid synthesis and carbon-carbon bond formation.
Common processes using heterogeneous catalysts include hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis, sulfuric acid synthesis, and alkane synthesis.

C.text: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.

alt.organic: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.
alt.inorganic: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.
alt.physical: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.

l3.text: A system of nomenclature is applied based on the classification of the substance.

l4.text: Anyone who works with chemicals needs to be able to name compounds, including binary inorganic compounds, acids, and some organic chemicals.

organic.text: Experimental measures provide data to determine whether desired products are obtained.
Measures of products can include stereochemical specificity.

inorganic.text: The parameters used in a synthesis (relative amounts, temperature, reaction time, pH, light/air/water exposure, etc.) can influence the identity and relative amounts of the product(s) obtained.
Exothermic and endothermic reactions are affected differently by temperature.
Many reactions fall into general reaction classes that have characteristic behavior under changing conditions, and knowledge of these reaction types can be used in the informed design of a synthesis.
Analysis using one or more techniques is used to determine identity and purity of products and understand effect of changing reaction conditions.

physical.text: Laser based photochemical reactions can be controlled in a state to state manner.
Reaction products in laser photochemistry may be influenced by state specific excitation of the reactants.
Insights into controlled synthesis of modern materials, including nanoparticles, often requires detailed understanding of reaction conditions.
Synthesis of nanoparticles requires different reaction controls than traditional bulk chemical reactions.
Understanding the role of solvent polarity in control of a reaction requires knowledge of polarity of product, reactant and intermediate substances.

D.text: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.

alt.organic: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, or interaction with electrons or photons.
alt.inorganic: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, or interaction with electrons or photons.
alt.physical: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, temperature, pressure, volume or interaction with electrons or photons.

l3.text: One key way to control reactions is to control the amount of reactants by varying concentrations.

l4.text: Le Châtelier’s principle is demonstrated by varying the concentration of one species and observing the outcome on the overall reaction.

inorganic.text: The chemical formula of a compound is determined using a combination of analysis techniques.
The elemental composition of compounds is measured using a variety of methods including combustion analysis, atomic absorption, and atomic emission.

The behavior of ions in the presence of an electric field or magnetic field can be a function of the mass of the ion. Mass spectrometric techniques involve analysis of this behavior to identify chemical formulas and presence of common structural fragments within molecules.
The percent yield for an experiment can be calculated from reactant and product masses.
UV-VIS absorption spectroscopy is used to observe valence shell electron transitions within molecules.
Intensity of UV-Vis transition corresponds to type of electronic transition and the concentration of analyte present.
The symmetry of a molecule determines the types of allowed transitions that can occur and hence the intensity of the observed absorption.
A Tanabe-Sugano diagram is used to interpret the energy information obtained from UV-Vis spectroscopy of transition metal compounds.
Multinuclear NMR experiments are used to identify the structures of inorganic complexes.
The number and locations of chemical shifts observed in an NMR spectrum can be used to identify the chemical environments present in a molecule.
Splitting patterns in observed chemical shifts result from interactions with other NMR active nuclei in the molecule.
Redox reactions can be used quantitatively in analysis.
Potentiometric titrations can be used to analyze the composition of reaction mixtures.
The elemental forms of many active metals and nonmetals are obtained using electrolytic methods.
Cyclic voltammetry is commonly used to study redox processes occurring in solution.
Different spectroscopic techniques employ different types of electromagnetic radiation to measure transitions occurring at different energies within molecules.

The energies of microwave radiation correspond to the rotational states of a molecule. More commonly, long wavelength radiation is used in the NMR and EPR experiments to measure transitions occurring between different magnetic spin states of atoms within molecules.

Infrared radiation is used to measure vibrational transitions within molecules. Vibrational transitions are also observed as small deviations from the absorbance of visible light using Raman spectroscopy.
Absorption and emission of light within UV-Visible wavelengths is associated with valence electronic transitions within molecules.

Absorbance and emission of X-rays is usually associated with electronic transitions involving core energy levels, and is used to obtain information about the local environments of atoms within molecules.
Mossbauer spectroscopy involves the absorption of gamma rays to probe the energies associated with nuclear spin levels.

Diffraction methods employing X-rays, electrons, and neutrons are used to measure the interatomic distances within compounds, and information gained from these experiments can be used to obtain bond distances and angles.
Powder diffraction techniques are used to obtain basic structural information about solids including the phases present, crystallinity, and unit cell lattice parameters.
Single crystal diffraction techniques are used to obtain more specific information about unit cell contents and interatomic distances.
Magnetic measurements, including magnetic susceptibility and SQUID measurements, are employed to determine the individual and cooperative behavior of unpaired electrons within a compound.
Temperature dependent conductivity and resistivity measurements are used to characterize metals, semiconductors, and superconductors.
Metals become less conductive at higher temperatures as vibration of electrons interferes with conductance.
Semiconductors become more conductive at higher temperatures as more energy is available to promote electrons to the conductance band.
Superconductors can be so only when a (low) critical temperature is reached allowing Cooper pairs of electrons to form.

physical.text: Interaction of molecules with light is a powerful and routinely used method of molecular observation.
Molecular spectroscopy can provide detailed structural information for small molecule systems.
Spectroscopic frequencies and intensities depend on reduced mass and can be used to distinguish isotope effects.
Spectroscopy may be used to measure changes to physical properties due to adsorption onto surfaces.
Different forms of spectroscopy (IR, Microwave, UV-VIS, PES, Mossbauer, NMR, ESR) examine different aspects of molecules and molecular processes.
Electronic transitions are accessed with UV/visible light.
Vibrational transitions are accessed with IR light.
Pure rotational transitions are accessed with microwave light.
Temperature may be controlled by maintaining constant temperature, or measured to determine temperature effects.
Establishing temperature as a control variable in experiments is commonly accomplished using a constant temperature circulating bath.
Modern experiments often use thermistors or thermocouples to measure temperature and temperature changes.
Electrochemical experiments take advantage of charge and reactions where charge changes are observable by experiments.
Oxidation reduction reactions are an important category of chemical reactions and they may be observed both thermodynamically and kinetically via electrochemical methods.
Mass spectrometry represents an area of experimentation where mass is the primary observation variable.
High resolution mass spectrometry can utilize isotopic abundances to provide detailed identification of reactions.

E.text: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, temperature, pressure, volume, or interaction with electrons or photons.

alt.organic: Observations are verifiable, so experimental conditions, including considerations of the representativeness of samples, must be considered for experiments.
alt.inorganic: Observations are verifiable, so experimental conditions, including considerations of the representativeness of samples, must be considered for experiments.
alt.physical: Observations are verifiable, so experimental conditions, including considerations of the representativeness of samples, must be considered for experiments.

l3.text: Stoichiometry provides an example of mass measurements being used in the laboratory, particularly for percentage yield.

l4.text: Graphical analysis of reaction yields as a function of reagent amounts can reveal when a particular reactant is in excess and identify an unknown reaction stoichiometric ratio.
Calculation of percentage yield is an important skill and may help determine the relative utility of a laboratory synthesis method.

l3.text: Practical implications of laboratory reactions include the ability to generate species of interest (such as oxygen) or release energy (by combustion of fuels).

l4.text: Common laboratory reactions to generate known species, such as oxygen, are an important component of descriptive chemistry.
Many hydrocarbons can be used as fuels; the combustion of a hydrocarbon in air produces carbon dioxide and water.

l3.text: Atomic line spectra provide important evidence that led to the quantum model of the atom.

l4.text: Spectral data can be used to demonstrate quantized energy levels in atoms in the gas phase.

l3.text: Mass spectrometry can provide data that show the existence of isotopes of elements.

l4.text: Mass spectrum data can be used to illustrate the existence of isotopes of an element and the importance of isotopic abundances.

inorganic.text: Demonstration of purity and comparison to peer's results and standards is an essential process.
Magnitudes of many measurements can be sensitive to experimental conditions.

physical.text: Methods can be employed to isolate or reduce complicating variables in experiments.
Vibrational and rotational populations can be collapsed by cooling methods, such as supersonic expansion, to allow state-to-state detection.
Reaction intermediates can be quenched to show their existence even if their reactivity is such that direct observation is difficult.

F.text: Observations are verifiable, so experimental conditions, including considerations of the representativeness of samples, must be considered for experiments.

alt.organic: Fidelity of inferences from data requires appropriate experimental design.
alt.inorganic: Fidelity of inferences made from data requires appropriate experimental design.
alt.physical: Fidelity of inferences made from data requires appropriate experimental design.

l3.text: Laboratory methods can be devised so that conditions limit the possibilities of measurement errors.

l4.text: Techniques in setting up and carrying out laboratory experiments are an important component of instruction in introductory college chemistry.
Gaining familiarity with laboratory instruments and glassware is a key skill for the development of appropriate laboratory design methods.
Errors in measurement can occur when techniques (such as meniscus reading or incomplete transfer of chemicals between vessels) arise in the laboratory.

l3.text: The preparation of solutions and accurate determination of their concentrations are important components of defining experimental conditions.

l4.text: Correct uses of volumetric glassware and/or dilution methods are important techniques in the preparation of solutions for chemical experimentation.
Determination of solution concentration is often carried out via titration with a standard.

inorganic.text: The precision of measured data has limitations that are dependent on measuring equipment or the execution of the experiment.
Appropriate equipment, including glassware and balances, should be selected to obtain the desired precision for an experiment.
Experimental conditions, including sample preparation for analysis, should be clearly described in the associated procedure.
All relevant data, conditions, and procedures should be recorded in the lab notebook for a particular experiment.

physical.text: Rapid reaction rates call for careful control of laser pulse lengths and/or delays between pulses.
Time delays can be built into laser spectroscopy by beam splitting with one beam going a longer distance.
Kinetic experiments can be designed to observe reaction intermediates.
Reaction intermediates may be measured directly by spectroscopic probes or indirectly using quenching methods.
Experimental data and data analysis can be used to refine or create models and inform chemical systems.
Key experiments in the development of quantum mechanics led to the discovery of wave- particle duality

G.text: Fidelity of inferences made from data requires appropriate experimental design and data analysis.

alt.inorganic: Chemistry experiments have risks associated with them, so chemical safety is a key consideration in the design of any experiment.
alt.physical: Chemistry experiments have risks associated with them, so chemical safety is a key consideration in the design of any experiment.

l3.text: Data can be characterized by both accuracy and precision.

l4.text: While the words “accuracy” and “precision” can be used nearly interchangeably in everyday life, in the laboratory they have specific meanings that must be understood.

l3.text: Error in data can be either random or systematic.

l4.text: Significant figures are used to reflect the level of error.
Standard deviation is relatable to the level of error.

l3.text: Proper laboratory procedures record all observations and correct recording errors with cross-outs rather than erasures.

l4.text: Appropriate methods for keeping a laboratory notebook are important in the instruction of introductory college chemistry.

l3.text: Calibration with samples of known quantities is a common method for determining unknowns in a laboratory setting.

l4.text: Construction and use of calibrations curves is an important laboratory skill.
Standardization of laboratory solutions is a form of calibration that is an important laboratory skill.

inorganic.text: Many experiments in inorganic chemistry are conducted using light, air, and moisture sensitive compounds, and the proper precautions should be employed in their use.
Inert atmosphere techniques employing glove boxes or Schlenk glassware are often used to exclude moisture and/or oxygen from experiments.

Methods for extinguishing fires involving metals and pyrophoric liquids often differ from procedures used to extinguish more common types of fires. When working with these materials, appropriate extinguishing media must be readily accessible.
Experiments conducted at high and low pressures present an explosion hazard, and proper equipment should be selected to minimize the risk of harm from explosion.
Vacuum pumps used to create reduced pressure environments pose an additional risk of injury due to mechanical malfunction, and the proper safeguards should be in place during their use.
Compressed gas cylinders should be secured to avoid injury in case of breach.
Experiments involving cryofluids can pose a risk to burning of the skin or explosions due to the condensation and subsequent reaction of liquid oxygen.

Many resources containing toxicological and other potential safety hazards associated with specific compounds are available and should be consulted prior to working with unfamiliar compounds to ensure that proper safety precautions are being followed.
A fume hood or other method of containment should be used when working with volatile compounds.

Certain classes of compounds require specialized techniques to be utilized and that appropriate first aid measures be on hand in case of exposure. Examples include hydrofluoric acid and hydrogen cyanide

Certain chemicals can react to form harmful byproducts if kept in storage for long periods of time, and special procedures should be developed to catalog and dispose of these compounds. For example, ethers will react with oxygen over long storage times to form shock-sensitive peroxides.

In many cases, a safer alternative compound can be employed to achieve the same desired result in a chemical reaction. One common example is the replacement of perchlorate salts with safer alternatives in syntheses.
Green chemical methods are developed to minimize the environmental impact of an experiment.

physical.text: In addition to chemical risk, physical chemistry experiments often include high vacuum or intense light sources which require proper safety precaution.
Many types of lasers produce light that may harm eyes and appropriate eyewear is required when experiments using them are conducted.

H.text: Chemistry experiments have risks associated with them, so chemical safety is a key consideration in the design of any experiment.

l3.text: Knowledge of appropriate safety apparatus is important knowledge for any work being done in the laboratory.

l4.text: Students should be able to identify and use safety equipment in the laboratory.

l3.text: Knowledge of chemical hazards and safety procedures associated with chemicals is important in the chemistry laboratory.

l4.text: Assessing the hazards associated with chemical procedures, such as the dilution of strong acids or heating of chemicals, is an important skill for introductory chemistry courses.

Appropriate storage and labeling of chemicals is a constant component of good chemical safety practices. This includes understanding safety terminology and the language, signs, and symbols commonly found in Safety Data Sheets and on labels.
Basic knowledge about handling of exposure to chemicals due to spills or other accidents is an important component of chemical safety.
Basic knowledge of and appropriate use of personal protective equipment, such as safety goggles, gloves, and lab coats, are important features of chemical safety.
Basic knowledge of the possible hazards of chemicals, such as flammability, toxicity, and corrosiveness, is an important component of chemical safety.
Basic knowledge of the routes of exposure for chemicals, such as inhalation, ingestion, and dermal routes, is an important component of chemical safety.

l3.text: Appropriate disposal of chemical waste is a key component of chemical safety and hygiene.

l4.text: Appropriate disposal of chemical waste is needed in any laboratory and students should know general guidelines related to chemical waste handling.

l3.text: Students should develop an “awareness” of chemical safety when conducting experiments that involves continual consideration of hazards and risks due to chemicals, chemical procedures, and physical hazards that may be present.

l4.text: The concept of a “culture of safety” is an increasingly important component of chemical education.

l3.text: Radioactive chemicals require additional knowledge related to risks and use of radioactive materials must include appropriate protective measures.

l4.text: Exposure to different forms of radiation pose different levels of risk, and students should have a general knowledge of these differences.

X.title: Visualization
X.text: Visualization: Chemistry constructs meaning interchangeably at the particulate and macroscopic levels.

A.text: Many theoretical models are constructed at the particulate level, while many empirical observations are made at the macroscopic level.

alt.inorganic: Many theoretical constructs are constructed at the particulate level, while many observations are made at the macroscopic level.
alt.physical: Many theoretical models are constructed at the particulate level, while many observations are made at the macroscopic level.

l3.text: Kinetic molecular theory provides an important bridge for the particulate and macroscopic levels.

l4.text: Gases provide an important example of bridging particulate and macroscopic description at the general chemistry level through kinetic molecular theory.
The diffusion and effusion of gases may be understood in terms of kinetic molecular theory and described quantitatively through Graham’s laws.

l3.text: Understanding the relationship between symbolic, macroscopic, and particulate representations of matter and reactions is important.

l4.text: Schematic drawings can depict key concepts at the particulate level, such as mixtures versus pure substances, compounds versus elements, or dissociative processes.

organic.text: Spectroscopic probes are especially important in organic labs where instruments such as NMR, MS, IR, chromatography, and GC as well as techniques such as melting points, boiling points, optical activities, and refractive indices are used to study the reactants and products of organic reactions.
Ultraviolet–visible light (UV–vis) spectroscopy can be used to observe the π-bond structure (especially conjugation) of molecules.

Infrared (IR) spectroscopy uses electromagnetic radiation to probe functional groups through energy absorption in bending and stretching molecular motions. Observed vibrations result from a change in dipole moment from the bending and stretching motion.

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the result of observing the α and β spin-state transitions of atomic nuclei with odd mass numbers caused by radio-frequency radiation in an external magnetic field. NMR is most commonly used to observe 1H and 13C nuclei.

Proton NMR signals are characterized by number (denoting the number of “kinds” of chemically equivalent protons), chemical shift (relative shielding or deshielding due to electron density relative to tetramethylsilane), integration (number of each “kind” of proton relative to every other “kind”), and splitting (number of “kinds” of protons alpha to the kind of proton causing the observed signal).

Carbon-13 NMR signals are characterized by number (denoting the number of “kinds” of chemically equivalent carbons), and chemical shift (relative shielding or deshielding due to electron density relative to tetramethylsilane). Specialized methods can be used to determine the number of non-hydrogen substituents on the number of carbons.
Mass spectrometry utilizes ionizing energy to fragment larger molecules that are then observed based on charged mass. Isotopes and fragmentation data can be used to predict the original molecule.

inorganic.text: Physical properties, such as melting point, boiling point, and viscosity, observed for nano- and macromaterials arise from interactions between molecules and/or particles.
Band theory is an extension of molecular orbital theory to the macroscale, and is used to explain electrical conductivity associated with metals, insulators, and semiconductors.
Ligand field theory is used to explain many macroscopic observations made on coordination compounds.
The colors and energies associated with electronic transitions arise from ΔO, ΔT, and other energy differences between molecular orbitals.

Unpaired electrons within a molecule give rise to a magnetic moment. Cooperation between magnetic moments gives rise to ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, or ferrimagnetic properties that are observed on the macroscale.

physical.text: Quantum mechanical models include the premise by which probabilities lead to experimental observations.
The quantum model of the atom was developed when classical theories were incapable of explaining experimental observations.

A key postulate of quantum mechanics is that the particle is completely specified by the wave function and the probability of finding the particle is determined by the wave function times its complex conjugate.
In quantum mechanics there is a linear operator that corresponds to any observable in classical mechanics.
In quantum mechanics the only values that can be observed are the eigenvalues of the operator which satisfy the eigenvalue equation.
Some simple models, like the particle in a box, can be used to explain experiments such as the absorption of light in conjugated systems.
Graphical depictions of tunneling show probability outside the range of a potential energy curve that would be classically allowed.
Mathematical relationships are useful in deriving equations that define various models.
Characteristics of the total differential of variables in thermodynamics define relationships that explain the behavior of thermodynamic systems.
Relationships among partial derivatives, such as Maxwell's relations, are useful in defining how variables in thermodynamics are related to each other and to measurable quantities.
Determination of a non-zero commutator between operators in quantum mechanics indicates the existence of an uncertainty principle for those operators.
Wavefunction must be well behaved and act appropriately according to the boundary conditions of the problem.
Wave functions in quantum mechanics must be normalized.
Many quantum mechanical models are solved mathematically by finding ways to separate the wave function, changing one complicated problem into more (but solvable) problems.
The quantum mechanical model for chemical systems must be solved with approximations, and these methods serve as a way to categorize the model.
The gas kinetic model provides a way to envision the implications of molecular scale motions for atoms/molecules in a gas.
The gas kinetic model is predicated on a set of postulates that are reasonable for perfect gases but may break down for real gases.
The gas kinetic model depicts pressure in terms of the forces that arise from collisions of the gas molecules with the walls of the container.
Simple models can often provide key chemical insights more quickly than more complete mathematically detailed models.

While the shape of a molecule is determined by minimization of the complete wavefunction, a simple theory such as VSEPR can provide rudimentary understanding of the shape about any atom in a molecule.
The Huckel method provides a quick, approximate method to determine energies of pi electrons in conjugated systems.

B.text: The mole represents the key factor for translating between the macroscopic and particulate levels.

l3.text: The mole is a measurable quantity that is set by the choice that 12 C has a mass of exactly 12 amu.

organic.text: Reaction yields obtained in the laboratory at the macroscopic scale are often explained in terms of molecular-scale models of the reaction.

inorganic.text: Avogadro's number is used to convert between grams and atomic mass units, as well as between number of objects, typically atoms or molecules, and moles.

physical.text: Error due to sample fluctuations is minimal with large ensembles, so samples with particles on the order of a mole are well treated statistically.

Bulk observable quantities in thermodynamics deal with the average behavior of all particles in a sample, and with sample sizes including roughly a mole of particles, fluctuations away from average are essentially never observed.
The Stirling approximation is useful in statistical mechanics and has a negligible error when using samples sizes on the order of a mole.

C.text: Macroscopic properties result from large numbers of particles, so statistical methods provide a useful model for understanding the connections between these levels.

alt.inorganic: Macroscopic properties result from large numbers of particles, so statistical methods provide a useful model for understanding the connections between these levels

l3.text: The idea that the Boltzmann distribution is a distribution function can provide an entry point into the importance of statistical reasoning at the general chemistry level.
Many macroscopic observables are the result of gradients in a key, molecular-scale quantity.

l4.text: Gradients in temperature result in the flow of energy as heat.
Concentration gradients lead to diffusion or osmosis.

inorganic.text: Statistical methods can be used to analyze particle size distributions arising from the synthesis of materials.

physical.text: Statistical mechanics provides the key tool for understanding how samples of particles combine to give macroscopically observed phenomena.
Statistical mechanics considers the possible configurations of a system and assigns a "weight" to those configuration in terms of how many ways they can be achieved.
Statistical thermodynamics is predicated on probabilistic occupation of energy states in the system of interest.
Statistical mechanics includes the principle of equal a priori probabilities which asserts that all distributions of a certain energy are equally probable.
The distribution of states is given by the molecular partition function which enumerates the average number of thermally accessible states.
With sample sizes on the order of a mole, the dominant configuration can be used in statistical mechanical calculations, and the Boltzmann distribution provides the dominant configuration.
The canonical partition function is based on the Boltzmann distribution
Several thermodynamic variables, such as U, H, S, A, and G can be calculated from the canonical partition function.
The molecular partition function has contributions from translation, rotation, vibration and electronic states.

D.text: Quantitative reasoning within chemistry is often visualized and interpreted graphically.

l3.text: Energy profiles for reaction progress include both kinetic and thermodynamic information.

l4.text: Students should be able to distinguish exothermic and endothermic reaction depictions from an energy profile representation.
Students should be able to identify the concept of activation energy within an energy profile representation.

l3.text: Manipulation of data (e.g., taking the natural log or the inverse of the data) as part of graphical depictions can be helpful in making appropriate inferences of the phenomena the data represent.

l4.text: Direct plots of experimentally measured quantities are sometimes able to provide key inferences, but in other cases data manipulation tends to make the interpretation easier.
Some experimentally observed phenomena, such as absorbance or transmission of light, may be recorded either directly or as an inverse of the observation.
When data of interest can range over several orders of magnitude, logarithms are often useful in helping graphical interpretations.

inorganic.text: Periodic trends in atomic properties, such as ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, and atomic/ionic radii are often represented and interpreted using graphs.
Ionization energy is positive for every element, ranging from 3.894 eV for Cs to 24.587 for He.
Sequential ionization energy values for a given element always increase.
A molecular orbital diagram is used to describe the bonding interactions within molecules.
The symmetry and relative energies of the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals are easily discerned from a molecular orbital diagram.
Jahn-Teller effects can be predicted for molecules by examination of the molecular orbital diagram.
Drawings representing three dimensional shapes are often used in symmetry analyses of molecules.
Drawings of orbitals used to describe the distribution of electron density and bonding interactions within atoms and molecules.
Electron density in delocalized molecular orbitals spans more than two atoms within a structure.
Symmetry Adapted Linear Combinations (SALC's) of atomic orbitals are constructed using symmetry and group theory.
The oxidation-reduction chemistry of the elements is graphically represented using Latimer, Pourbaix, Frost, and Ellingham diagrams.
Phase diagrams and distribution diagrams are used to summarize the speciation of compounds under different reaction conditions.
Tanabe-Sugano and Orgel diagrams are used to aid interpretation of electronic spectra of d-metal coordination complexes.
The structures of crystalline solids are often represented using unit cell drawings and plan diagrams.
Energy profiles are used to interpret the kinetics of a reaction.

physical.text: Phase diagrams are a tool for visualizing properties of phase changes.
Interpretation of single component phase diagrams allow the visualization of temperature and pressure regimes of a single phase and the temperature and pressure of phase changes.
Two component liquid-vapor diagrams can be used to explain how distillation is achieved and it's limitations in separating two liquids.
Two component liquid-vapor diagrams allow immediate visualization of azeotropes and how they are challenging to separate.
Potential energy diagrams allow visualization of the energy consequences of reactions.
Schematic energy diagrams show potential energy against a hypothetical reaction coordinate and depict both net reaction energy and the activation energy of any step in the overall reaction.
Potential energy contour plots for triatomic reacting systems show reactants, products, transition states and the possible role of vibrational energy in the reactants or products.
The temperature effects on the Boltzmann distribution can be depicted graphically.
The Boltzmann distribution shifts to the right and flattens as temperature increases.
The importance of high velocity molecules in collision theory can be demonstrated by superimposing the Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures.
Orbitals are depicted graphically from the probability that arises from the wave function.
Because electron probability decays with distance from the nucleus, orbitals are typically shown as surfaces that incorporate 90% probability of locating an electron.
The shape that is commonly shown for atomic orbitals is the angular portion of the wavefunction.
Nodes arise in the radial portion of the wave function, so complete pictures of atomic orbitals should include both radial and angular depictions.
Graphical depictions of relationships between thermodynamic variables (T, V, P, n) can provide useful information of the system being studied.
Graphs of pressure-volume isotherms for gases can distinguish several thermodynamic features.
Absorption isotherms depict how surface coverage of an adsorbed gas depends on pressure.

E.text: Mathematical equations provide a tool to visualize chemical and physical processes.

l3.text: Rearrangement of common mathematical expressions can either isolate variables or identify relationships that enhance understanding of the system being described.

sts.s: Use the atomic-molecular model to decide whether a chemical statement is about atoms, molecules, elements, or compounds.

Infer whether cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles that are common to atoms.

Use Bohr's model to calculate allowed energies, radii, and transition photons for hydrogen and one-electron ions.

Use probability density and quantum numbers to identify orbital shape, orientation, size, and nodes.
Order orbital energies correctly in hydrogen and multi-electron atoms.
Fill orbitals and write ground-state electronic configurations using Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund rules.
Use half-filled and completely filled subshell stability to explain exceptional ground-state configurations.
